Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal listener gated on the V1 flag; V2-only deployments lose cleanup silently

The whole listener (role, client and group removal cleanup) is now wrapped in Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ, the V1 flag, while the calls it makes dispatch to MgmtPermissionsV2 when the V2 flag is on. With only V2 enabled, deleting a client, group or role no longer runs any cleanup. Nothing replaces it: ClientPermissionsV2 has no removal path, so the per-client admin-permissions resource (named by the client UUID) and its attached policies stay behind. The gate is not mentioned in the PR description. The gate should follow the flag that governs the active evaluator, and V2 cleanup should be implemented rather than suppressed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the removal event listener in AdminPermissions (which cleans up permissions on role, client, or group deletion) is gated solely on the V1 feature flag (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), causing cleanup to be skipped and leaving orphaned permissions when only the V2 feature flag (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) is enabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the literal 'Clients' and omits type-level grants

findByType(server, 'Clients', ...) also returns the all-clients resource itself, since its name and type are both 'Clients' (created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init). If the caller holds the scope on it, the string 'Clients' is added to the result as if it were a client id. Clients covered only by a type-level grant are never added, because only per-client resources are inspected, whereas hasPermission(client, ...) falls back to the type-level resource. The result therefore disagrees with canView/canManage for the same caller.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same bug in `getClientsWithPermission`: calling `findByType` with the `Clients` resource type returns the type-level 'Clients' resource itself, resulting in the literal string 'Clients' being returned instead of actual client IDs.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
init() never backfills the Clients resource type or new scopes for existing realms

init() returns early when the realm already has an admin-permissions client. Realms set up with ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 before this change never receive the new 'configure', 'map-roles-client-scope' and 'map-roles-composite' scopes or the 'Clients' all-resource, and nothing else backfills them. For such realms, creating a CLIENTS permission hits 'No scopes found.' (line 108), and ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(client, ...) passes a null resource into findByResource (ClientPermissionsV2 line 219) whenever no per-client resource exists. That will fail with an NPE or wrong result on client checks. No migration or test covers this path.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies that ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission passes a null resource into findByResource, resulting in an NPE. While the candidate frames this within the broader context of missing initialization/backfilling for existing realms, it accurately pinpoints the exact code location, method calls, and NullPointerException described in the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
canView(client) ignores per-client policies when the caller has type-level VIEW

canView(ClientModel) returns true as soon as canView() is true, and canView() is true for any caller holding VIEW on the all-'Clients' resource. In that case the per-client resource is never evaluated, so a negative or otherwise non-matching per-client VIEW permission is silently ignored and the client stays visible and listable. canManage(client) and hasPermission(client, ...) treat an existing per-client resource as overriding the type-level grant, and the users tests (testViewUserPermission) establish that per-object deny overrides the all-users VIEW grant. This method is inconsistent with that and lets an explicit deny be bypassed. No test covers a per-client deny on top of an all-clients VIEW grant.

setPermissionsEnabled throws, so the ClientRemovedEvent listener fails client deletion under V2

Before this PR MgmtPermissionsV2 inherited clients() from MgmtPermissions, so setPermissionsEnabled worked. Now clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled (and isPermissionsEnabled) throw UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.registerListener calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on every ClientRemovedEvent, and management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 when the V2 flag is on. When the listener is active (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ enabled alongside V2), deleting any client throws during event dispatch and the deletion request fails.

V2 branch of the 4-arg evaluator() drops the target realm

In the V2 branch, evaluator(session, realm, adminsRealm, admin) calls new MgmtPermissionsV2(session, adminsRealm, admin) and never passes realm, although MgmtPermissionsV2 has a 4-argument constructor (session, realm, adminsRealm, admin) that carries it. The V1 branch passes realm. This PR makes MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() build ClientPermissionsV2 from the realm field. Client permission checks made through this factory may therefore be evaluated against the admin's realm rather than the target realm, depending on what the 3-argument constructor assigns to realm.

Type-level grant is ignored when a per-client resource exists, contradicting the documented 'also if' contract

hasPermission(client, scope) consults the all-'Clients' resource only when no per-client resource exists. If a per-client resource exists (for example because some other client-specific permission was created), only that resource's policies are evaluated. A caller with MANAGE on all clients is then denied canManage(X) for such a client. The interface Javadoc added in this PR (ClientPermissionEvaluator) says canManage, canView, canConfigure and canMap* are also true for the 'all clients' permission, which this does not honor. Either the documentation or the precedence rule must change. canView(client) applies the opposite precedence, so the two methods disagree.

Inherited permission methods now throw UnsupportedOperationException on reachable paths

canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, the mapRoles/manage/configure/view permission factories, resource(), getPermissions(), isPermissionsEnabled() and setPermissionsEnabled() all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Previously clients() under V2 returned the inherited V1 implementation. These are methods of the public evaluator interface that existing code calls (for example the legacy token-exchange check calls canExchangeTo, and client management-permission endpoints call getPermissions/resource). A request that reaches them now fails with HTTP 500 instead of a denial or a valid response. Nothing in the PR shows that callers are guarded.

getResourceName has no CLIENTS branch, so client permission resources get no readable name

getResourceName special-cases USERS to return the username. There is no CLIENTS branch, so client resources fall back to resource.getDisplayName(). getOrCreateResource never sets a display name for client resources, so the name shown for a client permission would be null or the internal UUID rather than the clientId. The PR adds no mapping and no test for it.

void require* methods documented as 'Returns true'

requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() are void methods, but their Javadoc says 'Returns {@code true} if ...'. They should say they throw ForbiddenException when the corresponding can* method returns false, as the other require* methods in this interface do.

canView(client) repeats full policy evaluations for every client in a listing

canView(client) first calls canView(), which evaluates the all-clients resource, then canConfigure(client), which evaluates canManage(client) and hasPermission(client, CONFIGURE), and finally hasPermission(client, VIEW). Each hasPermission call does a resource lookup and a full evaluatePermission. Checking each client in a list therefore costs several policy evaluations per client, and the type-level evaluation is repeated N times. Nothing caches the type-level result.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle

The method builds a new, uninitialized KeyStore of the default type and returns its Provider, which is normally the JDK's SUN provider. Callers of getBouncyCastleProvider() that expect BouncyCastle, for example to look up algorithms by provider name, get the JDK provider silently. The method also allocates a throwaway KeyStore on every call. It should either return a real BC provider or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: the method returns the default keystore provider instead of the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder calls whose results are discarded

Lines 114 and 115 create ASN1Encoder instances and discard the result. The returned DER sequence on lines 117-121 recomputes the same encodings. The dead calls look like a leftover and make the method harder to read.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: dead code where ASN1Encoder instances are created and their results are discarded, while the actual encoding is recomputed in the subsequent return statement.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation. Any existing implementation that does not override it, including out-of-tree providers, is not broken at compile time but throws AbstractMethodError. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls order() on every discovered provider, so such a provider fails during crypto initialization. A default method, for example returning 0, would keep existing implementations working.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: adding the abstract `order()` method to the `CryptoProvider` interface without a default implementation breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Providers with equal order() are picked by classpath order, silently

detectProvider no longer rejects multiple providers. It stable-sorts by order() and takes the first entry. DefaultCryptoProvider (line 84), WildFlyElytronProvider (line 77) and FIPS1402Provider (line 115) all return 200. When two of them are on the same classpath, the winner is whichever ServiceLoader discovered first. Before this PR that case threw IllegalStateException; now it only logs at debug level. In a FIPS deployment that also has the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider on the classpath, the non-FIPS provider can be chosen with no error. Ties need a deterministic rule (for example, FIPS ranked above default) or should still fail. No test covers this selection logic.

Non-selected providers are constructed, and their constructors mutate global JVM security state

The ServiceLoader stream is collected into a list before sorting, so every discovered CryptoProvider constructor runs, including those that will not be selected. FIPS1402Provider's constructor (FIPS1402Provider.java line 94) inserts a KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at JVM security slot 1. When BCFIPS is absent it also inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE and rewrites the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties. DefaultCryptoProvider's constructor registers a non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider with Security.addProvider. Previously these side effects were followed by a hard failure when more than one provider was present. Now the multi-provider case succeeds, so the side effects persist in a JVM that runs a different provider. Discovery should avoid constructing unselected providers, for example by ranking on metadata before instantiation.

AuthzClient.create() can pin the process-wide crypto provider to the minimal one

CryptoIntegration.init is process-global and effectively runs once, using the class loader of AuthzClient. If that loader cannot see the full crypto provider (for example, when the real crypto jar is in another class loader, such as an application server module), or if an application creates an AuthzClient before anything else initializes crypto, the global provider becomes AuthzClientCryptoProvider. Because init is a no-op afterwards, later code that needs the real provider keeps getting AuthzClientCryptoProvider, and most of its methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Before this change AuthzClient did not touch the global provider. Consider not installing a placeholder provider globally from this entry point.

Most provider methods throw a 'Not supported yet.' placeholder

About 17 methods, including getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getKeyFactory, getSignature, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory and wrapFactoryForTruststore, throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'). That is leftover IDE template text, and it suggests the feature is planned. Because this provider is now a global ServiceLoader entry, callers that reach it through CryptoIntegration.getProvider() get an opaque failure. The message should say the provider is limited to ECDSA conversion, or the methods should be implemented.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate signature length

The method copies signature[len..2*len) without checking signature.length. A short or malformed signature triggers an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than an IOException or a clean verification failure. The method is copied from the BC implementation but is new code here, so it should check that signature.length equals signLength.

Test only checks the module's own encoder and decoder round-trip

The assertion compares the concatenated R||S produced by asn1derToConcatenatedRS with the value obtained after encoding and decoding it again, using the same class. If both directions share a defect, or if the produced DER is not accepted by a standard verifier, the test still passes. The test should verify the DER output from concatenatedRSToASN1DER with java.security.Signature.verify, or check it against a known test vector.

ES384 and ES512 are tested with a P-256 key, so the real component sizes are not exercised

A single default EC key pair is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so ES384 and ES512 sign with P-256 keys. The 48-byte and 66-byte component paths are not tested with matching curves. The P-521 case matters most: R can be 66 bytes plus a sign byte, which hits the truncation branch in integerToBytes, and that path is never exercised. The test therefore gives false confidence for ES384 and ES512. Each algorithm should be tested with its own curve, P-384 and P-521.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deleted group silently reports a null subgroup count

The NPE is replaced by returning null from a method whose contract is a count. The missing group is swallowed here and the null propagates into representations (populateSubGroupCount assigns it directly). true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is not joined, so late failures are ignored

deletedAll is set and the assertion runs at line 157 without joining the reader thread started at line 139. The reader may still be inside an in-flight request, and any exception it records after the assertion is evaluated is never checked. false_positives.candidate:
Paged subgroup listing still dereferences a possibly-null model

getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults) calls modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null check. The supplier resolves to null when another request has deleted the group, which is the race this PR targets, so this still throws the same NPE. The check 'if (group == null)' tests the Supplier<GroupModel> parameter. GroupAdapter always passes its non-null modelSupplier, so the guard never fires. When the underlying group has been deleted, the supplier returns null, and that null reaches the lazy loader. The comment describes exactly the case this guard was meant to handle, so the intended protection is missing and the PR does not address it. The check should be on group.get() == null before calling the loader.

Unlike getRoleMappings, getAttributes (lines 66-68) and getSubGroups (lines 90-92) pass the supplier straight to DefaultLazyLoader. The loaders at lines 55 and 57 dereference the source (source.getAttributes(), source.getSubGroupsStream()). Assuming the loader runs on the supplied source when the value is not yet loaded, a group deleted before its first attribute or subgroup access makes the supplier return null and the loader throws NPE. That affects getFirstAttribute, getAttributes, getAttributeStream and getSubGroupsStream() in GroupAdapter, so the concurrent NPE remains reachable.

Parent lookup result used without a null check during hierarchy build

session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId()) returns null if the parent was deleted between listing and this lookup. parentModel is then passed to groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel) at line 51 (when admin permissions are off), to toRepresentation inside computeIfAbsent at line 57, and to populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent) at line 60, which calls getSubGroupsCount() on null. This is the same concurrent-deletion NPE in the group listing path, and the PR edits this file without handling it. A null check that drops the orphaned child or skips the parent is needed.

Exception during deletion leaves a non-daemon busy-looping thread running

If group(...).remove() at line 153 throws (for example a 500 from the bug under test), the exception escapes the forEach and deletedAll.set(true) at line 155 never runs. The reader thread (lines 139-149) then loops forever issuing HTTP requests. As a non-daemon thread it also keeps the JVM alive, so the run hangs instead of failing cleanly. Race-based test may not reproduce the NPE and has no deterministic interleaving

The NPE requires a cached adapter with a loaded group, a concurrent deletion, and then a lazy access. This test depends on timing between one reader thread and 100 sequential deletes, and it only asserts that no exception reached the client. Nothing shows it fails on the base commit, so it may pass without the fix. The author should confirm it reproduces the failure without the change, or drive the interleaving deterministically (for example by deleting the group on the server between the read and the access).

Reader thread spins on HTTP requests with no pause

The reader loop at lines 139-149 issues back-to-back list requests over 100 groups for the whole deletion phase with no sleep or backoff. This saturates the shared test server, slows the test, and adds load that can cause timeouts on CI. A short pause between iterations would avoid this.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-auth skip is disabled for every user whenever passkeys are enabled in the realm

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key

BuildIndex no longer serializes builds: the lock was removed from the whole function and only the final cache write is locked. Nothing deduplicates concurrent builds for one key, and getOrCreateIndex's GetIndex-then-build sequence is not atomic. Two concurrent cold Search or watch-event calls for the same namespace now build two full indexes in parallel, roughly doubling memory and CPU. The second 'b.cache[key] = idx' silently replaces the first index, which is never closed. For file-backed indexes, the second bleve.New on the same directory races the first and can fail. The previous code built twice too, but serially. Use per-key singleflight or re-check under the lock.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition described in the golden comment: narrowing the lock in BuildIndex to only cover the final cache write allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while GetIndex takes RLock and BuildIndex writes the map under Lock. The new log line in search.go init (line 216) calls TotalDocs after the watch goroutine has started (lines 207-213). That goroutine can call handleEvent, then getOrCreateIndex, then BuildIndex, which writes the map concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error in Go and cannot be recovered. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock().
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same data race: calling TotalDocs() iterates over b.cache without a lock while the newly started event watcher goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex, leading to a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Storage init failures now abort NewResourceServer and block startup on the full index build

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init synchronously. Init runs lifecycle.Init (DB connect and ping) and the search init, which builds an index for every namespace above InitMinCount, and returns the error to the caller. Previously these failures only surfaced as errors on the first gRPC call and never stopped construction. Now a transient DB error or any index build error makes the constructor fail, which fails whatever wires the server, and startup (including HTTP and metrics) is blocked for the entire index build. Init is also never retried. This is the behavior change the PR description asks about. It should be called out explicitly, and the module init order should be checked to confirm the DB and dependencies are ready when the provider runs.

On-demand index build still runs under the gRPC request context

getOrCreateIndex still builds a missing index with the request context: s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0). The build's ListIterator and builder calls use that ctx. Namespaces at or below InitMinCount at startup are not indexed at init. If such a namespace has since grown, the first Search builds the whole index inside the RPC, and a client cancel or deadline aborts the build mid-way. The index is then never cached, so the same failure repeats on every request. This is the failure mode the PR says it fixes, and it remains on this path. The fixed size hint of 10 also always selects the memory-only index.

Data race on shared err and counter in the parallel init workers

Pre-existing, but it is in the function being edited. The errgroup closure assigns the outer function's err variable ('_, _, err = s.build(...)') and increments totalBatchesIndexed (line 189), and both run concurrently in up to initWorkers goroutines. That is an unsynchronized write from multiple goroutines, which the race detector flags and which can tear an interface value. The closure should use a local error (the return value already reaches group.Wait), and the counter should be atomic.

GetResourceStats never checks rows.Err, so a mid-iteration failure returns partial stats as success

The loop ends when rows.Next() returns false. If that was caused by an error (for example a dropped connection), rows.Err() holds it, but the code never checks it. The callback then returns err, which is nil at that point, and the function returns partial res with a nil error. search init then indexes only the namespaces that were read, logs success, and never retries. rows is also not closed on the early Scan-error return. Check rows.Err() after the loop and defer rows.Close().

Trace propagation fixed only in GetResourceStats; sibling methods still drop the span context

The PR says it fixes trace propagation, but only GetResourceStats was changed. WriteEvent (line 158), ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) still do '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and then pass the parent ctx down. As a result the create, update and delete spans and the DB transaction spans are siblings of the wrapper span, not children. bleve.go BuildIndex (line 88) has the same pattern. Either finish the change in these methods or narrow the PR description.

Removing the Init gate from every RPC silently allows requests after Stop

Before this change, each RPC called s.Init, which returned s.initErr. Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopped', so every request after Stop was rejected. With the gates removed, initErr is dead state and RPCs keep being served after Stop, even though the broadcaster context has been cancelled. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR. Either keep a stopped check in the RPCs or document the change.

Postgres skip removes the only startup test for the storage target in CI

The new skip disables the only test that exercises starting the storage-server target, for postgres, with a TODO and the reason 'Works locally'. This PR changes exactly that startup path, because Init now runs inside NewResourceServer. CI therefore has no coverage of the new startup behavior on postgres. The PR description does not mention this test change. Either fix the test or track the skip with an issue and explain why the change is safe.

NewResourceServer leaks its context and started goroutines when Init fails

The context and cancel func are created at line 229, but on the Init error path the constructor returns without calling s.cancel(). If initWatcher failed after the broadcaster started, its goroutines keep running on s.ctx. The lifecycle hooks, which may already have been initialized, are not stopped either. The same applies to the error return at line 254. Call s.cancel() (and stop the lifecycle) before returning the error.

Watcher goroutine dereferences nil event when the backend stops, panicking at shutdown

Pre-existing, but in the function being edited. When the backend stops, the poller returns and runs 'defer close(stream)'. The loop 'v := <-events' then receives nil forever, and handleEvent reads evt.Type on a nil pointer, which panics and crashes the process during shutdown. The same pattern exists in server.go initWatcher (around lines 762-765, where v.Type is read). Use 'v, ok := <-events' and return when !ok.

false_positives.candidate:
close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped after the first rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and passed to every strategy that create_with_partitions() builds. Arroyo closes the current strategy on partition revocation and creates a new one on assignment, so after the first rebalance the pool's queues are already shut down and its workers have exited. The new strategy's submit() calls FixedQueuePool.submit -> queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. The except branch in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (lines 317-325) then marks the offset as added and completed, so the message is never processed but its offset becomes committable. Work that was still queued when the old pool shut down keeps its offsets in `outstanding` forever, which stalls commits for those partitions. Net effect: uptime results are silently lost after any rebalance and the commit point stops advancing. No test runs close() followed by create_with_partitions() on the same factory, so this is not caught. Pool ownership should stay with the factory; the strategy's close() should only stop its own commit thread.

Enqueue failures mark the offset as completed, so unprocessed messages get committed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, any exception raised while decoding, grouping, or enqueueing a message reaches an except block that calls add_offset and then complete_offset for that message. The message is never handed to a worker, yet its offset is now treated as processed, so the commit loop advances past it and the message is dropped with only a log line. This is the mechanism that hides the ShutDown failure described above. Poison messages (decode or grouping errors) may reasonably be skipped, but a failure to enqueue must not mark the offset complete. Failed enqueues should keep the offset outstanding or propagate the error.

Per-queue work queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure

Each per-queue work queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), so FixedQueuePool.submit() never blocks. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 255) promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills. If the handlers are slower than the Kafka fetch rate, the main thread keeps polling and queued WorkItems (each holding a full Message) accumulate without bound. Because commits are contiguous, the last committed offset stays pinned behind the slowest item, so the outstanding and all_offsets sets also grow. Either bound the queues and make submit block or pause the consumer, or remove the backpressure claim.

A hole in the offset sequence permanently stalls all commits for that partition

get_committable_offsets breaks out of the scan on any offset that is not in all_offsets (line 90), so a missing offset blocks commits forever. Within a partition, Kafka delivers messages in offset order, so if offset 102 arrives after 100, offset 101 will never arrive later; it is a hole from compaction or a transaction marker, and the tracker waits for it indefinitely. Consequences: the committed point never moves past the hole, mark_committed never prunes all_offsets so it grows without bound, and every restart reprocesses everything after the hole. test_offset_gaps_block_commits in the queue consumer tests only passes because it submits offset 101 after 102 and 103, which real delivery cannot produce. The tracker should treat offsets skipped by a newer delivered offset as complete.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread without synchronization

_commit_loop runs on its own thread and calls commit_function (line 287), which is the Arroyo commit callback from create_with_partitions. Arroyo's consumer is driven from the StreamProcessor thread (poll, stage, commit); nothing here coordinates with that loop, so commits can race with the main thread's consumer calls. There is also a shutdown race: after shutdown_event is set, the loop does not re-check the flag after shutdown_event.wait(1.0) (line 276), so it can run one more get_committable_offsets and commit_function after close() has begun or returned, and close() only joins for 5 seconds. Commit calls should be made from the processor thread (for example from poll()), and the loop should exit once the event is set.

Sequential 5-second joins make shutdown block for up to 100 seconds per rebalance

FixedQueuePool.shutdown joins each worker with a 5-second timeout, one after another (line 243). With the default 20 queues, if the workers are all stuck in slow result handlers (the exact case this PR targets), shutdown can block for up to 100 seconds. Because the strategy's close() also calls this shutdown (see the close() bug above), this delay occurs on every rebalance. That risks exceeding the consumer's poll or session timeouts and getting the consumer evicted from the group. Use one shared deadline for all joins, or avoid blocking joins on the rebalance path.

Racy assertion that queued items remain right after submission

test_stats_reporting asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 immediately after ten submits (line 200), while worker threads are already draining the queues. If the workers dequeue everything before this line runs (possible under CI load or GIL switching), the test fails intermittently. The check adds no coverage that the later == 0 assertion does not already provide, so either remove it or make the precondition deterministic, for example by blocking the workers first.

Test named for concurrency does not check concurrency

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims to verify that different groups are processed concurrently, but its only assertion (line 173) is that three group labels appear in the processed output. That would pass if every item ran serially on one thread, and with only three queues the groups can hash onto the same queue. The name and the assertion disagree, so the test gives false confidence about concurrency.

Worker transaction is named with a 'monitors.' prefix copied from another consumer

The worker transaction name is built as monitors.{identifier}.worker_{id} (line 138). This module is generic remote-subscription code used by the uptime results consumer, and the same prefix is copied into the result processor. Performance data for these workers will be filed under the monitors namespace, which misleads anyone looking at traces. The prefix should reflect the actual consumer or be derived from the identifier alone.

Strategy created in test is never closed, leaking a commit thread

test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy creates a SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy through the factory (line 415) but only calls factory.shutdown(), which stops the pool and not the strategy. The strategy's commit thread loops every second for the rest of the test session because its shutdown event is never set. The test should call strategy.close() so the thread is stopped and the test does not leak threads into later tests.

false_positives.candidate:
Span eviction at 1000 is silent: no log or metric when spans are dropped

When span_count exceeds 1000, zpopmin silently removes the lowest-scored (oldest by end timestamp) spans from the segment. The Python side previously logged 'Skipping too large segment' and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded, and that guard was removed in buffer.py. Dropped spans are now invisible to operators, and the limit is hardcoded here rather than configured. Emit a metric (and ideally a log) from the script or the caller when eviction occurs.

Key type change from Redis set to sorted set breaks in-flight buffers during deploy

The span-buf:s:* keys change from SET to ZSET but keep the same name prefix. Any segment key written by the old code is a SET. After deploy, ZADD in process_spans, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE in add-buffer.lua, and ZSCAN in _load_segment_data all fail with WRONGTYPE. Ingestion raises for those traces, and flush_segments raises before done_flush_segments runs, so the queue entries are not cleared until the keys expire (redis_ttl, default 3600s). The PR needs a new key prefix or a drain/migration plan.

ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, doubling scores of duplicate payloads

zunionstore is called without AGGREGATE, so the default SUM applies. When the same payload already exists in the destination (for example a redelivered Kafka message, or a span present in both merged sets), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps. That corrupts the eviction ordering, which relies on score = end_timestamp_precise. Use AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score is preserved.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and caveat comment removed

The loop bound changed from 10000 to 1000 with no mention in the PR description, and the comment explaining the limit's consequence was deleted. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 are now cut off silently, so their spans are attached to an intermediate segment rather than the root. Either keep the old limit or document the change and keep the caveat.

Hard key access on end_timestamp_precise can fail an entire batch

val['end_timestamp_precise'] is a strict lookup, and the cast(SpanEvent, ...) is type-only and does not validate anything at runtime. Before this PR the field was not read. A single message missing it raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and can leave the consumer retrying the same poison batch. Use val.get with a fallback, or validate and skip the bad message with a metric.

max_segment_spans config is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit

After this PR the span-count check in _load_segment_data was removed, so the max_segment_spans constructor argument (default 1001) is never read. The effective limit is the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Configuration that appears to control the limit no longer does, and the two defaults disagree. Remove the parameter or wire it into the script.

No test covers the new 1000-span eviction, the set-to-zset change, or the redirect depth change

The headline feature of this PR, evicting spans beyond 1000 during insert, has no test. The added lines only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures, so nothing checks that the segment is capped, that the oldest spans are the ones evicted, that merges keep the right scores, or that the loop limit behaves as intended. Add tests that insert more than 1000 spans through process_spans and assert the resulting count and which payloads survive.

optimized_pagination path is untested and crashes on the first page

The new branch gated by optimized_pagination=true has no test. Such a test would immediately expose the datetime TypeError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, so the endpoint's new path is broken and unverified. Add a test for a superuser request with that parameter and at least one audit log entry.

Comment claims a negative-offset feature that this change does not implement

The added comment says Cursor now allows negative offsets for advanced pagination and enables reverse pagination from arbitrary positions. The diff changes nothing in this constructor (self.offset = int(offset) is unchanged), and the paginators that consume negative offsets crash on them. The comment describes behavior that does not exist, so it should be removed or corrected.

Module docstring still describes span-buf:s:* keys as sets

The glossary says span-buf:s:* are 'the actual set keys', but after this PR they are sorted sets (ZADD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZSCAN, ZPOPMIN). Update the docstring so future readers do not assume SET commands.

Unrelated pagination changes and an undocumented query parameter are bundled into a spans PR

The PR title is about span buffer eviction, but this file, paginator.py, and cursors.py add an experimental audit-log paginator switch. That switch is an undocumented optimized_pagination query parameter, and the PR description is just 'Test 2', so reviewers have no rationale for it. Split these changes into their own PR with a description, or revert them from this one.

Allowlist option read via options.get with no registration in the diff

The allowlist comes only from options.get('issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist', []). None of the eight changed files registers this key in the options defaults. Sentry's options manager raises an UnknownOption error for unregistered keys, so on a cache miss _are_all_projects_error_upsampled would raise. That call happens in is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects before any dataset gating, so every events-stats request with a project could fail, not only error queries. The tests patch options in this module, so the real lookup never runs and CI would not catch it. Register the option or confirm it already exists.

Substring match classifies negated and compound event.type filters as error queries

The check 'event.type:error' in query is a substring test. Queries such as '!event.type:error', 'event.type:errors', or '(event.type:error OR event.type:transaction)' all return True. For those queries the count is rewritten to sum(sample_weight), but non-error rows have no sample_weight, so the sum drops them and the count is wrong (for '!event.type:error' it can come out as 0). The filter should be parsed as a token rather than matched as a substring. No test covers negation or compound queries.

sum(sample_weight) silently drops events that lack a weight

sum() ignores NULLs, so any error event without a sample_weight contributes 0 instead of 1 to upsampled_count. This includes events ingested before the rollout and events with no client sample rate. The docstring in error_upsampling.py (lines 85-86) says no null handling is needed because the schema guarantees the column, but nothing in the diff enforces that. Time ranges spanning the rollout would silently undercount for allowlisted projects. The fallback for a missing weight should be defined explicitly, for example coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

Transform is not gated on metrics or on-demand routing

The count() rewrite to upsampled_count() is applied regardless of use_metrics, has_metrics, use_metrics_layer, or on_demand_metrics_enabled, which can route a discover-dataset query to a metrics or on-demand builder. upsampled_count is registered only in discover.py's function converter, so in those routes the function would not resolve, or the query would silently fall back to a non-upsampled count. The transform should be gated on the builder actually used.

Equations containing count() are not upsampled alongside the rewritten yAxis

Only the exact count() entries in query_columns are rewritten. Equations passed through equations=self.get_equation_list(...) are not transformed, so an equation such as equation|count() * 2 returns un-upsampled values while the plain count() yAxis returns upsampled values in the same response. The inconsistency is not handled or documented.

Upsampling branch in the RPC path is unreachable

use_rpc is true only when dataset is spans_rpc or ourlogs. _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns False for both, so upsampling_enabled is always False when this block runs. The block is dead code, and it gives the false impression that RPC datasets get upsampled. Remove it, or rework the gating if RPC upsampling was intended.

Allowlist check and cache write run before the dataset gate

On every cache miss, _are_all_projects_error_upsampled runs options.get and cache.set, even for spans, metrics, and transactions queries. The dataset check on line 40 then discards the result. The cache get and set happen on every _get_event_stats call. Checking the dataset and request gate first, then returning early, would avoid the Redis round trips and the option lookup for queries that can never be upsampled.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code, so allowlist changes are only picked up after 60s

invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called in the diff, and no allowlist write path invokes it. Its docstring says it should be called when the allowlist changes, but nothing does. An allowlist change therefore takes up to 60 seconds to affect upsampling, because of the cache.set at line 38. Either wire it to the option update path or remove it and correct the docstring.

Comments claim caching and consistency that the code does not provide

The comments say the cached result 'ensures consistent behavior across query execution' and that storing the decision 'allows for better query optimization and caching'. Nothing is cached at this point. The decision is recomputed on every _get_event_stats call, and the underlying eligibility is a 60-second cache in error_upsampling.py. Calls within one request can therefore disagree if the cache entry expires between them. The comments should be corrected.

Unrelated change to an existing error message

The topEvents validation message changes from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This has nothing to do with upsampling and is not mentioned in the PR. Any client matching the exact string will see a change. It should be split out or called out in the description.

Bare except blocks silently ignore malformed sample rates

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling wraps dict access and float conversion in bare 'except Exception: pass'. A malformed client_sample_rate is silently dropped and the event is stored without sample_rate. This helper runs inside store_event, which many tests use, so a bad test payload gives no signal. The try around a plain dict .get chain is unnecessary. Validation should be explicit or errors should surface.

upsampled_count is a public aggregate with a different result type from count()

The function is registered without private=True, so users can request upsampled_count() in any discover query, including transaction queries the upsampling guard is meant to exclude. Its default_result_type is 'number' while count() is 'integer', so the field type reported in meta changes for upsampled responses. Either mark it private or document and validate the new public aggregate and its result type.

Stray file committed at repository root

A regular file named sentry-repo containing 'Subproject commit a5d29095...' is added at the repository root. It is not a real gitlink and appears to be an accidental artifact that pins the base commit. It should not be part of this change and should be removed from the PR.

Query-classification and cache paths are untested

test_is_error_focused_query and test_should_apply_sample_weight_transform only check the exact strings 'event.type:error' and 'event.type:transaction'. Nothing covers negated filters ('!event.type:error'), compound queries, or 'event.type:errors', which is exactly where the substring check goes wrong. is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects itself is not tested, so the cache hit and miss paths and the dataset gate are unverified. The endpoint tests also never exercise the topEvents or RPC branches where the transform is applied.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" passes even if the denial cache is ignored

The test is meant to prove that the denial cache short-circuits the check. But the permCache entry it sets is {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}, a deny, so the cached-permission path also denies. The fallback then reads the DB, where setupService's fakeStore has no permissions, so it denies too. Removing the permDenialCache lookup in Check() leaves this test green. The comment on line 981 ('Allow access ... to prove this is not checked') contradicts the value set. There is also no test that a denial is written after a DB deny and then bypassed once the permission exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because '_' separates fields that can contain '_'

userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, user UID, action, name and parent with '_', and Grafana UIDs and names often contain underscores. Different tuples collide: name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce "...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c". If the first is denied and cached, the second (which the user may be allowed) is wrongly denied for the 30s TTL. The key needs an unambiguous encoding (length prefix, escaping or a hash).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys using underscore concatenation without escaping or length prefixing, leading to key collisions when fields contain underscores, which causes incorrect permission denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache short-circuits before the DB refresh, so a fresh grant is ignored for up to 30s

Check() returns a cached deny as soon as the denial key is present, before it tries the cached permissions or re-queries the DB. The denial entry is written from a fresh DB result (line 154) but is never invalidated when permissions are granted. Sequence: user U checks dashboard X and is denied (denial entry stored, 30s TTL); U is then granted access to X (or X is created by U and U gets access); U checks X again within 30s. The denial hit returns Allowed=false, so the new 'requery DB when the resource is not in cached permissions' fallback never runs. That is exactly the 'creator cannot access what they just created' symptom this PR is meant to fix, and the denial cache re-introduces a stale-deny window that the fallback removed. The same applies to name-less checks (create flows, where the result only depends on whether any permission exists for the action). No test covers denial-then-grant.

Every DB denial is cached under a request-controlled key with no size bound

The denial key is built from the request's name and parent folder, and an entry is written for every denied request. The local cache used here (authlib cache.NewLocalCache) has no size cap in its configuration. A user can issue requests with many distinct names (including nonexistent ones) and fill the cache with entries for 30s each. Denial entries also add a write per denied request on top of the DB query. A bounded cache or a cap on what is cached would limit this.

Failed user lookup is performed twice per request in Check and List

getCachedIdentityPermissions calls GetUserIdentifiers, and its error is then ignored. The fallback getIdentityPermissions path calls GetUserIdentifiers again. Failed lookups are not cached, so for an unknown or deleted user every request issues two identical DB queries (Check at line 123 then line 139; List at lines 180 and 186). The identifier lookup should be done once and reused.

Remote/cloud client still keeps the 30s authlib client cache, so the stale-result symptom remains there

The PR removes the authlib client cache only for the in-proc client (ProvideAuthZClient). newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the client in a 30s LocalCache, which caches Check results on the client side. A creator using a remote or standalone authz server will therefore still see stale results for a newly created resource for up to 30s, regardless of the server-side fallback. The PR description only mentions in-proc, so either this is intentional and should be documented, or the remote path is not fixed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when an existing Integration has no sender metadata

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` raises KeyError if the Integration row has no `sender` key. `build_integration` only writes `sender` when the pipeline state contains one (lines 376-377), and integrations created by the pipeline without a webhook do not have it (test_basic_flow asserts metadata with no sender). This line is reached for any Integration row that exists without an OrganizationIntegration, so the install flow returns a 500 instead of the error page. Use `.get()` and return `error(...)` when the sender is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` directly raises a `KeyError` when the `sender` key is missing from the metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user check is skipped entirely when no Integration row exists yet

When no Integration row exists for `installation_id`, the `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch returns `pipeline.next_step()` before the new authenticated-user check (lines 501-505) runs. That check only executes when an Integration already exists with `metadata["sender"]`, which the installation webhook normally creates. The webhook is delivered asynchronously while the browser is redirected back to Sentry, so if the browser returns first, or the webhook is delayed or dropped, the pipeline completes without verifying that the authenticated GitHub user is the one who installed the app. This fail-open path defeats the guarantee the PR describes. The check should fail closed when there is no installer record to compare against, or the installer identity should be obtained another way.

Installer check compares mutable GitHub logins instead of immutable user IDs

The check compares `login` strings. GitHub usernames can be renamed, and the old name then becomes claimable by another account. The webhook `sender` payload and the `/user` response both include the numeric `id`, which is immutable. If the installer renames their account and another user claims the old login, that second account would pass this check. Comparing `id` values would close this gap.

Integration lookups for the security check are not scoped by provider

The lookups at lines 478 and 494-496 filter only on `external_id` and not on `provider`. `external_id` is unique only per provider, so `get` can raise an unhandled MultipleObjectsReturned (500), or it can return a non-GitHub row whose metadata is then used for the sender comparison at line 503. The lookup used for the security decision should include `provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key`.

Network and API failures during token exchange and user lookup are not handled

`safe_urlopen` at line 423 and `get_user_info` at line 434 are not wrapped in error handling, unlike the body parsing at lines 425-429. A connection failure, timeout, or non-2xx response from GitHub propagates out of the view and produces a 500 instead of the failure page that the rest of this view renders. These calls should be wrapped so the view returns `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

Installation now hard-requires GitHub OAuth client credentials

The new step reads the GitHub OAuth client ID and secret (lines 394-395) and places the client ID into the authorize URL without checking that it is set. On deployments that have the GitHub App configured but not GitHub login OAuth credentials, the authorize URL contains `client_id=None`, so users are sent to a GitHub error page and cannot install the integration. This new requirement is not mentioned in the PR description.

No test for the success path of the new installer check or for the skipped-check path

The only test exercising the new check (`test_github_user_mismatch`) covers the failure case. Nothing verifies that a webhook-created Integration whose `sender` matches the OAuth user completes the pipeline. Nothing covers an installation with no Integration row yet, which is the path where the check is skipped entirely (see the fail-open finding in integration.py). Both cases need tests.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the not-found path

The original assertion for 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' was removed. The test now sends a mismatched state, which fails at the state check before `build_integration` runs. The `IntegrationError` raised on a GitHub API 404 (integration.py lines 352-357) is therefore untested, and the `responses.replace(... status=404)` mock is never hit. Restore coverage by sending a matching state, or keep the original test.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update evaluates the stored IDP through the org-aware wrapper, so updates to IDPs in a disabled org skip invalidation

In update(), `idpById` comes from getById(), which wraps the model in createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the bound organization is disabled, while `model` (the updated raw representation) reports the IDP's own enabled flag. For an IDP bound to a disabled org, getLoginPredicate().test(original) is therefore always false. The login lists are built from the JPA query, which does not consider org state, so such an IDP can be cached. If the update then disables it (or hides it / makes it link-only), both sides evaluate to false, registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate returns early, and the cached login list keeps the now-disabled IDP. A later getForLogin cache hit returns it; the uncached path would exclude it. The stale entry persists after the org is re-enabled. Callers that do not re-check isEnabled() will expose a disabled IDP. The login decision should use the raw stored model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById), not the org-aware wrapper.

getForLogin javadoc omits the new organization BROKER_PUBLIC requirement

The javadoc says an IDP can be used for login if it is enabled, not link-only, and not hidden on login. The getLoginPredicate() change in this PR adds a further rule: an IDP bound to an organization must also have BROKER_PUBLIC=true to qualify. The public contract documented here is now incomplete, and callers of getForLogin cannot learn the rule from the interface.

REALM_ONLY lookups get separate cache entries per organizationId even though the organization is ignored

searchKey is derived from organizationId for every mode. For FetchMode.REALM_ONLY the delegate ignores organizationId, so getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, orgA) and getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, null) produce identical results but are stored under different searchKeys in the same IdentityProviderListQuery. The same realm-only list is duplicated per distinct organization id that is passed in. Normalising searchKey to "" for REALM_ONLY would avoid the duplicate entries.

No test covers the invalidation cases the new BROKER_PUBLIC predicate and org disable handling exist for

The new `idp.getOrganizationId() == null || BROKER_PUBLIC` clause in getLoginPredicate() is only exercised indirectly. Step 4 links a realm-level login IDP to an organization, but nothing checks that flipping BROKER_PUBLIC from true to false on an organization-bound login IDP invalidates the login caches. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. Any goroutine that missed the cache while another goroutine was already populating it will still re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, one at a time, even though the cache is now filled. At startup, N concurrent requests produce N serialized manifest reads. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after taking the Lock would return the cached value immediately.

Exclusive lock held across file I/O serializes all dev-mode calls and ignores caller context

The write Lock is taken on every call in dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), because the early return is skipped. Each call then reads and parses the manifest from disk while holding the exclusive lock, so concurrent dev requests that previously ran in parallel now run one at a time. In non-dev mode, while the cache is nil (for example, the manifest is missing or failed to load), every request blocks on Lock without honouring its ctx, so a slow operation inside readWebAssetsFromCDN (which uses http.DefaultClient with no timeout) holds up all waiters. The CDN path is currently unreachable because cdn is the constant "", so this is latent, but the lock scope is wider than the data race requires. Doing the I/O outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result would avoid both problems.

The PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Without a test run under `go test -race`, nothing guards against the race being reintroduced, for example by a future change that reads the global outside the lock. A small test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently with a temp manifest, with the cache reset between cases, would lock in the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

The legacy write runs in a goroutine but its context is derived from ctx, the incoming request context. net/http cancels a request's context when ServeHTTP returns, which happens right after Storage.Create returns and the response is written. The 10s timeout wrapper is built on that already-canceled context, so Legacy.Create typically fails with context canceled before it writes anything. Legacy writes will be lost for most requests, silently, which defeats the purpose of mode 3. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The background write should detach from the request context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the timeout.

The goroutine only feeds a boolean into a duration metric and drops the error. The base code logged legacy failures with the object attached. Now a failed legacy create (including a timeout) produces no log line and no error detail, so the unified/legacy divergence this mode is meant to guard against is invisible to operators. The same omission exists in Delete (line 113), Update (line 140) and DeleteCollection (line 166).

Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered per object

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object serialization. Two quick successive operations on the same playlist (for example update then update, or update then delete) can reach the legacy store out of order, leaving legacy with the older state while unified storage holds the newer one. Nothing detects or repairs this, and the 10s timeout makes it more likely. This needs either per-key serialization or an explicit, documented eventual-consistency guarantee with tests.

Legacy update recomputes the change from its own state instead of writing the unified result

The base code wrapped the Storage.Update result in updateWrapper so the legacy store received exactly what unified storage produced. This version passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update. objInfo.UpdatedObject is then applied to the legacy store's current object, which can differ from the unified object (different resourceVersions, stored fields, defaults, or a patch applied against a different base). Both writes can succeed and the stores still diverge. The same objInfo is also consumed a second time after the first UpdatedObject call.

Unified storage failures are recorded as legacy failures

When the storage write fails, Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The failed unified write is counted in the legacy metrics and the storage error metric is never set, so storage error rates are under-reported and legacy stats are polluted.

Destroy tears down Legacy while fire-and-forget writes may still be running

Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but background legacy goroutines may still be executing against the legacy store. Those writes then run against a destroyed backend and fail or panic. Destroy has no way to wait for in-flight legacy writes.

Background legacy goroutines have no panic recovery

Legacy calls used to run on the request goroutine, where net/http recovers panics per request. The bare goroutines added here have no recover, so a panic in any legacy storage method crashes the whole Grafana process instead of failing one request.

Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write

Storage and Legacy share a single mock.Mock, so the test cannot tell which store was called. The tests never call AssertExpectations, so the legacy expectations set up in TestMode3_Create, _Update and _DeleteCollection are never checked. Nothing verifies that Legacy is called, or with what object, which is the core of this change. The background goroutine can also call the mock after the test returns, so those calls are not observed at all.

Legacy-side reads run immediately after writes that are now asynchronous

In mode 3, the k8s create at line 496 returns before its legacy write completes. getFromBothAPIs then reads the legacy endpoint right away (and the legacy list comparison around line 523 does the same). These checks race the background write and will be flaky. If the legacy endpoint is actually served from unified storage, the checks do not exercise the legacy write at all. Either way the assertion does not test what it claims without waiting or polling for the legacy write.

The case is named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented', but List is now implemented in this PR and the case only checks that a storage error is propagated. The name is misleading to future readers.

Create test name contradicts its setup

The case is named 'creating an object only in the unified store', but its setup registers a legacy Create expectation and the implementation writes to legacy as well. The name describes the old behavior.

The line 'github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery ... /go.mod' is added a second time, duplicating the entry immediately above it. The hunk also adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporters and genproto rpc), which this dual-writer change does not touch. These look like an accidental go mod tidy or merge artifact and should be removed or verified.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries are now split because the range check runs after interpolation

querySupportsSplitting() (line 287) exists so that queries containing $__range are not split, because $__range has to be evaluated against the full time range of the request. Before this change it saw the raw expression. Now runSplitQuery interpolates first (line 299) and partitions on the result (line 300). Any $__range that applyTemplateVariables resolves from request.scopedVars (Grafana supplies __range for panel queries) has already been replaced by a literal, so isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false and the query is split. Each time chunk then runs with the full-range literal as its window and combineResponses merges the chunks, which gives wrong results for range aggregations. No test in the PR covers this exclusion.

Shard path no longer drops targets whose expression interpolates to empty

The old code interpolated first and then filtered on expr, so a target whose expression is a variable expanding to an empty string was dropped. The filter now runs on the raw expression (line 50), before the map on line 52, so such targets survive. They are passed to runSplitQuery as a subrequest, where the empty expr is filtered out (querySplitting.ts line 298). If nothing is left, runSplitGroupedQueries reads requests.filter(...)[0].partition (querySplitting.ts line 96) on an empty array and throws a TypeError. On the sharded path that throw happens inside the groupTargetsByQueryType().then() callback, so the rejection is unhandled and the observable never emits. Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, so expressions that expand to empty are not dropped

The filter on line 298 checks query.expr before applyTemplateVariables runs on line 299. A target such as $query whose variable expands to an empty string passes the filter and goes to runQuery with an empty expr, which the backend will reject. If that target is the only one, the requests array ends up empty and runSplitGroupedQueries throws a TypeError at line 96. The empty check should run after the interpolation step, as the old shard code did.

Targets are interpolated twice on the sharded path

runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already calls applyTemplateVariables on every target. Each shard subrequest is then passed to runSplitQuery, which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the already expanded expression (line 299) with the same scopedVars and filters. Expansion is not idempotent: if a variable value contains a $name token that matches a template variable, it gets expanded a second time and the query changes. The test change shows the redundancy: 'Interpolates queries before running' went from toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) to toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), which codifies the repeated calls instead of removing them. Interpolation should happen once per request, with the sharded path skipping the second pass.

The added test asserts only the expr and step passed to runQuery. The point of the fix for #107530 is that interpolated values drive splitting: calculateStep reads query.step (used for metric partitioning) and querySupportsSplitting reads the expression. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Limit check is a separate COUNT followed by a separate insert, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit

The check at lines 110-116 counts devices, then the insert/upsert runs later in a separate statement with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from different new devices can all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the stored device count can overshoot the configured limit by up to the number of concurrent requests. The limit is only soft under load. If it is meant to be strict, the check and insert must be atomic (for example a conditional insert within a transaction).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same race condition where concurrent requests can bypass the device limit check and insert more devices than allowed, and both suggest using a transaction or lock to make the operation atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device is admitted on its next request

tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry for the device before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and never removes it when the store fails. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate rejects the request, but the device key stays cached for the default 29-minute expiry. The device's next request hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds without any database record. A rejected device is therefore admitted on retry and stays admitted for up to ~29 minutes, so the configured device limit is not enforced for that device. The cache entry should only be set after a successful tag, or be deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same bug described in the golden comment: `tagDeviceUI` caches the device ID before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, meaning if `ErrDeviceLimitReached` occurs, the cached entry remains for 29 minutes and allows subsequent requests to bypass the device limit.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit keys off a client-supplied, unverified header

The device identity is the raw X-Grafana-Device-Id request header, accepted without any server-side verification. A client that sends a fresh ID on each request is counted as a new device every time, so the cap can be bypassed trivially. Clearing browser storage has the same effect. If the limit is meant to be enforced rather than advisory, the device identity needs a server-verifiable basis; otherwise the limit should be documented as not being a security control.

Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so anonymous authentication never waited on the database. Now it runs inline with the request context. Each device that misses the local cache (the first request per device and again every ~29 minutes) performs a COUNT(*) over the 30-day window plus an upsert or update before the request can be authenticated. With many devices or a slow database this adds latency to those requests and holds request goroutines and DB connections. The cap check makes this worse because it adds a COUNT to the hot path. Consider keeping the non-blocking write for the normal path, or bounding the synchronous call with a timeout.

Tests only cover rejection of a new device at the limit, not the update path or the authentication flow

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a brand-new device is rejected when the table is at the limit. Not covered: (a) an existing in-window device being updated successfully while the limit is reached, which is the updateDevice success path; (b) devices outside the 30-day window not being counted; (c) TagDevice or Authenticate actually returning ErrDeviceLimitReached to the caller; (d) a rejected device retrying. The retry bug in impl.go (device cached after rejection) would be caught by a test that calls TagDevice twice for a rejected device.

RowsAffected()==0 used as 'device not found' is unreliable on MySQL

updateDevice treats RowsAffected()==0 as meaning the device is not in the window, and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. MySQL reports changed rows by default (unless clientFoundRows is set on the connection), so an UPDATE that sets the same client_ip and user_agent and a updated_at with the same second-precision value reports 0 even though the row matched. In that case an existing, legitimate device is wrongly rejected. The window is narrow (a same-second retag), so the impact is limited, but the check should not rely on affected rows on MySQL, for example by verifying existence with a SELECT.

New [auth.anonymous] device_limit option is undocumented
