false_positives.candidate:
close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped after the first rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and passed to every strategy that create_with_partitions() builds. Arroyo closes the current strategy on partition revocation and creates a new one on assignment, so after the first rebalance the pool's queues are already shut down and its workers have exited. The new strategy's submit() calls FixedQueuePool.submit -> queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. The except branch in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (lines 317-325) then marks the offset as added and completed, so the message is never processed but its offset becomes committable. Work that was still queued when the old pool shut down keeps its offsets in `outstanding` forever, which stalls commits for those partitions. Net effect: uptime results are silently lost after any rebalance and the commit point stops advancing. No test runs close() followed by create_with_partitions() on the same factory, so this is not caught. Pool ownership should stay with the factory; the strategy's close() should only stop its own commit thread.

Enqueue failures mark the offset as completed, so unprocessed messages get committed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, any exception raised while decoding, grouping, or enqueueing a message reaches an except block that calls add_offset and then complete_offset for that message. The message is never handed to a worker, yet its offset is now treated as processed, so the commit loop advances past it and the message is dropped with only a log line. This is the mechanism that hides the ShutDown failure described above. Poison messages (decode or grouping errors) may reasonably be skipped, but a failure to enqueue must not mark the offset complete. Failed enqueues should keep the offset outstanding or propagate the error.

Per-queue work queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure

Each per-queue work queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), so FixedQueuePool.submit() never blocks. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 255) promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills. If the handlers are slower than the Kafka fetch rate, the main thread keeps polling and queued WorkItems (each holding a full Message) accumulate without bound. Because commits are contiguous, the last committed offset stays pinned behind the slowest item, so the outstanding and all_offsets sets also grow. Either bound the queues and make submit block or pause the consumer, or remove the backpressure claim.

A hole in the offset sequence permanently stalls all commits for that partition

get_committable_offsets breaks out of the scan on any offset that is not in all_offsets (line 90), so a missing offset blocks commits forever. Within a partition, Kafka delivers messages in offset order, so if offset 102 arrives after 100, offset 101 will never arrive later; it is a hole from compaction or a transaction marker, and the tracker waits for it indefinitely. Consequences: the committed point never moves past the hole, mark_committed never prunes all_offsets so it grows without bound, and every restart reprocesses everything after the hole. test_offset_gaps_block_commits in the queue consumer tests only passes because it submits offset 101 after 102 and 103, which real delivery cannot produce. The tracker should treat offsets skipped by a newer delivered offset as complete.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread without synchronization

_commit_loop runs on its own thread and calls commit_function (line 287), which is the Arroyo commit callback from create_with_partitions. Arroyo's consumer is driven from the StreamProcessor thread (poll, stage, commit); nothing here coordinates with that loop, so commits can race with the main thread's consumer calls. There is also a shutdown race: after shutdown_event is set, the loop does not re-check the flag after shutdown_event.wait(1.0) (line 276), so it can run one more get_committable_offsets and commit_function after close() has begun or returned, and close() only joins for 5 seconds. Commit calls should be made from the processor thread (for example from poll()), and the loop should exit once the event is set.

Sequential 5-second joins make shutdown block for up to 100 seconds per rebalance

FixedQueuePool.shutdown joins each worker with a 5-second timeout, one after another (line 243). With the default 20 queues, if the workers are all stuck in slow result handlers (the exact case this PR targets), shutdown can block for up to 100 seconds. Because the strategy's close() also calls this shutdown (see the close() bug above), this delay occurs on every rebalance. That risks exceeding the consumer's poll or session timeouts and getting the consumer evicted from the group. Use one shared deadline for all joins, or avoid blocking joins on the rebalance path.

Racy assertion that queued items remain right after submission

test_stats_reporting asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 immediately after ten submits (line 200), while worker threads are already draining the queues. If the workers dequeue everything before this line runs (possible under CI load or GIL switching), the test fails intermittently. The check adds no coverage that the later == 0 assertion does not already provide, so either remove it or make the precondition deterministic, for example by blocking the workers first.

Test named for concurrency does not check concurrency

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims to verify that different groups are processed concurrently, but its only assertion (line 173) is that three group labels appear in the processed output. That would pass if every item ran serially on one thread, and with only three queues the groups can hash onto the same queue. The name and the assertion disagree, so the test gives false confidence about concurrency.

The worker transaction name is built as monitors.{identifier}.worker_{id} (line 138). This module is generic remote-subscription code used by the uptime results consumer, and the same prefix is copied into the result processor. Performance data for these workers will be filed under the monitors namespace, which misleads anyone looking at traces. The prefix should reflect the actual consumer or be derived from the identifier alone.

test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy creates a SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy through the factory (line 415) but only calls factory.shutdown(), which stops the pool and not the strategy. The strategy's commit thread loops every second for the rest of the test session because its shutdown event is never set. The test should call strategy.close() so the thread is stopped and the test does not leak threads into later tests.

Denial cache short-circuits before the DB refresh, so a fresh grant is ignored for up to 30s

Check() returns a cached deny as soon as the denial key is present, before it tries the cached permissions or re-queries the DB. The denial entry is written from a fresh DB result (line 154) but is never invalidated when permissions are granted. Sequence: user U checks dashboard X and is denied (denial entry stored, 30s TTL); U is then granted access to X (or X is created by U and U gets access); U checks X again within 30s. The denial hit returns Allowed=false, so the new 'requery DB when the resource is not in cached permissions' fallback never runs. That is exactly the 'creator cannot access what they just created' symptom this PR is meant to fix, and the denial cache re-introduces a stale-deny window that the fallback removed. The denial key is built from the request's name and parent folder, and an entry is written for every denied request. The local cache used here (authlib cache.NewLocalCache) has no size cap in its configuration. A user can issue requests with many distinct names (including nonexistent ones) and fill the cache with entries for 30s each. The PR removes the authlib client cache only for the in-proc client (ProvideAuthZClient). newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the client in a 30s LocalCache, which caches Check results on the client side. A creator using a remote or standalone authz server will therefore still see stale results for a newly created resource for up to 30s, regardless of the server-side fallback. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-checked cache lookup after acquiring the write lock

The fast path reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, then releases it and takes the write Lock with no re-check. Any goroutine that missed the cache while another goroutine was already populating it will still re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, one at a time, even though the cache is now filled. At startup, N concurrent requests produce N serialized manifest reads. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after taking the Lock would return the cached value immediately.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, allowing goroutines that initially saw an empty cache to redundantly load assets even after another goroutine populated it.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across file I/O serializes all dev-mode calls and ignores caller context

The write Lock is taken on every call in dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), because the early return is skipped. Each call then reads and parses the manifest from disk while holding the exclusive lock, so concurrent dev requests that previously ran in parallel now run one at a time. In non-dev mode, while the cache is nil (for example, the manifest is missing or failed to load), every request blocks on Lock without honouring its ctx, so a slow operation inside readWebAssetsFromCDN (which uses http.DefaultClient with no timeout) holds up all waiters. The CDN path is currently unreachable because cdn is the constant "", so this is latent, but the lock scope is wider than the data race requires. Doing the I/O outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result would avoid both problems.

No regression test for concurrent access to the cached web assets

The PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Without a test run under `go test -race`, nothing guards against the race being reintroduced, for example by a future change that reads the global outside the lock. A small test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently with a temp manifest, with the cache reset between cases, would lock in the fix.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup logs every batch at Error level, including successes, with full ID lists

The new per-batch closures log at Error level on every batch, including successful ones. This applies to 'Annotations to clean by time' and 'cleaned annotations by time' here (lines 534 and 537), to 'Annotations to clean by count' and 'cleaned annotations by count' (554 and 557), and to 'Tags to clean' and 'cleaned tags' (576 and 579). Each message includes the full ID slice, which can be up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries (32767 in the new test). A large backlog therefore produces many very large error-level log lines per cleanup cycle, and error-based alerting will fire on routine success. The "err" field is also always nil at these points, because fetchIDs errors return earlier. These should be Debug-level, without the full ID list.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify routine debugging or successful cleanup messages logged at Error level, polluting production error logs, and recommend a lower log level. The candidate adds details about ID lists and alerting but describes the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unrelated change: cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is not mentioned in the PR description and has nothing to do with the annotation deadlock fix. It makes every cleanup job in this loop (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, old annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history with its row-limit enforcement) run about 10 times as often in production, adding continuous DB load. It looks like a leftover debugging change and should be reverted, or split into its own justified PR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker reduction from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting increased database load from more frequent cleanup execution. The candidate adds context and a stronger recommendation but describes the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite

In the SQLite branch, `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` rebuilds the entire string on every iteration, so building an IN list of n IDs copies O(n^2) bytes. For the 32767-ID batch exercised by the new test, each id adds about 7 bytes, so the total copying is roughly 7*n^2/2, about 3.8 GB of allocation and copying per batch. This repeats for every batch of the cleanup loop whenever the batch size exceeds 999 on SQLite. Use strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt to build the list in linear time.

IN list with one placeholder per ID can exceed MySQL's 65535 placeholder limit

On non-SQLite databases the DELETE uses one placeholder per ID, and the batch size is the configured annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size. MySQL prepared statements are limited to 65535 placeholders, so a batch size above that makes the DELETE fail on every batch and stops cleanup. The previous LIMIT-based statement had no such limit. The only special handling in this diff is for SQLite. Either cap the batch size or chunk the IDs for this case.

Subtest cleanup is registered after setup and assertions that can fail

t.Cleanup is registered only after createTestAnnotations and the assertAnnotationCount/assertAnnotationTagCount calls (lines 116-118). Those helpers call require, which stops the test with FailNow. If any of them fails, the rows are never deleted, and every following subtest starts with leftover annotations and fails on counts, which hides the real failure. The cleanup should be registered before the data is created, as the previous top-level version did.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the request-scoped logger

Delete builds log with name, kind and method, then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) using the base logger. Downstream logs from the storage and legacy calls lose those fields, unlike the other methods, which pass log.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that klog.NewContext uses d.Log instead of the enriched log variable, preventing name, kind, and method fields from propagating to downstream logs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the kind label on storage metrics

recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes name where every other call passes options.Kind. Each distinct object name becomes a new Prometheus label value, which creates unbounded metric cardinality and breaks per-kind dashboards and alerts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same metrics inconsistency: Delete passes the object name instead of options.Kind to recordStorageDuration. The candidate adds consequences of the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context, which is canceled when the handler returns

The legacy write runs in a goroutine but its context is derived from ctx, the incoming request context. net/http cancels a request's context when ServeHTTP returns, which happens right after Storage.Create returns and the response is written. The 10s timeout wrapper is built on that already-canceled context, so Legacy.Create typically fails with context canceled before it writes anything. Legacy writes will be lost for most requests, silently, which defeats the purpose of mode 3. The same pattern appears in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163). The background write should detach from the request context first, e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx), before applying the timeout.

Legacy write failures are no longer logged anywhere

The goroutine only feeds a boolean into a duration metric and drops the error. The base code logged legacy failures with the object attached. Now a failed legacy create (including a timeout) produces no log line and no error detail, so the unified/legacy divergence this mode is meant to guard against is invisible to operators. The same omission exists in Delete (line 113), Update (line 140) and DeleteCollection (line 166).

Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered per object

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object serialization. Two quick successive operations on the same playlist (for example update then update, or update then delete) can reach the legacy store out of order, leaving legacy with the older state while unified storage holds the newer one. Nothing detects or repairs this, and the 10s timeout makes it more likely. This needs either per-key serialization or an explicit, documented eventual-consistency guarantee with tests.

Legacy update recomputes the change from its own state instead of writing the unified result

The base code wrapped the Storage.Update result in updateWrapper so the legacy store received exactly what unified storage produced. This version passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update. objInfo.UpdatedObject is then applied to the legacy store's current object, which can differ from the unified object (different resourceVersions, stored fields, defaults, or a patch applied against a different base). Both writes can succeed and the stores still diverge. The same objInfo is also consumed a second time after the first UpdatedObject call.

DeleteCollection records the legacy outcome in the storage metric

The goroutine calls recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy), so legacy delete-collection latency and failures are counted under the storage series, and the legacy histogram is never updated for this method. It should be recordLegacyDuration.

Unified storage failures are recorded as legacy failures

When the storage write fails, Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The failed unified write is counted in the legacy metrics and the storage error metric is never set, so storage error rates are under-reported and legacy stats are polluted.

Destroy tears down Legacy while fire-and-forget writes may still be running

Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but background legacy goroutines may still be executing against the legacy store. Those writes then run against a destroyed backend and fail or panic. Destroy has no way to wait for in-flight legacy writes.

Background legacy goroutines have no panic recovery

Legacy calls used to run on the request goroutine, where net/http recovers panics per request. The bare goroutines added here have no recover, so a panic in any legacy storage method crashes the whole Grafana process instead of failing one request.

Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write

Storage and Legacy share a single mock.Mock, so the test cannot tell which store was called. The tests never call AssertExpectations, so the legacy expectations set up in TestMode3_Create, _Update and _DeleteCollection are never checked. Nothing verifies that Legacy is called, or with what object, which is the core of this change. The background goroutine can also call the mock after the test returns, so those calls are not observed at all.

Legacy-side reads run immediately after writes that are now asynchronous

In mode 3, the k8s create at line 496 returns before its legacy write completes. getFromBothAPIs then reads the legacy endpoint right away (and the legacy list comparison around line 523 does the same). These checks race the background write and will be flaky. If the legacy endpoint is actually served from unified storage, the checks do not exercise the legacy write at all. Either way the assertion does not test what it claims without waiting or polling for the legacy write.

Test case name says List is not implemented, but it is

The case is named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented', but List is now implemented in this PR and the case only checks that a storage error is propagated. The name is misleading to future readers.

Create test name contradicts its setup

The case is named 'creating an object only in the unified store', but its setup registers a legacy Create expectation and the implementation writes to legacy as well. The name describes the old behavior.

Duplicate go.work.sum entry and unrelated checksum additions

The line 'github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery ... /go.mod' is added a second time, duplicating the entry immediately above it. The hunk also adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporters and genproto rpc), which this dual-writer change does not touch. These look like an accidental go mod tidy or merge artifact and should be removed or verified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list without a key

The grafana branch of the switch now renders <GrafanaRuleListItem> without a key prop, while the datasource and unknown branches still use key={key}. React emits 'unique key' warnings for this list. The component comment explicitly says the keys exist to prevent duplicates, so the removal looks accidental. Since rules are append-only today the visible impact is small, but row-level state is then keyed by index.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing React key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list, with potential rendering or row-state issues when list order changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence notifications menu item is a no-op in the list view

In the list view AlertRuleMenu now shows 'Silence notifications' when the Grafana promRule silence ability is true, and its handler `handleSilence` sets showSilenceDrawer=true. But the drawer is rendered only when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` (the ruler DTO) is always undefined in the list view after this PR. Clicking Silence therefore sets state and nothing appears. No test clicks this item, so the gap is not caught.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same list-view bug: silencing is offered based on Grafana Prom abilities, but clicking it only toggles state because the silence drawer requires a Grafana Ruler rule that is not provided.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete (and Pause) never render in the list view even though their abilities are computed from promRule

canDelete is now computed from the Grafana promRule abilities, but the Delete item is rendered only under `canDelete && rulerRule`. The list view no longer passes rulerRule (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule), so Delete never appears in the list-view menu. Pause has the same gating on line 123 (`rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`), so Pause also disappears. Before this PR both were available in the list view, and the new promRule-based ability code for them is effectively dead. The GrafanaGroupLoader test asserts exactly 4 menu items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), which locks in the missing Delete/Pause instead of catching the regression.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously derived isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) (source_tenants). It now delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. Federated groups therefore lose the immutability guard, so Update/Delete/Pause/DeletePermanently can be enabled for them. The isFederatedRuleGroup import was also dropped. This affects every caller of useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities, not only the list view.

Duplicate is offered for data-source rules via the Grafana-side fallback, bypassing ruler and datasource permission checks

For non-Grafana rules AlertRuleMenu passes skipToken to useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. With an undefined rule, useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets Duplicate to [AlwaysSupported, hasPermission(AlertingRuleCreate)] (useAbilities.ts line 318). canDuplicate ORs this with the ruler result, so Duplicate is shown for datasource-managed rules whenever the user holds the Grafana-wide create permission. This bypasses the ruler-availability check (duplicateSupported = isRulerAvailable) and the isPluginProvided check, and ignores the datasource's own write permission (AlertingRuleExternalWrite). The other OR'd actions (Edit, Delete, Silence, Export, Pause) are false on this path, so Duplicate is the only leak.

Rule view link drops the returnTo parameter

The previous GrafanaRuleLoader built the view href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo })` using createReturnTo(). The new GrafanaRuleListItem silently drops returnTo, so navigating from the list to the rule view and back no longer returns to the list context. This is unrelated to removing the ruler and appears accidental.

Every list row now evaluates both ruler and Grafana ability hooks, duplicating folder and silence-config subscriptions

AlertRuleMenu (and RuleActionsButtons.V2 the same way) now calls useRulerRuleAbilities and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities for each row. Each full evaluation calls useFolder, the Grafana alerting-config RTK query, and folder permission lookups. For Grafana rows the ruler evaluation runs with an undefined rule and contributes nothing useful, so each row ends up with about four full ability evaluations. The hook comment already warns about ~80 rows on the list page. Only the applicable hook should be invoked per row.

Doc comments still describe the removed ruler request

The component docstring says it loads 'from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', and the expectedRulesCount prop doc (line 19) says the ruler response may contain a different number of rules. After this change the component uses only the Prometheus endpoint, so both comments are wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ad-hoc filters are now passed on the sharded path and then applied again per subrequest

The removed call interpolateVariablesInQueries(request.targets, request.scopedVars) did not pass request.filters. The new applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters) does. The subRequest built at line 154 keeps the original request's filters, so runSplitQuery applies them again (querySplitting.ts line 299). If applyTemplateVariables applies ad-hoc filters to the expression, sharded queries get the filter matchers added twice, and that behavior change is not covered by any test, because the mock in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts ignores the third argument.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly notes that applyTemplateVariables receives request.filters as its third argument while the test mock ignores that argument, matching the golden comment's test-setup concern. Its additional double-application claim does not negate that match.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries are now split because the range check runs after interpolation

querySupportsSplitting() (line 287) exists so that queries containing $__range are not split, because $__range has to be evaluated against the full time range of the request. Before this change it saw the raw expression. Now runSplitQuery interpolates first (line 299) and partitions on the result (line 300). Any $__range that applyTemplateVariables resolves from request.scopedVars (Grafana supplies __range for panel queries) has already been replaced by a literal, so isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false and the query is split. Each time chunk then runs with the full-range literal as its window and combineResponses merges the chunks, which gives wrong results for range aggregations. No test in the PR covers this exclusion.

Shard path no longer drops targets whose expression interpolates to empty

The old code interpolated first and then filtered on expr, so a target whose expression is a variable expanding to an empty string was dropped. The filter now runs on the raw expression (line 50), before the map on line 52, so such targets survive. They are passed to runSplitQuery as a subrequest, where the empty expr is filtered out (querySplitting.ts line 298). If nothing is left, runSplitGroupedQueries reads requests.filter(...)[0].partition (querySplitting.ts line 96) on an empty array and throws a TypeError. On the sharded path that throw happens inside the groupTargetsByQueryType().then() callback, so the rejection is unhandled and the observable never emits. For example, a panel with a metric query plus a query like $q, where $q is empty, would hang instead of returning the metric results.

Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, so expressions that expand to empty are not dropped

The filter on line 298 checks query.expr before applyTemplateVariables runs on line 299. A target such as $query whose variable expands to an empty string passes the filter and goes to runQuery with an empty expr, which the backend will reject. If that target is the only one, the requests array ends up empty and runSplitGroupedQueries throws a TypeError at line 96. The empty check should run after the interpolation step, as the old shard code did.

Targets are interpolated twice on the sharded path

runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) already calls applyTemplateVariables on every target. Each shard subrequest is then passed to runSplitQuery, which calls applyTemplateVariables again on the already expanded expression (line 299) with the same scopedVars and filters. Expansion is not idempotent: if a variable value contains a $name token that matches a template variable, it gets expanded a second time and the query changes. The test change shows the redundancy: 'Interpolates queries before running' went from toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) to toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5), which codifies the repeated calls instead of removing them. Interpolation should happen once per request, with the sharded path skipping the second pass.

New interpolation test checks only runQuery arguments, not the splitting decisions

The added test asserts only the expr and step passed to runQuery. The point of the fix for #107530 is that interpolated values drive splitting: calculateStep reads query.step (used for metric partitioning) and querySupportsSplitting reads the expression. Nothing checks that a $step value changes the metric stepMs grouping, or that a $__range query is excluded from splitting after interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Limit check is a separate COUNT followed by a separate insert, so concurrent requests can exceed the limit

The check at lines 110-116 counts devices, then the insert/upsert runs later in a separate statement with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from different new devices can all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, so the stored device count can overshoot the configured limit by up to the number of concurrent requests. The limit is only soft under load. If it is meant to be strict, the check and insert must be atomic (for example a conditional insert within a transaction).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a separate device count check and then insert devices beyond the limit. Both recommend making the check and insert atomic using a transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device is admitted on its next request

tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry for the device before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and never removes it when the store fails. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate rejects the request, but the device key stays cached for the default 29-minute expiry. The device's next request hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds without any database record. A rejected device is therefore admitted on retry and stays admitted for up to ~29 minutes, so the configured device limit is not enforced for that device. The cache entry should only be set after a successful tag, or be deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, leaving the entry cached after ErrDeviceLimitReached and allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit for the 29-minute cache lifetime.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit keys off a client-supplied, unverified header

The device identity is the raw X-Grafana-Device-Id request header, accepted without any server-side verification. A client that sends a fresh ID on each request is counted as a new device every time, so the cap can be bypassed trivially. Clearing browser storage has the same effect. If the limit is meant to be enforced rather than advisory, the device identity needs a server-verifiable basis; otherwise the limit should be documented as not being a security control.

Device tagging moved from a background goroutine onto the synchronous auth path

Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so anonymous authentication never waited on the database. Now it runs inline with the request context. Each device that misses the local cache (the first request per device and again every ~29 minutes) performs a COUNT(*) over the 30-day window plus an upsert or update before the request can be authenticated. With many devices or a slow database this adds latency to those requests and holds request goroutines and DB connections. The cap check makes this worse because it adds a COUNT to the hot path. Consider keeping the non-blocking write for the normal path, or bounding the synchronous call with a timeout.

Tests only cover rejection of a new device at the limit, not the update path or the authentication flow

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a brand-new device is rejected when the table is at the limit. Not covered: (a) an existing in-window device being updated successfully while the limit is reached, which is the updateDevice success path; (b) devices outside the 30-day window not being counted; (c) TagDevice or Authenticate actually returning ErrDeviceLimitReached to the caller; (d) a rejected device retrying. The retry bug in impl.go (device cached after rejection) would be caught by a test that calls TagDevice twice for a rejected device.

RowsAffected()==0 used as 'device not found' is unreliable on MySQL

updateDevice treats RowsAffected()==0 as meaning the device is not in the window, and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. MySQL reports changed rows by default (unless clientFoundRows is set on the connection), so an UPDATE that sets the same client_ip and user_agent and a updated_at with the same second-precision value reports 0 even though the row matched. In that case an existing, legitimate device is wrongly rejected. The window is narrow (a same-second retag), so the impact is limited, but the check should not rely on affected rows on MySQL, for example by verifying existence with a SELECT.

New [auth.anonymous] device_limit option is undocumented

The new device_limit option is read here, but the PR does not touch conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini or the docs, and the docs checkbox in the PR description is unchecked. Operators cannot discover that 0 means unlimited, or that the limit counts devices seen within a rolling 30-day window.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded during web requests, not for background or console lookups

translate() only calls load_locale(config.locale). The fallback chain (default locale and :en) is loaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Outside a web request (background jobs such as Sidekiq email delivery, rake tasks, the console, or a process that has not served a request yet), I18n.locale is e.g. :fr, so only :fr translations are loaded. Fallbacks#translate then asks the Simple backend for :en or default-locale strings that were never loaded, and keys missing from the non-English locale come back as 'translation missing' instead of the English text. That is the exact case this feature is meant to fix. The fallback chain should be loaded from the translate path (for example by loading I18n.fallbacks[config.locale] here), not only from the controller filter.

LRU translation cache key ignores the fallback chain it now depends on

With fallbacks enabled, the value returned for (key, locale) depends on the fallback chain, which depends on SiteSetting.default_locale and on which fallback locales happen to be loaded at lookup time. The cache key is only key + config.locale + backend object_id, and nothing in this change invalidates entries when default_locale changes or when a fallback locale is loaded later. The first computed value, including a 'translation missing' string that is frozen and cached at line 75, is then served until LRU eviction (300 entries) or reload!.

Every I18n lookup now reads SiteSetting and allocates a fallback array

Fallbacks#translate, included into the backend at line 9, calls I18n.fallbacks[locale] on every lookup that reaches the backend. That means this method runs for every translation, including calls with interpolation arguments that bypass the LRU cache (translate_accelerator.rb line 69). Each call reads SiteSetting.default_locale and builds and uniq/compacts a new array. I18n previously had no dependency on SiteSetting, so any I18n.t during boot or in tasks where settings are not yet readable (asset precompile, migrations) can now trigger a SiteSetting load and hit the database. Memoizing the chain per (locale, default_locale) would remove both costs.

No specs cover the new fallback behavior or the load path

This change affects global translation behavior: a new fallback chain, the fallback backend module included globally, pluralization moved from pluralization.rb into this file, config.i18n.fallbacks removed from three environment files, and a new ensure_loaded! path in set_locale and the accelerator. The PR adds no specs. Nothing verifies that a key missing in a non-English locale resolves through the site default and then :en, that the fallback works when the fallback locale has not been loaded (the gap described in translate_accelerator.rb line 68), or that pluralization still works after the include was moved. A unit test for FallbackLocaleList#[] and a request spec exercising set_locale with a missing key would catch these regressions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted-attribute restriction for TL0 users

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), so for a TL0 user seen by an anonymous viewer (`scope.restrict_user_fields?`) the raw website URL is omitted. It contains the host and, when the host matches the forum, the full path, so the restricted URL is effectively exposed again. The 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' spec checks that bio, location, website and profile/card background are not serialized. The new `website_name` attribute is not in this list, so the spec does not catch the leak where a TL0 user's website host and path are serialized to anonymous viewers. Add `website_name` to this list and make the untrusted check cover it.

For a website such as `http://example.com/` on a forum at `example.com`, `URI(...).path` returns `"/"`, so `website_name` becomes `"example.com/"`. Users who type a bare domain with a trailing slash will see a stray slash that the previous client-side `split('/')[2]` logic did not produce. Consider stripping a bare `/` path, for example by treating a path of `/` as empty.

`URI(...).host` preserves the case typed by the user, while `Discourse.current_hostname` is normally lowercase. A website entered as `http://Example.com/user` on a forum at `example.com` fails the `==` test on line 141 and falls through to the else branch. The result is `Example.com` with no path, so the feature silently does not apply. Downcase both hosts before comparing, including in the `ends_with?` and sibling comparisons.

The branch on line 146 compares everything after the first label. For a forum at `y.co.uk` and a website at `x.co.uk/page`, both have three labels and the comparison yields `co.uk == co.uk`, so the full path is shown as if the website belonged to the forum's site. The heuristic does not account for public suffixes such as `co.uk` or `github.io`. `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is a substring test, not an origin comparison. Any sender whose origin is a prefix of the forum URL passes. With `discourseUrl = "https://community.example.com/"`, a page served from the registrable domain `https://community.example.co` has an origin that is a prefix, so `indexOf` returns 0 and the message is accepted. The handler also never checks `e.source === iframe.contentWindow`. The practical effect is that a lookalike site can resize the iframe, but the check is wrong. Compare the exact origin (scheme, host, port) of `discourseUrl` with `e.origin`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same security flaw: using indexOf substring matching for origin validation allows a malicious lookalike origin to bypass the check. The candidate gives a different bypass example and an additional source-check concern, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options 'ALLOWALL' is not a valid value and is ignored by browsers

Valid X-Frame-Options values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM. Browsers ignore unknown values, so this header does nothing; framing is permitted only because the browser ignores it. It also overwrites any X-Frame-Options set earlier in the request. If the intent is to allow framing from the configured host, use `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` with the embeddable host and remove this header.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that setting X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL leaves framing unrestricted and removes clickjacking protection. The candidate explains that browsers ignore the invalid value rather than treating it as an explicit allowance. Although it omits the referer-validation weaknesses, it identifies the same core security issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Imported-from footer interpolates the URL into HTML without escaping The footer is built as `I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")`. The URL comes from the feed link or id and is inserted unescaped into a body stored as raw HTML. A link such as `http://x.test/'>` injects markup. The URL check on line 11 uses `^`, which matches after any newline, so the scheme check is also weaker than intended. Escape the URL before interpolating it, and anchor the scheme check at the start of the string.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by interpolating an unescaped URL into the imported-from HTML footer. It does not mention the nil contents NoMethodError, but it directly matches the XSS issue in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dangling `if` modifier in `<%- end if %>` makes the embed template invalid

`<%- end if %>` closes the `if` opened on line 2 but leaves a stray `if` modifier with no condition. Once ERB compiles this, the result is not valid Ruby (the modifier is followed by the compiler's statement separator), so the `best` template fails whenever it is rendered. The intent is clearly `<%- end %>`. This breaks the main embed page for every request that finds an existing topic. The controller specs do not catch it because they never render views (no `render_views`), so a view or request spec is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify `<%- end if %>` as invalid Ruby/ERB that fails during rendering and specify replacing it with `<%- end %>` to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One bad feed item aborts the whole poll, and nil content raises NoMethodError

The `rss.items.each` loop has no per-item error handling. `i.content` can be nil for feed items that only supply a description, so `i.content.scrub` on line 35 raises NoMethodError. `i.title` can also be nil. `TopicEmbed.import` can raise too, for example when the URL exceeds 255 characters, or when the embed's post has been deleted. Any of these aborts the loop, and the job has `retry: false`, so nothing retries. The next hourly run reaches the same item and fails again, so every item after it is never imported. Guard nil content and title, and rescue and log errors per item.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that i.content may be nil for feeds providing only a description, causing i.content.scrub to raise NoMethodError. This matches the golden issue, despite additional concerns and a less specific mitigation.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed content is double-unescaped and stored as raw HTML, giving stored XSS on the forum

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` decodes entities that SimpleRSS has already decoded from the XML, so text meant to be shown literally (for example `&lt;img onerror=...&gt;` in the feed) becomes live markup. `TopicEmbed.import` then creates the post with `cook_method: raw_html` (topic_embed.rb:22). `Post#cook` returns `raw` directly (app/models/post.rb:133), which skips the Sanitize/PrettyText pipeline and the `after_post_cook` plugin filters. The embed view then renders `raw post.cooked` unescaped (app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19), and the same cooked HTML appears in the forum topic. A feed item containing a script or event-handler payload therefore runs on the forum origin for every visitor, including staff. Feed content is third-party data, so this crosses a trust boundary. Run imported content through the normal sanitizer before storing raw HTML, and remove the extra unescape.

PostCreator enqueues jobs inside an outer transaction that has not committed

`TopicEmbed.import` wraps `PostCreator#create` in `Topic.transaction`. `PostCreator#create` calls `enqueue_jobs` (which triggers `process_post` and `feature_topic_users`) before the outer transaction commits. PostCreator's own comment says jobs must be enqueued after the transaction because workers may start on uncommitted data. With Sidekiq, a `process_post` job can run before the post and the TopicEmbed row are visible, find nothing, or fail, so the post is never processed (oneboxes, image sizes, and so on). Enqueue after the outermost commit, or do not wrap the creator in an outer transaction.

Anonymous requests can force unlimited outbound fetches and full feed polls

For any unknown `embed_url`, each request enqueues a `retrieve_topic` job without checking the host (the controller only checks the referer). The only throttle is `retrieved:#{@embed_url}` in topic_retriever.rb:26-28, which runs inside the worker and is keyed on the exact URL string. An attacker can vary a query string to get a fresh key every time. Each new key causes an outbound HTTP fetch of the embeddable host, and when feed polling is enabled it runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` (topic_retriever.rb:41), which downloads and re-imports the entire feed. Nothing rate-limits the endpoint, so this is a cheap way to exhaust outbound bandwidth and Sidekiq capacity. Validate the host in the controller before enqueueing, throttle per normalized URL in the request path, and do not run a full feed poll from a request-driven job.

`force: true` on a new table migration drops any existing topic_embeds table

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` drops an existing `topic_embeds` table before creating it. A migration that creates a new table gains nothing from this option and makes it destructive: running it in an environment where the table already exists (a partially migrated database, or another branch that created the table) silently deletes every embed-to-topic mapping. The importer depends on those mappings to avoid duplicate topics. Remove `force: true`.

Unrelated migration gains `force: true`, which drops existing top_topics data if rerun

This change adds `force: true` to the `top_topics` table creation. It is unrelated to embedding. If the migration runs in an environment where `top_topics` already exists with data, the table and all its counters are dropped. If the schema needs changing, add a new migration instead of editing one that may already have run.

setnx followed by a separate expire can leave a throttle key with no TTL

`$redis.setnx` and `$redis.expire` are two separate commands. If the process dies or the connection drops between them, `retrieved:<url>` persists with no TTL. Non-staff users are then permanently throttled for that URL and it is never retried. Use one atomic command, `SET key 1 NX EX 60`.

Missing post for an existing embed causes NoMethodError on update

`post = embed.post` can be nil if the post was deleted. When the content hash differs, `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` raises NoMethodError on `@post.raw`. The stale embed row is never repaired, and in PollFeed this exception aborts the whole loop (poll_feed.rb:31), so every later item is skipped. Handle a missing post explicitly, for example by recreating the post or removing the stale embed.

Readability attribute whitelist does not restrict URL schemes

`attributes: %w[href src]` limits which attribute names survive, but it does not check URL schemes. A `<a href="javascript:...">` from the fetched page can survive into the body. That body is stored as raw_html (cook_method), so the link runs script on the forum when clicked. The source is the configured embeddable host, so exploiting this needs that site to be compromised or malicious, but the forum should not accept unsanitized HTML from it. Pass the output through the normal sanitizer with an allowed-scheme list.

embed_url is varchar(255) with no length check, so long URLs fail at insert

`t.string :embed_url` creates varchar(255) in PostgreSQL. The value comes from unauthenticated request params (embed_controller.rb:9) and from feed links, and nothing checks its length. A longer URL makes `TopicEmbed.create!` raise StatementInvalid after the page has been fetched and the post built. The transaction rolls back, and every retry fails the same way. Validate the length at the controller and model, or use a text column.

Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the entire posts table

On PostgreSQL releases before 11, `add_column` with a default and `null: false` rewrites the whole posts table while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. On a large forum, reads and writes to posts are blocked for the duration. Add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then add the default and NOT NULL constraint, or schedule the downtime explicitly.

The --category option is silently removed from the Disqus import CLI

Removing `method_option :category` means `thor disqus:import --category X` now fails with an unknown-option error, and imported topics no longer get a category. This is a breaking change to the command-line interface that the PR description does not mention. Restore the option or document the removal.

Disqus import now fetches every thread live with no error handling and duplicates comments on re-run

Replacing PostCreator with `TopicEmbed.import_remote` makes the import fetch each thread's live URL with `open(url).read`. There is no timeout, no rescue, and no per-thread handling, so one 404 or network error aborts the import midway. The `ensure` block restores settings, but earlier threads are already imported. Re-running the import also appends every comment again: `import` returns the existing post, and the loop keeps creating posts for it. Rescue per thread, and skip comment creation when the topic already existed.

`ruby-readability` and `simple-rss` are added unconditionally, and Rails 3 mode uses the same Gemfile with the default `Gemfile.lock`. Only `Gemfile_rails4.lock` is updated in this PR. In Rails 3 mode, `bundle install --deployment` or `--frozen` will fail because the lockfile is missing these gems. Update the Rails 3 lockfile too, or gate the gems by mode.

The example is titled 'is 404 without an embed_url' but only checks `should_not be_success`. It passes because the `ensure_embeddable` filter raises first when embeddable_host is unset, so `params.require` is never exercised. No spec renders the `best` or `loading` templates (no `render_views`), so a broken template like the one in best.html.erb:6 goes undetected. Add a request spec that checks the status code and renders the templates.

Every TopicRetriever example stubs the method under test, leaving the throttle and feed logic untested

Each example in the 'with a valid host' context stubs `retrieved_recently?` or `perform_retrieve`. The Redis throttle, the feed-first branch in `perform_retrieve` (topic_retriever.rb:40-43), the existing-embed early return, and `fetch_http` are never exercised. The most important behavior, that a second request within 60 seconds does not fetch again, has no coverage. Add examples that use a real or mock Redis and exercise `perform_retrieve` directly.

PollFeed import logic has no test coverage, only the gating conditions

The spec only checks when `poll_feed` is called and stubs `poll_feed` in the delegation example. The actual import path, including URL filtering, nil title or content handling, the `TopicEmbed.import` call per item, and the error behavior, is untested. That is the riskiest code in the feature (see the XSS and per-item abort findings above). Add examples that feed a sample RSS document through `poll_feed`.

Kernel#open is used on an admin-supplied URL

`SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Kernel#open. In Ruby 2.x, a string beginning with `|` is executed as a shell command rather than fetched. The setting is admin-only, so the exposure is limited, but the call should be explicit. Use `URI.parse(url).open` (open-uri) so only HTTP(S) fetches are possible.

String#scrub requires Ruby 2.1 or later

`String#scrub` was added in Ruby 2.1. If this application still targets Ruby 2.0 (as Discourse did in late 2013), every poll that reaches this line raises NoMethodError. Confirm the supported Ruby version, or use an encoding-safe alternative.

cook_method is accepted from any opts hash and can bypass sanitization

`setup_post` now copies `opts[:cook_method]` onto the post. Setting it to raw_html stores the body unsanitized, because `Post#cook` returns raw HTML directly. If any controller forwards request parameters into PostCreator, an API or web user could create raw_html posts. Check that user-facing controllers whitelist their params and never pass `cook_method`, or only honor it from trusted server-side callers.

Documented options list omits the new cook_method option

The header comment lists the accepted PostCreator options, but `cook_method`, which this PR adds and which changes how the body is rendered and sanitized, is not documented. Add it, with its accepted values and the fact that raw_html skips the sanitizer.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

The `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` lookup is replaced by a hardcoded 10 MB for every upload type. Consequences: images larger than max_image_size_kb now pass client validation up to 10 MB, and an admin who sets max_image_size_kb above 10 MB can never upload between 10 MB and that limit from the UI, so the setting above 10 MB has no effect. Attachments are now checked against 10 MB instead of max_attachment_size_kb, so attachments the admin has forbidden pass client validation. false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failures and never verifies the final size before uploading

The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize at most five times and then continues to Upload.create_for with whatever is in tempfile. Two problems. First, nothing re-checks tempfile.size against max_image_size_kb after the loop, so an image that is still over the limit is stored. Each pass scales both dimensions by 0.8 (pixel count by 0.64), so five passes leave about 11% of the original pixels, which is not enough for a large original. Second, downsize returns false when convert exits non-zero (convert_with does not log that case), and the return value is discarded. A failing conversion is retried five times on an unchanged file and the failure is invisible. On this path nothing enforces max_image_size_kb for uploaded images any more.

API URL downloads are now capped at a hardcoded 10 MB instead of max_image_size_kb

The download cap changes from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes to a hardcoded 10.megabytes. Consequences: (a) a site that sets max_image_size_kb above 10 MB can no longer fetch images between 10 MB and its own limit through the API URL path, which contradicts the setting; (b) the new downsizing cannot help images above 10 MB fetched by URL, which is the case the feature is for; (c) when FileHelper.download fails or exceeds the cap, the `rescue nil` leaves tempfile nil, and line 72 then calls `tempfile.size` on nil and raises NoMethodError, giving a 500 rather than a validation error. The 10 MB value is also duplicated in utilities.js with no shared source.

Up to five ImageMagick and ImageOptim passes per oversized upload, run inline on the synchronous API path

Each loop iteration runs a full convert pass, and convert_with also runs ImageOptim.new.optimize_image! on the output, so an oversized upload can cost five decode/encode cycles plus five optimizer runs. On the synchronous API path (`synchronous` param) this runs inline in the request and blocks the web worker for the duration. This code does not bound the input size: the client-side check is browser-only, the URL path cap is 10 MB, and the multipart path has no size check in this diff. A very large image makes every pass expensive.

Downsizing writes in place to the uploaded file, so a failed pass can corrupt the only copy

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with the same path as input and output, so ImageMagick overwrites the uploaded file in place. If a pass fails partway (disk full, process killed, ImageMagick error during write), the file is left truncated or corrupt. Because the return value is ignored (see the loop above), the damaged file is then passed to Upload.create_for. Writing to a separate temp file and replacing the original only on success would avoid this.

Oversized animated GIFs are flattened to their first frame when allow_animated_thumbnails is off

The loop reuses the thumbnail setting `allow_animated_thumbnails` for the user's original upload. When that setting is off, OptimizedImage.optimize uses downsize_instructions, which reads `#{from}[0]`, so an oversized animated GIF is replaced by a static first frame. The animation is lost permanently in the stored upload, and the user is not told. This may be intended, but it is not documented or surfaced anywhere in the PR.

No specs for the changed downsize/optimize signatures or the new upload downsizing path

The PR changes the signatures of optimize, resize and downsize, removes the public OptimizedImage.dimensions helper, and adds a loop in UploadsController#create_upload. Such an override then falls through to the overlap comparisons, where a slot starting exactly at the override start is treated as inside the override and returned as available (line 133). true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: comparing distinct Dayjs objects with === checks reference identity rather than date values, making the equality check always false. Both recommend using .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, once a slot falls inside a date override, the function returns true at line 134 before reaching the busy.every(...) check at line 153. The busy array holds the host's existing Cal bookings and calendar events. For any fixed or round-robin host with a date override covering the slot, a booking or external calendar event at that time is ignored and the slot is still offered. Before this PR the busy check always ran for fixed hosts, so this is a regression that can produce double bookings on exactly the days that have date overrides. The override should only decide the working-hours question; the slot should still fall through to the busy check.

Working-hours check rejects slots that fall in a second same-day range

workingHours.find(...) returns truthy as soon as any entry for the weekday does not contain the slot (the if at line 143 returns true for any entry where the slot is before its start or after its end). Users commonly have several availability rows for one weekday (split shifts such as 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, or a lunch break). A 14:00 slot is then rejected because the 09:00-12:00 entry does not contain it. This affects fixed hosts in individual events and fixed/round-robin hosts in team events, and removes roughly half of a split-shift user's slots. The logic should be: reject only if no entry for that day contains the slot. Also, a weekday with no entries (a day off) passes this check unchecked because find never matches, so the check does not enforce the intent stated in its comment.

Two date-override ranges on the same day make every slot on that day unavailable

dateOverrides.find(...) returns true for the first same-day override that does not contain the slot (the returns at lines 115, 121 and 124). The outer check then treats this as 'slot is outside the override' and returns false at line 130. The predicate never asks whether some other override on that day contains the slot. With two override rows for one date, for example 14:00-15:00 and 16:00-17:00 (the data model allows multiple date-override rows per date), a 14:00 slot is rejected because the 16:00 override does not contain it, and a 16:00 slot is rejected because the 14:00 override does not contain it. All slots on that day disappear for that host. The check should be whether some same-day override contains the slot (some, not find-with-rejection).

Override day matching mixes server-local and UTC dates and can attach an override to the wrong day

The override's day is computed as dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD'). dayjs(date.start) is in the server process's local timezone, while the slot side, slotStartTime.format(...), is in UTC (time.utc()). On a server whose TZ is not UTC the two sides use different calendars, so the override may match the wrong day or none. Separately, the day is taken from the UTC date of the shifted instant rather than the organizer's local date. An override at 02:00 on 22 Jan in Asia/Kolkata becomes 20:30Z on 21 Jan, so it also rejects the organizer's daytime 21 Jan slots (for example 09:30 IST), which have no override. Day matching should be done on organizer-local dates for both the override and the slot.

Override UTC offset is taken at the wall-clock-as-UTC instant, so it is off by an hour on DST-change days

Overrides are stored as organizer wall-clock time encoded as UTC. The offset is computed with dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone) at that encoded instant, which can differ from the real instant by up to 14 hours. When the encoded instant and the real instant fall on opposite sides of a DST transition, the wrong offset is used. Example: America/New_York override at 03:30 on 2023-03-12 (already on EDT). The encoded instant 03:30Z is before the 07:00Z switch, so offset -5 is used, and the bound becomes 08:30Z instead of 07:30Z. The same pattern is used in packages/lib/slots.ts lines 212-213, so the lib and the trpc check share the error.

packages/types/schedule.d.ts now declares TimeRange.timeZone as optional, and this code passes override.timeZone straight into .tz(...) with no guard. If a caller omits it, dayjs falls back to the process's local timezone with no error. Offsets are then computed for the server's zone rather than the organizer's, and slots are shifted silently. The caller contract should be made explicit (required parameter, or an explicit guard and fallback).

The only new test is a second timezone assertion on a single-user event with hosts: []. Nothing covers the headline fix, a round-robin event where a fixed host has a date override, so the fixed-host path in getSchedule is never exercised with overrides. Nothing covers busy bookings or calendar events that fall inside a date override (which would catch the busy-check bypass). Nothing covers two override rows on the same date, or split same-day working hours, or a slot that runs past the end of working hours. The existing suite therefore passes with all of these defects present. Tests for each of these should be added.

On the next call, googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) in googleAuth (line 75) finds no top-level access_token/refresh_token and throws, so Google Calendar stops working for that user after the first hourly refresh. Callers are written against the latter: Google reads res?.data (line 94 of googlecalendar CalendarService), and a fetch Response has no .data, so token.access_token throws. The catch swallows that and the stale access token is used silently. zoho-bigin and zohocrm read tokenInfo.data.error / .data.expiryDate on the result and throw TypeError. Hubspot treats it as a token object. Also response.ok is not checked, so a 500 HTML page is passed on as if it were tokens, and there is no timeout, so a hung endpoint blocks every calendar or video call for that user. true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

Zoho Bigin passes the credential id as the Cal.com userId to the sync endpoint

In sync mode the endpoint is asked for tokens of user <credential row id>, which is not necessarily the credential's owner. The returned tokens are then written into this credential (lines 102-109), which can attach another user's Zoho tokens to this user's credential. true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
