Salesforce refresh checks response.statusText === 'OK' instead of response.ok

statusText is the HTTP reason phrase. It is not defined for HTTP/2 responses and is often empty, so a successful refresh can be rejected. The thrown HttpError also reports statusText with a fixed 400 regardless of the real status, and the response body (which contains Salesforce's error_description) is never read. Check response.ok and include the status and error body in the error.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: checking response.statusText rather than response.ok when handling Salesforce OAuth token refresh responses, which can incorrectly reject successful refreshes. The additional error-handling concerns do not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid payloads and undecryptable keys surface as unhandled 500s

appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws a ZodError on malformed input (line 31). symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse (lines 57-59) throw on a wrong key or non-JSON plaintext. None are caught, so the caller gets a 500 with a stack trace in logs instead of a 400, and a self-hoster's retry logic will treat client errors as server failures. Use safeParse and wrap decryption and parsing, returning 400.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same issue: appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws on invalid payloads without being caught, causing 500 responses instead of 400 responses. Its additional concerns about decryption and JSON parsing do not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Helper both throws on failure and returns a SafeParse result, so callers' .success checks are dead

On schema failure this throws, yet on success it returns the safeParse wrapper. Callers that check `!parsed.success` (Zoom VideoApiAdapter around line 108, Salesforce around line 92) can never reach that branch, and the error text is generic. Office365 previously logged the provider's response on schema failure; that logging was removed in this PR, so the provider error is now lost. Pick one contract: return the parsed data or throw.

HubSpot refresh writes the sync Response object into the credential key

In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response. hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn is then undefined, so expiryDate becomes NaN (line 192), and line 198 stores the Response instance as the credential key. A Response does not carry the token fields as enumerable properties, so the stored key either becomes an empty or garbage object (losing accessToken and refreshToken) or the update fails. The catch at lines 203-205 only logs, so nothing surfaces. The HubspotToken annotation on line 177 hides the mismatch from the type checker.

Zoom refresh sends appSlug 'zoomvideo' but the Zoom app slug is 'zoom'

Zoom credentials are created with appId 'zoom' (zoomvideo/api/callback.ts line 73), and the webhook resolves app slugs the same way. Here refreshOAuthTokens is called with 'zoomvideo', the directory name rather than the app slug. A self-hoster's sync endpoint keyed on appSlug will not recognize it or will look up the wrong app. Use 'zoom'.

Salesforce CalendarService uses prisma without importing it

The new refresh code calls prisma.credential.update (line 96), but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript compile error, and at runtime constructing the client throws a ReferenceError, so every Salesforce calendar operation (contact search, event creation, availability) fails for all users. Add the import.

Salesforce refreshes its token on every client construction, bypassing the sync endpoint

getClient now posts to login.salesforce.com and writes the credential row on every CalendarService construction, even when the stored access token is still valid. Each calendar operation therefore costs an extra network round trip and a DB write, and concurrent operations each refresh and overwrite the same row. The refresh also goes directly to Salesforce with the Cal.com consumer secret and does not use refreshOAuthTokens, so with CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set Salesforce still refreshes on its own, contrary to the sync design. Refresh only when the token is expired and route it through refreshOAuthTokens.

Webhook secret compared with !== instead of a constant-time comparison

The shared webhook secret is checked with plain string inequality, which short-circuits at the first differing byte and leaks timing information. For an authentication check on a network endpoint, compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers (for example, hash both values first).

Concurrent deliveries can create duplicate credentials for the same user and app

The handler does findFirst (line 62) then create (line 83) with no transaction or lock. Two deliveries for the same user and app can both see no row and both create one, unless the schema has a unique constraint on (userId, appId), which this PR does not add. Later lookups that take the first matching credential may then pick a row that is not the one just synced.

Sync update leaves a credential flagged invalid even after fresh tokens arrive

Refresh failure paths set invalid: true on the credential (for example googlecalendar CalendarService lines 112-118 on invalid_grant, and Webex/Zoom invalidateCredential). The update branch here only writes key (lines 73-80), so after the self-hoster pushes fresh tokens the credential stays flagged invalid and remains unusable in code paths that check the flag. Clear invalid on update.

Documented sync response contract is narrower than what the callers read

The comment says the endpoint should return only the access token and expiry date, but callers read more. Google reads expiry_date. Hubspot reads expiresIn. Zoom, Webex and Office365 video read expires_in, and Office365 video stores the whole response as the credential key. Lark parses a {code, data} envelope and needs refresh_token and refresh_expires_in. Following the comment gives NaN expiry, or in Office365 video expiry_date = now (line 84), which forces a sync call on every request, and loses refresh tokens. The actual contract (field names, units, envelope) should be documented, for example next to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT in .env.example (line 240, currently undocumented). The PR description also says docs are required, but none are included.

No tests for the webhook, the sync refresh path, or the schema helper

The PR adds a webhook that writes credentials, a refresh indirection touching about twelve integrations, and a new schema helper, and the PR description says no tests were added. Several defects above (wrapper stored as the key, stripped fields, placeholder refresh token, wrong userId, missing prisma import) would be caught by unit tests of parseRefreshTokenResponse and refreshOAuthTokens with sync on and off, and by webhook tests for auth, validation and create/update.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cancellation flag write is fire-and-forget, so the reminder's fate is not guaranteed

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is async, but it is called without `await` here (and the same pattern appears in bookings.tsx line 490 and workflows.tsx). The `cancelled: true` UPDATE that now decides whether the reminder is sent may not complete before the handler returns, and on a serverless runtime the process can be frozen after the response. Errors are swallowed inside the helper's try/catch, so a failed write leaves the booking cancelled with no record that its reminder must be stopped, and nothing retries it. The helper's result should be awaited and failures surfaced or retried.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: async reminder deletion/cancellation helpers are called without await in booking and workflow handlers, so cancellation may not complete and scheduled reminders can remain active. Its focus on email reminders and additional failure details do not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Immediate cancel path reuses the call that hits SendGrid's 100-pending-cancellation cap

The `immediateDelete` branch sends `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid's `/v3/user/scheduled_sends`. The PR description identifies this exact mechanism as the root cause: each cancelled send stays pending until its scheduled date, and once 100 are pending new cancels fail while the emails are still sent. This branch is used for rescheduling (handleNewBooking.ts line 968), workflow deletion (workflows.tsx line 214) and step deletion (workflows.tsx line 521), which can cancel many reminders at once. When the cap is hit, the error is swallowed by the catch at the bottom of the function, so the reminders are silently still sent. The branch also returns without touching the DB row, so the reminder keeps `scheduled: true` and a `referenceId` pointing at a cancelled batch until its scheduled date passes. The name `immediateDelete` is also misleading because the row is not deleted. These paths should use the same deferred `cancelled` flag and cron-based cancellation as the rest of the PR.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the immediateDelete branch leaves the WorkflowReminder database row untouched rather than deleting it, and uses SendGrid cancellation instead of deletion. These match the golden issue, despite the candidate emphasizing cancellation limits and recommending a different remedy.

false_positives.candidate:
Paid-booking cancellation returns before workflow reminders are cancelled

For a paid booking the handler takes the `bookingToDelete.paid` branch (starts at line 363), refunds, sets status REJECTED, and returns at this line. The workflow reminder cancellation block (lines 484-493) and the zapier `cancelScheduledJobs` call come after this return, so they never run for paid bookings. The booking is cancelled, but its scheduled BEFORE_EVENT email and SMS reminders are still sent, which is the exact bug this PR is meant to fix. The same gap exists at line 437 (`return null` when the payment service is not implemented), and any throw between the status update at line 255 and line 484 leaves reminders uncancelled. Reminder cancellation should happen before the paid branch, or be duplicated into it.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and skips all deletes

The loop awaits `client.request` for every cancelled reminder inside a single try block. If any call throws (for example SendGrid rejects a batch that was already sent or already cancelled), the catch at lines 75-77 runs and the loop is abandoned, so the remaining reminders in the window are never cancelled. Also, `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` returns a lazy PrismaPromise that only executes when awaited in `Promise.all` at line 74. Because that await is never reached after an error, the deletes for reminders already cancelled earlier in the loop never run either. Those rows keep `cancelled: true`, and the next cron run (about 15 minutes later) hits the same failing reminder first. A single bad batch therefore blocks cancellation of every other reminder in its one-hour window, and emails for cancelled bookings still go out. Each cancel should be isolated (try/catch per reminder), and the delete should be awaited right after its own successful cancel.

SMS reminder row is only deleted if the Twilio cancel succeeds

The Prisma `workflowReminder.delete` runs after `twilio.cancelSMS` in the same try block. If Twilio throws (for example because the message is already sent or no longer cancellable), the delete is skipped and the error is only logged. Before this change the callers deleted the row regardless of the Twilio result, so this is a regression: the row keeps `scheduled: true` and its `referenceId`. The row deletion should not depend on the external cancel succeeding.

Cron endpoint authorizes everyone when CRON_API_KEY is unset

If `CRON_API_KEY` is not configured and the request has neither an `authorization` header nor an `apiKey` query parameter, `apiKey` is `undefined` and the check `process.env.CRON_API_KEY !== apiKey` evaluates to `undefined !== undefined`, which is false, so the request proceeds. This is pre-existing, but the endpoint now also cancels SendGrid sends and deletes reminder rows, so an unauthenticated caller on a misconfigured deployment can trigger those side effects. The handler should reject when the key is missing.

Unrelated UI restructuring bundled into a reminder-cancellation fix

The condition changes from `(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded)` to `isPhoneNumberNeeded` and the phone block is unwrapped. This changes rendering for SMS_ATTENDEE steps, which no longer get an empty padded container. Nothing in the PR description or title mentions this UI change, and it is unrelated to cancelling reminders. It should be split into its own PR or described explicitly.

New cancel-and-delete cron logic and cancelled flag have no tests

The PR changes cancellation semantics across handleCancelBooking, bookings.tsx, handleNewBooking and workflows.tsx, adds a `cancelled` column with a migration, and adds a cron branch that calls SendGrid and deletes rows. None of this is covered by a test in the diff. The previous fix shipped broken with the failure silently swallowed. At minimum, tests should cover: a cancelled reminder inside the one-hour window being cancelled and deleted; a SendGrid failure for one reminder not blocking the others; and a paid booking's reminders being cancelled.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, so a caller must be both admin and owner. A team admin who is not the owner fails the check and gets FORBIDDEN, even though the UI shows the 'additional guests' action to them. The intended check is an OR of the two conditions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same permission-check bug: using AND requires the user to be both a team admin and owner, while OR should allow either role.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

Existing attendees who were re-submitted get the new-booking email

The handler passes the raw `guests` input (line 168 of addGuests.handler.ts) instead of the filtered `uniqueGuests`. Here, `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)` therefore matches existing attendees who were in the request, and they receive a full AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of the 'guests added' notice. The function should receive only the newly created guests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same email-classification bug: newGuests contains the raw input guests rather than only newly added guests, so existing attendees included in the request match newGuests.includes(attendee.email) and incorrectly receive AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate guests in one request, or case-variant duplicates, create duplicate attendee rows

The filter on lines 74-78 only removes guests already present in `booking.attendees` (exact, case-sensitive match). It does not dedupe within `guests` itself, and the server schema does not enforce uniqueness, so the same email sent twice passes and both copies go into `createMany` on line 102. Case variants such as `Bob@x.com` and `bob@x.com` are also both inserted. The result is duplicate attendee rows and duplicate invites. The uniqueness rule is enforced only in the client dialog.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the guest filter excludes existing attendees but fails to deduplicate repeated emails within the request, allowing createMany to insert duplicate attendee rows. The candidate's additional case-variant concern does not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores eventType disableStandardEmails metadata

Every other send function in this file gates host and attendee emails on `eventTypeDisableHostEmail(eventTypeMetadata)` / `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail(eventTypeMetadata)`. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata and always sends to organizers, team members, and attendees. The handler also does not pass the event type metadata. Organizers who disabled standard emails for this event type will still receive add-guest emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor EventType metadata flags disabling standard emails, causing host or attendee emails to be sent despite those settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Guests array has no size limit; any attendee can mass-mail arbitrary addresses

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no max length and no per-user rate limit. Each new guest receives a calendar invite and an email containing booking details, and the handler also sends an email to every existing attendee. Any authenticated user who is merely an attendee (the handler allows `isAttendee`) can send a single request with thousands of addresses to third parties through the platform's mail infrastructure, with no cap.

Guests are persisted before calendar sync, and calendar failure is unhandled

The attendees are written to the DB at lines 92-106. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` at line 165 is not wrapped in try/catch, unlike the email call. If the calendar update throws, the request fails after the guests were saved, and no invites are sent. A retry then hits the dedupe check on lines 74-81 and returns BAD_REQUEST, so the user cannot recover without manual DB cleanup. The writes should be ordered or wrapped so that a calendar failure does not leave persisted guests with no invite.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

`getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` returns the calling user's credentials, and the `EventManager` is built from them. When a team admin or an attendee (not the organizer) adds guests, the calendar event belongs to the organizer's connected calendar, so `updateCalendarAttendees` runs against the wrong account's credentials and either fails or does not update the organizer's event. The organizer's credentials are loaded on line 38 (`booking.user.credentials`) but never used.

No check on booking status or time; guests can be added to cancelled or past bookings

After the booking is loaded, the handler only checks existence and permissions. It never checks whether the booking is cancelled or rejected, or whether it has ended. A direct API call can add attendees and send calendar invites for a cancelled booking, which effectively reactivates it on the guest's calendar. The UI hides this action for cancelled bookings, but the server does not enforce it.

Email failure is logged with console.log and the error object is dropped

The catch block logs the constant string 'Error sending AddGuestsEmails' and discards `err`, so the failure cause is unrecoverable from logs. It should use the project logger and include the error. Swallowing the error is intentional, but the diagnostic detail should not be lost.

Misleading error when all guests are already attendees or blacklisted

When every submitted guest is already an attendee or on the blacklist, the handler throws BAD_REQUEST with message 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' ('Emails must be unique and valid'). That message does not explain the real cause. Blacklisted addresses are dropped silently, and the user is told their emails are invalid even when they are valid and simply already present.

Error toast shows raw error code, and the fallback is dead code

`message` is built as `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`, which always yields a non-empty string, so `message || t('unable_to_add_guests')` on line 44 never uses the fallback. The user sees raw tRPC codes such as 'FORBIDDEN: you_do_not_have_permission'. If `err.data` is missing, the toast starts with 'undefined:'. The toast should show the translated message, with the fallback used when it is absent.

Validation error flag is never cleared, so it persists after the user fixes input

`setIsInvalidEmail(true)` is called on validation failure, but it is only reset by the Cancel button. After a successful add, or after the dialog is closed via the overlay or X button, the 'Emails must be unique and valid' message is still shown the next time the dialog opens. The flag should be cleared on success and on open/close.

Hardcoded English tooltip text is not translated

`<Tooltip content="Remove email">` is a hardcoded English string in a shared UI component that elsewhere uses `t(...)` for all user-facing text (for example the 'Add another' button). Non-English users see English here, so it should use a translation key added to common.json.

No tests for a new permission-gated mutation with dedupe and email logic

The PR adds a mutation with authorization rules (organizer, team admin/owner, attendee), blacklist and duplicate filtering, calendar sync, and email fan-out, but no unit or integration tests. The permission `&&` bug and the duplicate-insertion problem would likely be caught by even basic tests of the handler's branches.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is an unlocked read-modify-write, allowing double use and restoration of spent codes

The code is read and checked at lines 139-145, then the entire array is rewritten at line 149 with no transaction, lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent logins using the same code can both pass indexOf before either write lands, so one backup code can be spent twice. Concurrent logins with different codes also race: each writes back its own copy of the array, so the later write can restore a code the other request already nulled. Use an atomic compare-and-swap on the stored value (or a transaction with row locking) so that consumption is single-use.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition in backup-code consumption: concurrent requests can read the same unused code and both accept it before the modified array is persisted, violating one-time-use semantics. The candidate also describes a related lost-update consequence.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plaintext backup codes and blob URL persist in component state after the dialog closes

resetState() clears password and step but not backupCodes or backupCodesUrl. After the dialog is closed, the plaintext recovery codes stay in React state, and the blob URL that encodes them is never revoked on close (it is only revoked on the next setup call). Clear the codes and revoke the URL when the dialog closes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify missing cleanup of the backup-code object URL, allowing it to persist and potentially leak memory. The candidate focuses on dialog closure rather than component unmount and additionally flags plaintext retention, but the underlying URL lifecycle issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Password check skipped whenever totpCode is non-empty, which also bypasses it for the new backup-code path

The password verification is gated by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`, so any non-empty totpCode skips the password check entirely. The new backup-code branch (line 131) runs whenever credentials.backupCode is non-empty, regardless of totpCode. A request with a valid email, a valid backup code, and any non-empty totpCode (for example 'x') logs in without the password ever being verified. Backup codes are meant to replace only the second factor, but this turns them into a single-factor credential (email plus a 40-bit code). The same gap already exists for TOTP, but this PR adds a new route that depends on it. Password verification should not be skippable by supplying an unrelated second-factor field.

Users who reach 2FA via Google/SAML cannot use backup codes at all

When 2FA is triggered after an OAuth/SAML sign-in (totpEmail set), the footer is ExternalTotpFooter, which only has a Cancel button, so the 'Lost access' toggle is never rendered. Even if the UI were reachable, authorize() in next-auth-options.ts (lines 113-115) throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled for non-CAL users when totpCode is empty, so a backupCode-only submission is always rejected for these users. Users who sign in with Google or SAML and lose their authenticator therefore have no recovery path on the login page. Every paginated page's Seer summary includes all error events of the replay

The endpoint paginates over recording segments and calls analyze_recording_segments once per page, passing the replay-wide error_events list each time. gen_request_data restarts error_idx at 0 for every page, and this trailing loop yields every error not yet consumed. Each page's Seer request therefore contains every error in the replay, including errors whose timestamps fall in other pages, so the same errors are repeated across page summaries. The new tests only exercise a single page with one error, so they pass despite this.

Error IDs are paired with nodestore results by position, not by key

nodestore.backend.get_multi returns a mapping keyed by node id that omits missing nodes, and its order is not guaranteed to match error_ids. zip(error_ids, events.values()) pairs each error id with whatever value comes next in the mapping. When any error's nodestore entry is missing (for example after retention expiry), every later error gets the title, message and timestamp of a different event. The 'data is not None' filter runs after the misalignment, so it does not prevent this. Each id should be looked up in the returned mapping.

Exceptions from blob deletes are silently discarded

pool.map returns a lazy iterator and its result is never consumed, so any exception raised by storage_kv.delete other than NotFound is never re-raised. The with-block only waits for completion. A failed blob delete (permissions, network error) produces no log or metric, and delete_replays then archives the replay anyway, leaving orphaned recording blobs with no trace. Consume the results (for example list(pool.map(...))) or submit futures and check their exceptions. This is pre-existing, but it is in a file this PR touches.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES is only applied when a search query is entered

The early return when searchQuery is empty returns the sorted list without applying the HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter. The filter only runs when the user types a search. With the default empty search, is_segment, project_id and received are shown, but they disappear as soon as any search is typed. The hidden-attribute rule should apply in both cases.

Comment points to a replacement migration that is not part of this change

The no-op body says the correct migration is 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py, but no such file appears in the changed files. 0917 and 0920 are both replaced with no-ops, and the 0917 test is deleted. If the replacement is not in this PR, org-level saved searches will never be converted into GroupSearchView rows, and the comment misleads readers. Either add the replacement or correct the reference.

Summary card renders with empty content when the API returns no summary

useFeedbackSummary returns summary as string or null. tooFewFeedbacks is only true when numFeedbacksUsed is 0 and success is false. If feedbacks were used but the LLM call failed (success false, summary null), this component still renders the 'Feedback Summary' header with an empty paragraph. The component should return null when summary is null.

Unescaped issue title is placed inside a markdown link in PR comments

The template renders '[**{title}**]({url})' with the raw issue title. Titles derive from error messages, which can be influenced by application input. A title containing ']' followed by '(' closes the link text early and lets the remaining text form an arbitrary link destination in a comment the Sentry bot posts on the PR. The environment name is also interpolated raw inside backticks. The title should be escaped or sanitized before interpolation.

Recommended event is loaded from nodestore for every issue in every PR comment

get_environment_info calls issue.get_recommended_event() and then get_environment() for each of up to five issues per comment. Each call does a nodestore fetch and a DB lookup, and this runs on every PR comment build. The environment could be fetched in a batch, or cached per issue.

Title truncation and environment formatting have no test coverage

The new _truncate_title path (titles longer than 50 characters get an ellipsis) and the non-empty environment suffix in get_environment_info are not exercised by the GitHub or GitLab PR comment tests. The existing tests use short titles and only check the happy path. A regression in truncation or the environment suffix would not be caught.

Default autofix tuning changed from low to off for every project without an explicit setting

Changing DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT (and the matching projectoptions default) to off changes live behavior for every project that never set sentry:autofix_automation_tuning, with no migration, backfill or release note. The tests were only updated to match the new default. This should be called out explicitly or handled with a data migration.

Environment filter silently dropped from the attribute keys request

The previous useTraceItemAttributeKeys sent environment: selection.environments to the trace-items attributes endpoint. The new makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions omits it and says it is intentionally unsupported, which contradicts the prior behavior. Attribute keys from every environment are now returned, which is a silent behavior change.

Analytics event name changed, breaking continuity of the View HTML metric

The trackAnalytics call for the View HTML click was renamed from replay.view_html to replay.view-html. Existing dashboards and queries keyed on the old name will stop receiving data for this action. The rename should be noted, or the old name kept for continuity.

Snuba query and nodestore fetch run on every page request, even when error context is disabled

The endpoint runs query_replay_instance and fetch_error_details before paginate, so both run on every paginated request, not once per replay. The Snuba query also runs when enable_error_context=false, where its result is discarded except for error_ids that are then ignored. Error details should be fetched once per replay or skipped when disabled.

A bug in the code path that fills every issued token id would not be caught by these tests.

Access token jti is no longer a UUID for every access token, with no compatibility note

initToken now sets the access token jti to a value like 'onrtac:<uuid>' instead of a plain UUID. Any consumer, event listener or client that validates or parses jti as a UUID will break. The PR does not document this as a change to the token format or mention a compatibility impact, and the only test updates are in AssertEvents. Other token-exchange providers that issue access tokens through the same TokenManager responseBuilder path do not set the attribute. Their token ids encode the grant as 'na' (UNKNOWN), even though the grant being served is token-exchange. That undermines the grant-type purpose the PR states for the token-exchange use case. The public copy constructor Context(Context) is deleted in this PR. The change is unrelated to the feature and is not mentioned in the description. Any external grant implementation that calls it will fail to compile. If the removal is intentional, it should be called out, or the constructor should be kept and deprecated.

Plaintext recovery codes are persisted in user storage

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes into a JSON array and passes that as the credential value to user storage via updateCredential. The local path does not do this: RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode and verifyRecoveryCodeInput (which compares against a hashed saved code) show that local storage keeps only hashes. Recovery codes act as a second factor that bypasses OTP/WebAuthn, so after this change they sit in plaintext in whatever external store backs the user storage (LDAP attribute, external DB). Anyone with read access to that store can obtain usable recovery codes for the user. The codes should be hashed before leaving Keycloak, or the trade-off should be explicitly justified and documented.

Exhausted federated recovery-code credential is never removed

getCredential now returns credentials from user storage first. When all codes are used, this calls removeStoredCredentialById with the id of that credential. removeStoredCredentialById only operates on the local store (and on user-storage providers that implement UserCredentialStore). For a federated credential the call is a silent no-op, so the spent credential stays in user storage. The CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is still added, but the spent credential is not cleaned up for user-storage-backed users. The test provider does not implement UserCredentialStore and keeps returning the credential. No test covers this path.

Undocumented, asymmetric data format for user-storage recovery codes

updateCredential receives a JSON array of raw codes (CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential). But getCredential passes whatever the provider returns from getCredentials into RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel (RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator around line 83 and RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean line 19), which expects the local serialized model. The test provider has to convert its stored list via createFromValues inside getCredentials to make this work. Nothing documents this contract for SPI implementers. A provider that returns the stored credential data unchanged, the natural round trip, will likely fail to parse at login or make the login bean throw.

Reference provider never consumes recovery codes; single-use is untested

The recovery branch of isValid returns true for any stored code and never removes or marks it as used, so this reference provider accepts the same recovery code indefinitely. The new test logs in once with code 0 and never checks that a reused code is rejected or that the next login asks for a different code. Single-use behaviour for user-storage recovery codes is therefore untested, and the provider silently demonstrates the wrong semantics for anyone copying it.

Class Javadoc claims this is an unchanged 4.8.3 fixture

The Javadoc says this is the Keycloak 4.8.3 implementation and that future versions should work without any change to this provider. This PR adds recovery-code support to the class, a credential type 4.8.3 never had. The comment is now wrong, and the class no longer serves as a frozen 4.8.3 compatibility baseline.

Switching to user storage leaves stale local recovery-code credentials

When updateCredential succeeds, the local recovery-codes credential is not removed. getCredential then prefers the federated credential, so any previously created local set becomes unreachable for authentication, but it remains in the local store and in stored-credential listings. Regenerating codes after user storage starts supporting the type leaves duplicate, dead recovery credentials.

This method is inconsistent with that and lets an explicit deny be bypassed. No test covers a per-client deny on top of an all-clients VIEW grant.

Before this PR MgmtPermissionsV2 inherited clients() from MgmtPermissions, so setPermissionsEnabled worked. Now clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled (and isPermissionsEnabled) throw UnsupportedOperationException. AdminPermissions.registerListener calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on every ClientRemovedEvent, and management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 when the V2 flag is on. When the listener is active (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ enabled alongside V2), deleting any client throws during event dispatch and the deletion request fails.

V2 branch of the 4-arg evaluator() drops the target realm

In the V2 branch, evaluator(session, realm, adminsRealm, admin) calls new MgmtPermissionsV2(session, adminsRealm, admin) and never passes realm, although MgmtPermissionsV2 has a 4-argument constructor (session, realm, adminsRealm, admin) that carries it. The V1 branch passes realm. This PR makes MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() build ClientPermissionsV2 from the realm field. Client permission checks made through this factory may therefore be evaluated against the admin's realm rather than the target realm, depending on what the 3-argument constructor assigns to realm.

Type-level grant is ignored when a per-client resource exists, contradicting the documented 'also if' contract

hasPermission(client, scope) consults the all-'Clients' resource only when no per-client resource exists. If a per-client resource exists (for example because some other client-specific permission was created), only that resource's policies are evaluated. A caller with MANAGE on all clients is then denied canManage(X) for such a client. The interface Javadoc added in this PR (ClientPermissionEvaluator) says canManage, canView, canConfigure and canMap* are also true for the 'all clients' permission, which this does not honor. Either the documentation or the precedence rule must change. canView(client) applies the opposite precedence, so the two methods disagree.

Inherited permission methods now throw UnsupportedOperationException on reachable paths

canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, the mapRoles/manage/configure/view permission factories, resource(), getPermissions(), isPermissionsEnabled() and setPermissionsEnabled() all throw UnsupportedOperationException. Previously clients() under V2 returned the inherited V1 implementation. These are methods of the public evaluator interface that existing code calls (for example the legacy token-exchange check calls canExchangeTo, and client management-permission endpoints call getPermissions/resource). A request that reaches them now fails with HTTP 500 instead of a denial or a valid response. Nothing in the PR shows that callers are guarded.

getResourceName has no CLIENTS branch, so client permission resources get no readable name

getResourceName special-cases USERS to return the username. There is no CLIENTS branch, so client resources fall back to resource.getDisplayName(). getOrCreateResource never sets a display name for client resources, so the name shown for a client permission would be null or the internal UUID rather than the clientId. The PR adds no mapping and no test for it.

void require* methods documented as 'Returns true'

requireView() and requireViewClientScopes() are void methods, but their Javadoc says 'Returns {@code true} if ...'. They should say they throw ForbiddenException when the corresponding can* method returns false, as the other require* methods in this interface do.

canView(client) repeats full policy evaluations for every client in a listing

canView(client) first calls canView(), which evaluates the all-clients resource, then canConfigure(client), which evaluates canManage(client) and hasPermission(client, CONFIGURE), and finally hasPermission(client, VIEW). Each hasPermission call does a resource lookup and a full evaluatePermission. Checking each client in a list therefore costs several policy evaluations per client, and the type-level evaluation is repeated N times. Nothing caches the type-level result.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle

The method builds a new, uninitialized KeyStore of the default type and returns its Provider, which is normally the JDK's SUN provider. Callers of getBouncyCastleProvider() that expect BouncyCastle, for example to look up algorithms by provider name, get the JDK provider silently. The method also allocates a throwaway KeyStore on every call. It should either return a real BC provider or throw UnsupportedOperationException like the other unimplemented methods.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default JDK keystore provider rather than the expected BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder calls whose results are discarded

Lines 114 and 115 create ASN1Encoder instances and discard the result. The returned DER sequence on lines 117-121 recomputes the same encodings. The dead calls look like a leftover and make the method harder to read.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same dead-code issue: ASN1Encoder instances are created and their results discarded, while the return statement recomputes the encodings with new instances.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation. Any existing implementation that does not override it, including out-of-tree providers, is not broken at compile time but throws AbstractMethodError. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider calls order() on every discovered provider, so such a provider fails during crypto initialization. A default method, for example returning 0, would keep existing implementations working.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider without a default implementation breaks existing providers (AbstractMethodError), and a default method would preserve compatibility.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-selected providers are constructed, and their constructors mutate global JVM security state

The ServiceLoader stream is collected into a list before sorting, so every discovered CryptoProvider constructor runs, including those that will not be selected. FIPS1402Provider's constructor (FIPS1402Provider.java line 94) inserts a KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at JVM security slot 1. When BCFIPS is absent it also inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE and rewrites the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory properties. DefaultCryptoProvider's constructor registers a non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider with Security.addProvider. Previously these side effects were followed by a hard failure when more than one provider was present. Now the multi-provider case succeeds, so the side effects persist in a JVM that runs a different provider. Discovery should avoid constructing unselected providers, for example by ranking on metadata before instantiation.

Most provider methods throw a 'Not supported yet.' placeholder

About 17 methods, including getAlgorithmProvider, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils, getKeyFactory, getSignature, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory and wrapFactoryForTruststore, throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'). That is leftover IDE template text, and it suggests the feature is planned. Because this provider is now a global ServiceLoader entry, callers that reach it through CryptoIntegration.getProvider() get an opaque failure. The message should say the provider is limited to ECDSA conversion, or the methods should be implemented.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate signature length

The method copies signature[len..2*len) without checking signature.length. A short or malformed signature triggers an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than an IOException or a clean verification failure. The method is copied from the BC implementation but is new code here, so it should check that signature.length equals signLength.

Test only checks the module's own encoder and decoder round-trip

The assertion compares the concatenated R||S produced by asn1derToConcatenatedRS with the value obtained after encoding and decoding it again, using the same class. If both directions share a defect, or if the produced DER is not accepted by a standard verifier, the test still passes. The test should verify the DER output from concatenatedRSToASN1DER with java.security.Signature.verify, or check it against a known test vector.

ES384 and ES512 are tested with a P-256 key, so the real component sizes are not exercised

A single default EC key pair is used for ES256, ES384 and ES512, so ES384 and ES512 sign with P-256 keys. The 48-byte and 66-byte component paths are not tested with matching curves. The P-521 case matters most: R can be 66 bytes plus a sign byte, which hits the truncation branch in integerToBytes, and that path is never exercised. The test therefore gives false confidence for ES384 and ES512. Each algorithm should be tested with its own curve, P-384 and P-521.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deleted group silently reports a null subgroup count

The NPE is replaced by returning null from a method whose contract is a count. The missing group is swallowed here and the null propagates into representations (populateSubGroupCount assigns it directly). Callers that unbox the Long or compare it will now throw NPE far from the cause. Other methods in this adapter throw IllegalStateException('Not found in database') when the group is gone, so behavior is inconsistent. Pick one defined behavior and document it on GroupModel.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getSubGroupsCount() returns null for a missing group, violating the non-null count contract and risking NPEs in callers. The candidate adds detail about propagation and inconsistent exception behavior, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is not joined, so late failures are ignored

deletedAll is set and the assertion runs at line 157 without joining the reader thread started at line 139. The reader may still be inside an in-flight request, and any exception it records after the assertion is evaluated is never checked. The test can therefore pass despite the failure it is meant to catch. The thread should be joined, with a timeout, before asserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same race: the reader thread is not waited/joined before deletedAll is flipped and the assertion runs, so exceptions recorded afterward can be missed and the test can pass incorrectly.

false_positives.candidate:
Paged subgroup listing still dereferences a possibly-null model

getSubGroupsStream(search, firstResult, maxResults) calls modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...) with no null check. The supplier resolves to null when another request has deleted the group, which is the race this PR targets, so this still throws the same NPE. The same unguarded pattern appears at lines 262 and 268 in the other two paged overloads. Only getSubGroupsCount was guarded, so the reported bug is only partly fixed.

Null guard in getRoleMappings tests the supplier instead of the group

The check 'if (group == null)' tests the Supplier<GroupModel> parameter. GroupAdapter always passes its non-null modelSupplier, so the guard never fires. When the underlying group has been deleted, the supplier returns null, and that null reaches the lazy loader. The comment describes exactly the case this guard was meant to handle, so the intended protection is missing and the PR does not address it. The check should be on group.get() == null before calling the loader.

getAttributes and getSubGroups have no null handling for a deleted group

Unlike getRoleMappings, getAttributes (lines 66-68) and getSubGroups (lines 90-92) pass the supplier straight to DefaultLazyLoader. The loaders at lines 55 and 57 dereference the source (source.getAttributes(), source.getSubGroupsStream()). Assuming the loader runs on the supplied source when the value is not yet loaded, a group deleted before its first attribute or subgroup access makes the supplier return null and the loader throws NPE. That affects getFirstAttribute, getAttributes, getAttributeStream and getSubGroupsStream() in GroupAdapter, so the concurrent NPE remains reachable.

Parent lookup result used without a null check during hierarchy build

session.groups().getGroupById(realm, currGroup.getParentId()) returns null if the parent was deleted between listing and this lookup. parentModel is then passed to groupEvaluator.canView(parentModel) at line 51 (when admin permissions are off), to toRepresentation inside computeIfAbsent at line 57, and to populateSubGroupCount(parentModel, parent) at line 60, which calls getSubGroupsCount() on null. This is the same concurrent-deletion NPE in the group listing path, and the PR edits this file without handling it. A null check that drops the orphaned child or skips the parent is needed.

Exception during deletion leaves a non-daemon busy-looping thread running

If group(...).remove() at line 153 throws (for example a 500 from the bug under test), the exception escapes the forEach and deletedAll.set(true) at line 155 never runs. The reader thread (lines 139-149) then loops forever issuing HTTP requests. As a non-daemon thread it also keeps the JVM alive, so the run hangs instead of failing cleanly. The flag should be set in a finally block, and the reader should be a daemon or be stopped explicitly.

Race-based test may not reproduce the NPE and has no deterministic interleaving

The NPE requires a cached adapter with a loaded group, a concurrent deletion, and then a lazy access. This test depends on timing between one reader thread and 100 sequential deletes, and it only asserts that no exception reached the client. Nothing shows it fails on the base commit, so it may pass without the fix. The author should confirm it reproduces the failure without the change, or drive the interleaving deterministically (for example by deleting the group on the server between the read and the access).

Reader thread spins on HTTP requests with no pause

The reader loop at lines 139-149 issues back-to-back list requests over 100 groups for the whole deletion phase with no sleep or backoff. This saturates the shared test server, slows the test, and adds load that can cause timeouts on CI. A short pause between iterations would avoid this.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

The new condition calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments. The only definition in this change is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` in UsernamePasswordForm.java, and no no-arg overload exists in the class hierarchy. The `services` module will not compile, so the whole PR (including all the new tests) cannot build or run. The intended call is presumably `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, which is already non-null inside this branch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is invoked without the required UserModel argument. The candidate adds that this breaks compilation and suggests passing context.getUser(), which is consistent with the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Re-auth skip is disabled for every user whenever passkeys are enabled in the realm

The shortcut that skips the username form during re-authentication is now bypassed for any user as soon as passkeys are enabled for the realm, regardless of whether that particular user has a passkey. A password-only user re-authenticating with prompt=login in a passkey-enabled realm is now shown the username page and must submit it, where previously they were skipped. The only new UsernameForm re-auth test uses a passkey-only user, so this regression for password-only users is not covered. If the intent is to only show the form when the user can use a passkey, the condition should check the user's passkey credentials rather than only the realm flag.

Negative webauthn-button check uses catch(Exception), so it can pass vacuously

In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey` (and again around line 312), the absence of the webauthn form is checked with `try { assertThat(driver.findElement(...), nullValue()); fail(...) } catch (Exception nsee) { }`. Any Exception thrown while looking up the element, such as a WebDriverException from a stale or not-yet-loaded page, is swallowed and the check passes without verifying anything. The same PR and file already use `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` for this kind of check, which only accepts the expected exception.

Unused import NoSuchElementException left behind

The two `Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...)` uses were replaced by `MatcherAssert.assertThat(...)` in this PR, so the `org.openqa.selenium.NoSuchElementException` import is now unused. This can fail a checkstyle or unused-import check in the build.

Unused PasswordCredentialModel import added by this PR

The import `org.keycloak.models.credential.PasswordCredentialModel` is added in this PR, but nothing in the file references it (the new tests only use string/nullValue checks). It should be removed to keep the build's unused-import checks clean.

false_negatives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offset is passed straight into a queryset slice, which Django rejects

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, `start_offset` is the raw negative offset and `queryset[start_offset:stop]` is evaluated. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative start indices and raises an error, so the request returns a 500. The branch that is supposed to reach data beyond normal pagination bounds therefore never returns data. A user can reach this with any crafted cursor string whose offset is negative, provided the advanced flag is set.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: a negative cursor offset is used as a queryset slice start, which Django QuerySets do not support and will reject. The candidate adds context about the advanced-features branch and resulting 500, but the underlying issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member is dereferenced without a None check

RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional, since a requester may not be a member of the organization. The expression `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` only avoids the dereference when the user is a superuser. For any other requester with no membership record, this raises AttributeError and returns a 500. Whether OrganizationAuditPermission guarantees membership for non-superusers is not visible in this diff, so this needs a None guard or a confirmed invariant.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: organization_context.member may be None and is accessed via has_global_access without a guard, causing AttributeError for non-superuser requesters. The candidate captures the core issue despite less specific auth context.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime, crashing any non-empty page

The endpoint sends `order_by="-datetime"` to this paginator, so `getattr(item, self.key)` returns a `datetime` for each AuditLogEntry. `math.floor()`/`math.ceil()` raise TypeError on a datetime. `build_cursor` calls this key function on the results, so with `optimized_pagination=true` every organization that has at least one audit entry gets a 500. Only the empty-result case avoids the call. DateTimePaginator.get_item_key avoids this by converting the datetime to a millisecond epoch value. This class did not copy that logic, so it cannot serve its only use case. Subclassing DateTimePaginator or porting its conversion would fix it.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to the datetime key produced by order_by=-datetime, causing a TypeError during pagination.

false_positives.candidate:
value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value, which is then bound against a DateTimeField

DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor converts the millisecond cursor value back into a timezone-aware datetime. This class returns `cursor.value` unchanged. `build_queryset` then appends that int to the `extra(where=...)` params against `auditlogentry.datetime`, so any request carrying a next/prev cursor either fails at the database (timestamp compared with integer) or fails Django's DateTimeField validation. Pagination past the first page cannot work on this path.

Comments justify exposing data beyond pagination bounds on the claim that queryset-level checks exist, which is false

The comments at lines 878-879 say the negative-offset branch 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' and that this 'is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. The queryset here is only filtered by organization_id (organization_auditlogs.py line 48). The role check that enables the mode is in the endpoint (line 71). Nothing checks permissions at the queryset level. The intent is a privilege-gated path that widens what an admin can reach, and its safety argument is wrong and unreviewed. The branch should be removed or its authorization model explicitly designed and documented.

Negative offsets are silently clamped to 0 in BasePaginator for every paginator, not only the new one

The change to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` affects BasePaginator.get_result, which DateTimePaginator, Paginator and every other cursor paginator inherit. It is not gated by the new query parameter. Before this change, a non-prev cursor with a negative offset (reachable through Cursor.from_string) raised a slicing error. Now it silently returns the first page with a cursor built from the original negative offset. The comment at lines 179-181 says negative offsets are being allowed, but the code does the opposite, clamping them. The comment and the global behavior change both need to be reconsidered, and the change should be separated from this feature.

Privileged mode is gated on the raw is_superuser flag rather than an active superuser session

The gate uses `request.user.is_superuser` directly. Sentry's superuser pattern normally checks an elevated, session-scoped superuser state (for example via is_active_superuser(request)). Using the raw user flag can grant the advanced mode to a superuser who has not elevated in this session. The impact is limited while the advanced path is broken, but the gate should follow the codebase's superuser convention.

Comment claims a Cursor behavior change that the diff does not make

The added comment says the Cursor now 'allows negative offsets ... enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets'. The code line below it, `self.offset = int(offset)`, is unchanged. The class already accepted negative offsets, and nothing in the change makes pagination more efficient. The comment documents a nonexistent optimization and should be removed.

New paginator, query-parameter path and negative-offset behavior change have no tests

The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, a new `optimized_pagination` branch in the endpoint, an advanced-features gate, and a global change to BasePaginator offset handling, but adds no tests. The first basic use (one page of audit entries with the param set) crashes, as described in the get_item_key and value_from_cursor findings. A simple endpoint test would have caught it. Tests are also needed for the default DateTimePaginator path, which the BasePaginator change now affects.

PR description is a placeholder and the 'performance' framing is unsupported

The description is only 'Test 1', so nothing explains why the endpoint gets an undocumented `optimized_pagination` query parameter or who it is for. The code comments at lines 68-75 call this a performance optimization, but the optimized branch issues the same ORM queries as DateTimePaginator (its only real difference is the broken negative-offset branch), and no measurements are included. The title and comments overstate what the change does.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds for the same key

BuildIndex no longer serializes builds: the lock was removed from the whole function and only the final cache write is locked. Nothing deduplicates concurrent builds for one key, and getOrCreateIndex's GetIndex-then-build sequence is not atomic. Two concurrent cold Search or watch-event calls for the same namespace now build two full indexes in parallel, roughly doubling memory and CPU. The second 'b.cache[key] = idx' silently replaces the first index, which is never closed. For file-backed indexes, the second bleve.New on the same directory races the first and can fail. The previous code built twice too, but serially. Use per-key singleflight or re-check under the lock.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: BuildIndex no longer holds the lock across the full build, so concurrent callers can build the same key in parallel and the later cache assignment overwrites the earlier index. This matches the golden comment's underlying bug and concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while GetIndex takes RLock and BuildIndex writes the map under Lock. The new log line in search.go init (line 216) calls TotalDocs after the watch goroutine has started (lines 207-213). That goroutine can call handleEvent, then getOrCreateIndex, then BuildIndex, which writes the map concurrently. A concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error in Go and cannot be recovered. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock().
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race: TotalDocs reads b.cache unsynchronized while the newly started watcher can concurrently BuildIndex and write the map, risking a fatal concurrent map iteration/write.

false_positives.candidate:
Storage init failures now abort NewResourceServer and block startup on the full index build

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init synchronously. Init runs lifecycle.Init (DB connect and ping) and the search init, which builds an index for every namespace above InitMinCount, and returns the error to the caller. Previously these failures only surfaced as errors on the first gRPC call and never stopped construction. Now a transient DB error or any index build error makes the constructor fail, which fails whatever wires the server, and startup (including HTTP and metrics) is blocked for the entire index build. Init is also never retried. This is the behavior change the PR description asks about. It should be called out explicitly, and the module init order should be checked to confirm the DB and dependencies are ready when the provider runs.

On-demand index build still runs under the gRPC request context

getOrCreateIndex still builds a missing index with the request context: s.build(ctx, key, 10, 0). The build's ListIterator and builder calls use that ctx. Namespaces at or below InitMinCount at startup are not indexed at init. If such a namespace has since grown, the first Search builds the whole index inside the RPC, and a client cancel or deadline aborts the build mid-way. The index is then never cached, so the same failure repeats on every request. This is the failure mode the PR says it fixes, and it remains on this path. The fixed size hint of 10 also always selects the memory-only index.

Data race on shared err and counter in the parallel init workers

Pre-existing, but it is in the function being edited. The errgroup closure assigns the outer function's err variable ('_, _, err = s.build(...)') and increments totalBatchesIndexed (line 189), and both run concurrently in up to initWorkers goroutines. That is an unsynchronized write from multiple goroutines, which the race detector flags and which can tear an interface value. The closure should use a local error (the return value already reaches group.Wait), and the counter should be atomic.

GetResourceStats never checks rows.Err, so a mid-iteration failure returns partial stats as success

The loop ends when rows.Next() returns false. If that was caused by an error (for example a dropped connection), rows.Err() holds it, but the code never checks it. The callback then returns err, which is nil at that point, and the function returns partial res with a nil error. search init then indexes only the namespaces that were read, logs success, and never retries. rows is also not closed on the early Scan-error return. Check rows.Err() after the loop and defer rows.Close().

Trace propagation fixed only in GetResourceStats; sibling methods still drop the span context

The PR says it fixes trace propagation, but only GetResourceStats was changed. WriteEvent (line 158), ReadResource (line 353) and ListIterator (line 388) still do '_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)' and then pass the parent ctx down. As a result the create, update and delete spans and the DB transaction spans are siblings of the wrapper span, not children. bleve.go BuildIndex (line 88) has the same pattern. Either finish the change in these methods or narrow the PR description.

Removing the Init gate from every RPC silently allows requests after Stop

Before this change, each RPC called s.Init, which returned s.initErr. Stop sets initErr to 'service is stopped', so every request after Stop was rejected. With the gates removed, initErr is dead state and RPCs keep being served after Stop, even though the broadcaster context has been cancelled. This behavior change is not mentioned in the PR. If initWatcher failed after the broadcaster started, its goroutines keep running on s.ctx. The lifecycle hooks, which may already have been initialized, are not stopped either. The same applies to the error return at line 254. Call s.cancel() (and stop the lifecycle) before returning the error.

Pre-existing, but in the function being edited. When the backend stops, the poller returns and runs 'defer close(stream)'. The loop 'v := <-events' then receives nil forever, and handleEvent reads evt.Type on a nil pointer, which panics and crashes the process during shutdown. The same pattern exists in server.go initWatcher (around lines 762-765, where v.Type is read). Use 'v, ok := <-events' and return when !ok.
