true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated intent and depends on timing

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors in processing must not block offset commits for other messages. Its final assertion requires that the partition is NOT committed: `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. By the design (the finally block completes the failed offset 100), both offsets 100 and 101 complete, so a later commit should reach 102. The assertion passes only because the test exits about 0.2 seconds after submission, before the commit thread's first one-second tick. The test therefore neither verifies the intended behavior nor is stable. It should wait for a commit and assert that the partition is committed at 102.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core problem: the test's stated intent (docstring) does not match its implementation/assertion. The candidate elaborates that the assertion is inverted and timing-dependent, which is a more detailed description of the same mismatch.

false_positives.candidate:
close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are silently dropped after the first rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and passed to every strategy that create_with_partitions() builds. Arroyo closes the current strategy on partition revocation and creates a new one on assignment, so after the first rebalance the pool's queues are already shut down and its workers have exited. The new strategy's submit() calls FixedQueuePool.submit -> queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown. The except branch in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit (lines 317-325) then marks the offset as added and completed, so the message is never processed but its offset becomes committable. Work that was still queued when the old pool shut down keeps its offsets in `outstanding` forever, which stalls commits for those partitions. Net effect: uptime results are silently lost after any rebalance and the commit point stops advancing. No test runs close() followed by create_with_partitions() on the same factory, so this is not caught. Pool ownership should stay with the factory; the strategy's close() should only stop its own commit thread.

Enqueue failures mark the offset as completed, so unprocessed messages get committed

In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, any exception raised while decoding, grouping, or enqueueing a message reaches an except block that calls add_offset and then complete_offset for that message. The message is never handed to a worker, yet its offset is now treated as processed, so the commit loop advances past it and the message is dropped with only a log line. This is the mechanism that hides the ShutDown failure described above. Poison messages (decode or grouping errors) may reasonably be skipped, but a failure to enqueue must not mark the offset complete. Failed enqueues should keep the offset outstanding or propagate the error.

Per-queue work queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure

Each per-queue work queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize (line 185), so FixedQueuePool.submit() never blocks. The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 255) promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever fills. If the handlers are slower than the Kafka fetch rate, the main thread keeps polling and queued WorkItems (each holding a full Message) accumulate without bound. Because commits are contiguous, the last committed offset stays pinned behind the slowest item, so the outstanding and all_offsets sets also grow. Either bound the queues and make submit block or pause the consumer, or remove the backpressure claim.

A hole in the offset sequence permanently stalls all commits for that partition

get_committable_offsets breaks out of the scan on any offset that is not in all_offsets (line 90), so a missing offset blocks commits forever. Within a partition, Kafka delivers messages in offset order, so if offset 102 arrives after 100, offset 101 will never arrive later; it is a hole from compaction or a transaction marker, and the tracker waits for it indefinitely. Consequences: the committed point never moves past the hole, mark_committed never prunes all_offsets so it grows without bound, and every restart reprocesses everything after the hole. test_offset_gaps_block_commits in the queue consumer tests only passes because it submits offset 101 after 102 and 103, which real delivery cannot produce. The tracker should treat offsets skipped by a newer delivered offset as complete.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread without synchronization

_commit_loop runs on its own thread and calls commit_function (line 287), which is the Arroyo commit callback from create_with_partitions. Arroyo's consumer is driven from the StreamProcessor thread (poll, stage, commit); nothing here coordinates with that loop, so commits can race with the main thread's consumer calls. There is also a shutdown race: after shutdown_event is set, the loop does not re-check the flag after shutdown_event.wait(1.0) (line 276), so it can run one more get_committable_offsets and commit_function after close() has begun or returned, and close() only joins for 5 seconds. Commit calls should be made from the processor thread (for example from poll()), and the loop should exit once the event is set.

Sequential 5-second joins make shutdown block for up to 100 seconds per rebalance

FixedQueuePool.shutdown joins each worker with a 5-second timeout, one after another (line 243). With the default 20 queues, if the workers are all stuck in slow result handlers (the exact case this PR targets), shutdown can block for up to 100 seconds. Because the strategy's close() also calls this shutdown (see the close() bug above), this delay occurs on every rebalance. That risks exceeding the consumer's poll or session timeouts and getting the consumer evicted from the group. Use one shared deadline for all joins, or avoid blocking joins on the rebalance path.

Racy assertion that queued items remain right after submission

test_stats_reporting asserts stats['total_items'] > 0 immediately after ten submits (line 200), while worker threads are already draining the queues. If the workers dequeue everything before this line runs (possible under CI load or GIL switching), the test fails intermittently. The check adds no coverage that the later == 0 assertion does not already provide, so either remove it or make the precondition deterministic, for example by blocking the workers first.

Test named for concurrency does not check concurrency

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups claims to verify that different groups are processed concurrently, but its only assertion (line 173) is that three group labels appear in the processed output. That would pass if every item ran serially on one thread, and with only three queues the groups can hash onto the same queue. The name and the assertion disagree, so the test gives false confidence about concurrency.

Worker transaction is named with a 'monitors.' prefix copied from another consumer

The worker transaction name is built as monitors.{identifier}.worker_{id} (line 138). This module is generic remote-subscription code used by the uptime results consumer, and the same prefix is copied into the result processor. Performance data for these workers will be filed under the monitors namespace, which misleads anyone looking at traces. The prefix should reflect the actual consumer or be derived from the identifier alone.

Strategy created in test is never closed, leaking a commit thread

test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy creates a SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy through the factory (line 415) but only calls factory.shutdown(), which stops the pool and not the strategy. The strategy's commit thread loops every second for the rest of the test session because its shutdown event is never set. The test should call strategy.close() so the thread is stopped and the test does not leak threads into later tests.

Span eviction at 1000 is silent: no log or metric when spans are dropped

When span_count exceeds 1000, zpopmin silently removes the lowest-scored (oldest by end timestamp) spans from the segment. The Python side previously logged 'Skipping too large segment' and emitted spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded, and that guard was removed in buffer.py. Dropped spans are now invisible to operators, and the limit is hardcoded here rather than configured. Emit a metric (and ideally a log) from the script or the caller when eviction occurs.

The span-buf:s:* keys change from SET to ZSET but keep the same name prefix. Any segment key written by the old code is a SET. ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, doubling scores of duplicate payloads

zunionstore is called without AGGREGATE, so the default SUM applies. When the same payload already exists in the destination (for example a redelivered Kafka message, or a span present in both merged sets), its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps. That corrupts the eviction ordering, which relies on score = end_timestamp_precise. Use AGGREGATE MIN or MAX so the score is preserved.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 and caveat comment removed

A single message missing it raises KeyError inside process_batch, which fails the whole batch and can leave the consumer retrying the same poison batch. max_segment_spans config is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit

After this PR the span-count check in _load_segment_data was removed, so the max_segment_spans constructor argument (default 1001) is never read. The effective limit is the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Configuration that appears to control the limit no longer does, and the two defaults disagree. The headline feature of this PR, evicting spans beyond 1000 during insert, has no test. The added lines only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures, so nothing checks that the segment is capped, that the oldest spans are the ones evicted, that merges keep the right scores, or that the loop limit behaves as intended. optimized_pagination path is untested and crashes on the first page

The new branch gated by optimized_pagination=true has no test. Such a test would immediately expose the datetime TypeError in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key, so the endpoint's new path is broken and unverified. Add a test for a superuser request with that parameter and at least one audit log entry.

Comment claims a negative-offset feature that this change does not implement

The added comment says Cursor now allows negative offsets for advanced pagination and enables reverse pagination from arbitrary positions. The diff changes nothing in this constructor (self.offset = int(offset) is unchanged), and the paginators that consume negative offsets crash on them. The comment describes behavior that does not exist, so it should be removed or corrected.

The PR title is about span buffer eviction, but this file, paginator.py, and cursors.py add an experimental audit-log paginator switch. Allowlist option read via options.get with no registration in the diff

The allowlist comes only from options.get('issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist', []). None of the eight changed files registers this key in the options defaults. Sentry's options manager raises an UnknownOption error for unregistered keys, so on a cache miss _are_all_projects_error_upsampled would raise. The tests patch options in this module, so the real lookup never runs and CI would not catch it. Register the option or confirm it already exists.

Substring match classifies negated and compound event.type filters as error queries

For those queries the count is rewritten to sum(sample_weight), but non-error rows have no sample_weight, so the sum drops them and the count is wrong (for '!event.type:error' it can come out as 0). The filter should be parsed as a token rather than matched as a substring. No test covers negation or compound queries.

sum(sample_weight) silently drops events that lack a weight

sum() ignores NULLs, so any error event without a sample_weight contributes 0 instead of 1 to upsampled_count. This includes events ingested before the rollout and events with no client sample rate. The docstring in error_upsampling.py (lines 85-86) says no null handling is needed because the schema guarantees the column, but nothing in the diff enforces that. Time ranges spanning the rollout would silently undercount for allowlisted projects. The fallback for a missing weight should be defined explicitly, for example coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

Transform is not gated on metrics or on-demand routing

The count() rewrite to upsampled_count() is applied regardless of use_metrics, has_metrics, use_metrics_layer, or on_demand_metrics_enabled, which can route a discover-dataset query to a metrics or on-demand builder. upsampled_count is registered only in discover.py's function converter, so in those routes the function would not resolve, or the query would silently fall back to a non-upsampled count. The transform should be gated on the builder actually used.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. The fast path reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, then releases it and takes the write Lock with no re-check. Any goroutine that missed the cache while another goroutine was already populating it will still re-read and re-parse assets-manifest.json from disk, one at a time, even though the cache is now filled. At startup, N concurrent requests produce N serialized manifest reads. Re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after taking the Lock would return the cached value immediately.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across file I/O serializes all dev-mode calls and ignores caller context

The write Lock is taken on every call in dev mode (cfg.Env == setting.Dev), because the early return is skipped. Each call then reads and parses the manifest from disk while holding the exclusive lock, so concurrent dev requests that previously ran in parallel now run one at a time. In non-dev mode, while the cache is nil (for example, the manifest is missing or failed to load), every request blocks on Lock without honouring its ctx, so a slow operation inside readWebAssetsFromCDN (which uses http.DefaultClient with no timeout) holds up all waiters. The CDN path is currently unreachable because cdn is the constant "", so this is latent, but the lock scope is wider than the data race requires. Doing the I/O outside the lock and only taking the lock to publish the result would avoid both problems.

No regression test for concurrent access to the cached web assets

The PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache, but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Without a test run under `go test -race`, nothing guards against the race being reintroduced, for example by a future change that reads the global outside the lock. A small test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently with a temp manifest, with the cache reset between cases, would lock in the fix.

The goroutine only feeds a boolean into a duration metric and drops the error. The base code logged legacy failures with the object attached. Now a failed legacy create (including a timeout) produces no log line and no error detail, so the unified/legacy divergence this mode is meant to guard against is invisible to operators. The same omission exists in Delete (line 113), Update (line 140) and DeleteCollection (line 166).

Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered per object

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no per-object serialization. Two quick successive operations on the same playlist (for example update then update, or update then delete) can reach the legacy store out of order, leaving legacy with the older state while unified storage holds the newer one. Nothing detects or repairs this, and the 10s timeout makes it more likely. This needs either per-key serialization or an explicit, documented eventual-consistency guarantee with tests.

Legacy update recomputes the change from its own state instead of writing the unified result

The base code wrapped the Storage.Update result in updateWrapper so the legacy store received exactly what unified storage produced. This version passes the raw objInfo to Legacy.Update. objInfo.UpdatedObject is then applied to the legacy store's current object, which can differ from the unified object (different resourceVersions, stored fields, defaults, or a patch applied against a different base). Both writes can succeed and the stores still diverge. The same objInfo is also consumed a second time after the first UpdatedObject call.

Unified storage failures are recorded as legacy failures

When the storage write fails, Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The failed unified write is counted in the legacy metrics and the storage error metric is never set, so storage error rates are under-reported and legacy stats are polluted.

Destroy tears down Legacy while fire-and-forget writes may still be running

Destroy calls Storage.Destroy and Legacy.Destroy immediately, but background legacy goroutines may still be executing against the legacy store. Those writes then run against a destroyed backend and fail or panic. Destroy has no way to wait for in-flight legacy writes.

Background legacy goroutines have no panic recovery

Legacy calls used to run on the request goroutine, where net/http recovers panics per request. The bare goroutines added here have no recover, so a panic in any legacy storage method crashes the whole Grafana process instead of failing one request.

Tests never verify the asynchronous legacy write

Storage and Legacy share a single mock.Mock, so the test cannot tell which store was called. The tests never call AssertExpectations, so the legacy expectations set up in TestMode3_Create, _Update and _DeleteCollection are never checked. Nothing verifies that Legacy is called, or with what object, which is the core of this change. The background goroutine can also call the mock after the test returns, so those calls are not observed at all.

Legacy-side reads run immediately after writes that are now asynchronous

In mode 3, the k8s create at line 496 returns before its legacy write completes. getFromBothAPIs then reads the legacy endpoint right away (and the legacy list comparison around line 523 does the same). These checks race the background write and will be flaky. If the legacy endpoint is actually served from unified storage, the checks do not exercise the legacy write at all. Either way the assertion does not test what it claims without waiting or polling for the legacy write.

Test case name says List is not implemented, but it is

The case is named 'error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented', but List is now implemented in this PR and the case only checks that a storage error is propagated. The name is misleading to future readers.

Create test name contradicts its setup

The case is named 'creating an object only in the unified store', but its setup registers a legacy Create expectation and the implementation writes to legacy as well. The name describes the old behavior.

Duplicate go.work.sum entry and unrelated checksum additions

The line 'github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery ... /go.mod' is added a second time, duplicating the entry immediately above it. The hunk also adds checksums for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, several otel exporters and genproto rpc), which this dual-writer change does not touch. These look like an accidental go mod tidy or merge artifact and should be removed or verified.

Any $__range that applyTemplateVariables resolves from request.scopedVars (Grafana supplies __range for panel queries) has already been replaced by a literal, so isQueryWithRangeVariable() returns false and the query is split. Each time chunk then runs with the full-range literal as its window and combineResponses merges the chunks, which gives wrong results for range aggregations. No test in the PR covers this exclusion.

The old code interpolated first and then filtered on expr, so a target whose expression is a variable expanding to an empty string was dropped. The filter now runs on the raw expression (line 50), before the map on line 52, so such targets survive. They are passed to runSplitQuery as a subrequest, where the empty expr is filtered out (querySplitting.ts line 298). The filter on line 298 checks query.expr before applyTemplateVariables runs on line 299. A target such as $query whose variable expands to an empty string passes the filter and goes to runQuery with an empty expr, which the backend will reject. If that target is the only one, the requests array ends up empty and runSplitGroupedQueries throws a TypeError at line 96. Targets are interpolated twice on the sharded path

The query at lines 9-11 returns a PG::Result. When no row matches, `[0]` is nil and `['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the upgrade. This is the common case: embed_category only exists in site_settings if an admin set it (default ''), and the join requires it to equal an existing category name. The uncategorized fallback at lines 14-16 is only reached when the id is 0, which never happens for a real category, so the intended default is never applied. The empty result needs explicit handling, and the uncategorized_category_id lookup needs a guard too, since that setting may not be stored.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the migration indexes execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking for an empty result, so a missing embed_category row yields nil and raises NoMethodError, aborting the upgrade. The extra note about the uncategorized fallback is consistent with the same failure path.

false_positives.candidate:
Migration is irreversible and create_table uses force: true

`def change` contains raw `execute` calls, which Rails cannot invert, so rolling this migration back raises ActiveRecord::IrreversibleMigration. Separately, `create_table :embeddable_hosts, force: true` (line 3) silently drops an existing embeddable_hosts table and its rows if one exists. Use explicit up/down methods and drop force: true.

Stored hosts with a port can never match a lookup

The format validator explicitly allows an optional port, e.g. 'eviltrout.com:8080'. But record_for_host (line 14) looks up by URI#host, which drops the port, so a host saved with a port never matches and embedding silently fails for it. Either reject ports in validation or compare including the port.

Duplicate hosts allowed and lookup returns an arbitrary row

There is no uniqueness validation or unique index on host, and the admin UI can add the same host twice. `.first` has no ORDER BY, so record_for_host returns an arbitrary row, and TopicEmbed.import will use an arbitrary category for that site. Add a case-insensitive uniqueness validation and a unique index.

TLD length limit rejects valid domains

The TLD pattern `[a-z]{2,5}` rejects valid hosts with longer TLDs such as example.community or example.technology. The setting this replaces accepted any string, so admins with such sites can no longer configure them.

category_id is never checked against existing categories

The submitted category_id is only defaulted when blank. It is never checked against Category, and the column has no foreign key. A nonexistent id is stored, and TopicEmbed.import then passes it to PostCreator, creating topics in a missing category. The same happens after a category is deleted. Validate that the category exists.

Admin hosts controller has no behavioral tests

The only spec asserts that the class inherits from Admin::AdminController. Nothing exercises create, update, destroy, the uncategorized default in save_host, validation failures, the not-found path, or non-admin access. The core of the new write endpoint is untested.

_hydrateEmbedded now rewrites every *_ids key and can leave undefined entries

The regex now matches every `*_ids` key in REST-serialized payloads, and the original key is deleted. When the referenced collection is not in the root payload, _lookupSubType returns undefined for each id, so the result is an array of undefined values. The `hydrated || []` fallback never runs because map always returns an array. Previously such keys were left intact, and now the id list is lost and consumers get undefined items. This matters for the new feature: EmbeddingSerializer uses `embed: :ids` without `include: true`, so the root may have no embeddable_hosts collection and the admin list would iterate undefined hosts. Unresolved ids should be filtered out, and conversion should only happen when the collection is present.

find embedded test passes for the wrong record

The test calls store.find('fruit', 2) but asserts apple's data. The /fruits/:id pretender in create-pretender.js.es6 (line 227) always returns fruits[0] regardless of the id, so the change from id 1 to 2 has no effect and the test would still pass if lookup by id were broken. The fixture should use request.params.id.

Stale test named for a host check that no longer exists

The test 'is false if embeddable_host is blank' sets up no host. expandable_first_post? no longer checks hosts, and embed_truncate defaults to false, so the test passes trivially and no longer tests what its name says. It should be removed or rewritten to test the behavior that actually matters.

Delete has no error handling

delete() calls destroyRecord().then(...) with no failure handler, unlike save() which uses popupAjaxError. On a server error the row silently stays with no feedback, and the promise rejection is unhandled. A .catch(popupAjaxError) is needed.

false_positives.candidate:
Public group members page silently truncated to 50 members

The members endpoint now defaults to a page size of 50 for every group (previously non-automatic groups returned all members and automatic groups were capped at 200). The public members page (`group/members.hbs`) renders `members` with `{{#each}}` and has no pagination controls, and the shared `Discourse.Group` model also defaults `limit: 50`. For any non-automatic group with more than 50 members, users see only the first 50 and have no way to reach the rest. This is a functional regression on the public group page.

Remove link is rendered for automatic groups because `automatic` is looked up on the member

Inside `{{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}` the item context is the member User object, not the group, so `{{#unless automatic}}` resolves `automatic` against the user and is always falsy. The remove link therefore appears for automatic groups too. The server rejects those removals with a 422, and `removeMember` in the admin controller and model has no failure handler, so the click appears to do nothing. The flag needs to come from the controller or be passed into the item view.

create ignores alias_level even though the client now sends it

`Discourse.Group#asJSON` now includes `alias_level`, and the new-group form shows the alias-level selector. `create` assigns only name and visible, so the chosen alias_level is silently dropped and the group gets the default. The PR rewrote `create` but left this gap in place.

Removing a non-member raises RecordNotFound instead of succeeding

`group.users.delete(user_id)` with an integer id makes Rails 4 look the record up with `find` on the association, which raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound when that user is not a member. The old PATCH path tolerated removing non-members, and the deleted spec ('succeeds silently when removing non-members') asserted that. A double-click or a stale member list now produces a 404 that the Ember client does not handle.

limit/offset are unvalidated: negative values cause a 500, and limit has no cap

`limit` and `offset` come straight from `params.to_i`. A negative `limit` produces `LIMIT -1`, which PostgreSQL rejects, so the request fails with a 500; a negative offset fails the same way. There is also no upper bound on limit, so a single request can pull the full membership of any visible group. Clamp limit to a sane range and floor offset at 0.

GET /groups/:name/members.json response shape changed from an array to an object

The endpoint now returns `{members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}}` instead of a bare array of users, and the default page size changed. Any other consumer of this public JSON endpoint (plugins, API clients) will break silently. The PR description does not mention the contract change.

Admin update silently resets visible for clients using the old nested params

`update` now reads flat top-level params and no longer reads `group[...]`, and the PATCH membership path is removed. A client still sending the old nested payload (`group[name]`, `group[visible]`) gets `params[:visible]` nil, so `group.visible` is set to false without any error. The name change is also silently skipped.

No positive test for updating a non-automatic group

The `.update` context only checks that renaming an automatic group is ignored. The rename, visible, and alias_level paths for normal groups, which are the main behavior of the rewritten `update` action, have no test. The old test covering name changes for regular groups was removed.

New public members endpoint and its pagination have no spec

The `members` action changed its response shape, default limit, and query logic, and the group members UI now depends on the meta fields. No spec in this PR exercises pagination, meta values, the 50-member default, or access to hidden groups through `find_group`.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocklist match counter is inflated because the check writes from inside validation

`should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the row, but it is called from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs on every `valid?` or `save` of a User whose email changed. In `UsersController#create` the code calls `user.valid?` (line ~168) and then `user.save` (line ~172), so one blocked signup attempt increments `match_count` twice, and any other validation call adds more. The statistic therefore does not reflect the number of blocked attempts. Also, a validator that mutates blocklist state couples every model using `validates :email, email: true` to that side effect. Record the match once in the controller or a single save path, and keep validation read-only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the block-check method mutates match statistics as a side effect of a read/validation call, inflating counts and coupling validation to writes. The candidate adds concrete call-path details but points to the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocklist lookup is case-sensitive, so case variants bypass a blocked address

`should_block?` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, an exact, case-sensitive match. Nothing normalizes the address first: `User.new_from_params` assigns `params[:email]` verbatim, and the domain restriction in the same validator is case-insensitive (`Regexp.new(..., true)`). If 'spam@example.com' is blocked, a signup with 'Spam@Example.com' passes validation and is stored. The unique index on blocked_emails is also case-sensitive, so case variants can coexist as separate entries. Normalize both the stored value and the lookup key (for example with Email.downcase, which the codebase already uses for lookups).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: case-sensitive exact matching in BlockedEmail.should_block? lets case variants of a blocked email bypass the block. The candidate adds normalization guidance but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write loses match_count increments under concurrency

`record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save` reads the count into Ruby, increments it, and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts that read the same value both write value+1, so an increment is lost. `save` also reruns validations, including the uniqueness query, just to bump a counter. Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` or `update_counters`.

rejectedEmails is never cleared, so any server email error blocks that address until reload

Every response with `errors.email` pushes the address into `rejectedEmails`, and `emailValidation` then fails that exact address (line 69) for the controller's lifetime. That includes errors that are not about the blocklist, such as 'has already been taken'. The field then shows the generic `user.email.invalid` reason for an address that is well-formed but registered, and submit stays disabled for it even if the server-side condition changes (for example, an admin removes the blocklist entry). Consider clearing the list when the email changes or limiting it to the blocked-email error.

New errors and values keys in the failed-signup response have no spec

The failed-create JSON now includes `errors` and `values`, and the new client code depends on that shape (`result.errors.email && result.values`). No request or controller spec in this PR checks these keys, so renaming or dropping them would silently break the rejected-email handling in the frontend.

Moved domain whitelist/blacklist logic and the real blocklist path are untested here

The whitelist and blacklist checks were moved from User into EmailValidator in this PR, but this spec only covers the blocked-email branch, and it stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the real lookup is never exercised. Nothing in this PR checks the domain restrictions through the new validator, the short-circuit (no blocklist lookup once a domain error is added), or case-insensitive matching. Regressions in the moved logic or the case-sensitivity issue would not be caught by these specs.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted-attribute restriction for TL0 users

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), so for a TL0 user seen by an anonymous viewer (`scope.restrict_user_fields?`) the raw website URL is omitted. The new `website_name` attribute is not in that list, and `include_website_name?` only checks `website.present?`, so it is serialized for those users. It contains the host and, when the host matches the forum, the full path, so the restricted URL is effectively exposed again. This defeats the anti-spam restriction the `untrusted_attributes` mechanism exists to enforce. Fix: add `:website_name` to the `untrusted_attributes` list, or gate `include_website_name?` on `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

Untrusted-attribute spec does not cover website_name

The 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' spec checks that bio, location, website and profile/card background are not serialized. The new `website_name` attribute is not in this list, so the spec does not catch the leak where a TL0 user's website host and path are serialized to anonymous viewers. Add `website_name` to this list and make the untrusted check cover it.

Trailing slash on same-domain website is shown as 'example.com/'

For a website such as `http://example.com/` on a forum at `example.com`, `URI(...).path` returns `"/"`, so `website_name` becomes `"example.com/"`. Users who type a bare domain with a trailing slash will see a stray slash that the previous client-side `split('/')[2]` logic did not produce. Consider stripping a bare `/` path, for example by treating a path of `/` as empty.

Domain comparison is case-sensitive

`URI(...).host` preserves the case typed by the user, while `Discourse.current_hostname` is normally lowercase. A website entered as `http://Example.com/user` on a forum at `example.com` fails the `==` test on line 141 and falls through to the else branch. The result is `Example.com` with no path, so the feature silently does not apply. Downcase both hosts before comparing, including in the `ends_with?` and sibling comparisons.

Sibling-domain heuristic treats different registrable domains as the same site

The branch on line 146 compares everything after the first label. For a forum at `y.co.uk` and a website at `x.co.uk/page`, both have three labels and the comparison yields `co.uk == co.uk`, so the full path is shown as if the website belonged to the forum's site. The heuristic does not account for public suffixes such as `co.uk` or `github.io`. The result is misleading display text for unrelated sites, not a security issue, but it does not match the stated intent of the feature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open is used on an admin-supplied URL

`SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Kernel#open. In Ruby 2.x, a string beginning with `|` is executed as a shell command rather than fetched. The setting is admin-only, so the exposure is limited, but the call should be explicit. Use `URI.parse(url).open` (open-uri) so only HTTP(S) fetches are possible.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same unsafe call: open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) in the PollFeed job. The golden comment frames it as SSRF (arbitrary URL fetch), while the candidate highlights Kernel#open's pipe-command execution risk and recommends URI.parse(url).open to restrict to HTTP(S). Same underlying bug and code location, different emphasis.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check uses substring matching, so a prefix origin is accepted

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is a substring test, not an origin comparison. Any sender whose origin is a prefix of the forum URL passes. With `discourseUrl = "https://community.example.com/"`, a page served from the registrable domain `https://community.example.co` has an origin that is a prefix, so `indexOf` returns 0 and the message is accepted. The handler also never checks `e.source === iframe.contentWindow`. The practical effect is that a lookalike site can resize the iframe, but the check is wrong. Compare the exact origin (scheme, host, port) of `discourseUrl` with `e.origin`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) performs substring/prefix matching rather than exact origin comparison, allowing a lookalike domain to bypass the check. The candidate's example and extra source-check note don't change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
X-Frame-Options 'ALLOWALL' is not a valid value and is ignored by browsers

Valid X-Frame-Options values are DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM. Browsers ignore unknown values, so this header does nothing; framing is permitted only because the browser ignores it. It also overwrites any X-Frame-Options set earlier in the request. If the intent is to allow framing from the configured host, use `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` with the embeddable host and remove this header.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same core bug: setting X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL fails to provide clickjacking protection. The candidate correctly explains that ALLOWALL is invalid and ignored by browsers, even though it omits the golden comment's additional referer-validation concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Imported-from footer interpolates the URL into HTML without escaping The footer is built as `I18n.t('embed.imported_from', link: "#{url}")`. The URL comes from the feed link or id and is inserted unescaped into a body stored as raw HTML. A link such as `http://x.test/'>` injects markup. The URL check on line 11 uses `^`, which matches after any newline, so the scheme check is also weaker than intended. Escape the URL before interpolating it, and anchor the scheme check at the start of the string.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment flags two problems: a nil-contents NoMethodError and an XSS from unescaped URL interpolation. The candidate precisely identifies the XSS issue (URL interpolated unescaped into the imported-from HTML footer, plus the weak ^ scheme check), which is the same underlying vulnerability, though it omits the nil NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dangling `if` modifier in `<%- end if %>` makes the embed template invalid

`<%- end if %>` closes the `if` opened on line 2 but leaves a stray `if` modifier with no condition. Once ERB compiles this, the result is not valid Ruby (the modifier is followed by the compiler's statement separator), so the `best` template fails whenever it is rendered. The intent is clearly `<%- end %>`. This breaks the main embed page for every request that finds an existing topic. The controller specs do not catch it because they never render views (no `render_views`), so a view or request spec is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same ERB syntax bug: `<%- end if %>` is invalid Ruby/ERB and should be `<%- end %>` to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
One bad feed item aborts the whole poll, and nil content raises NoMethodError

The `rss.items.each` loop has no per-item error handling. `i.content` can be nil for feed items that only supply a description, so `i.content.scrub` on line 35 raises NoMethodError. `i.title` can also be nil. `TopicEmbed.import` can raise too, for example when the URL exceeds 255 characters, or when the embed's post has been deleted. Any of these aborts the loop, and the job has `retry: false`, so nothing retries. The next hourly run reaches the same item and fails again, so every item after it is never imported. Guard nil content and title, and rescue and log errors per item.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same core bug: i.content can be nil when a feed item only supplies a description, so role-based access like i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError. Its additional points about broader error handling do not change the shared underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed content is double-unescaped and stored as raw HTML, giving stored XSS on the forum

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` decodes entities that SimpleRSS has already decoded from the XML, so text meant to be shown literally (for example `&lt;img onerror=...&gt;` in the feed) becomes live markup. `TopicEmbed.import` then creates the post with `cook_method: raw_html` (topic_embed.rb:22). `Post#cook` returns `raw` directly (app/models/post.rb:133), which skips the Sanitize/PrettyText pipeline and the `after_post_cook` plugin filters. The embed view then renders `raw post.cooked` unescaped (app/views/embed/best.html.erb:19), and the same cooked HTML appears in the forum topic. A feed item containing a script or event-handler payload therefore runs on the forum origin for every visitor, including staff. Feed content is third-party data, so this crosses a trust boundary. Run imported content through the normal sanitizer before storing raw HTML, and remove the extra unescape.

PostCreator enqueues jobs inside an outer transaction that has not committed

`TopicEmbed.import` wraps `PostCreator#create` in `Topic.transaction`. `PostCreator#create` calls `enqueue_jobs` (which triggers `process_post` and `feature_topic_users`) before the outer transaction commits. PostCreator's own comment says jobs must be enqueued after the transaction because workers may start on uncommitted data. With Sidekiq, a `process_post` job can run before the post and the TopicEmbed row are visible, find nothing, or fail, so the post is never processed (oneboxes, image sizes, and so on). Enqueue after the outermost commit, or do not wrap the creator in an outer transaction.

Anonymous requests can force unlimited outbound fetches and full feed polls

For any unknown `embed_url`, each request enqueues a `retrieve_topic` job without checking the host (the controller only checks the referer). The only throttle is `retrieved:#{@embed_url}` in topic_retriever.rb:26-28, which runs inside the worker and is keyed on the exact URL string. An attacker can vary a query string to get a fresh key every time. Each new key causes an outbound HTTP fetch of the embeddable host, and when feed polling is enabled it runs `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` (topic_retriever.rb:41), which downloads and re-imports the entire feed. Nothing rate-limits the endpoint, so this is a cheap way to exhaust outbound bandwidth and Sidekiq capacity. Validate the host in the controller before enqueueing, throttle per normalized URL in the request path, and do not run a full feed poll from a request-driven job.

`force: true` on a new table migration drops any existing topic_embeds table

`create_table :topic_embeds, force: true` drops an existing `topic_embeds` table before creating it. A migration that creates a new table gains nothing from this option and makes it destructive: running it in an environment where the table already exists (a partially migrated database, or another branch that created the table) silently deletes every embed-to-topic mapping. The importer depends on those mappings to avoid duplicate topics. Remove `force: true`.

Unrelated migration gains `force: true`, which drops existing top_topics data if rerun

This change adds `force: true` to the `top_topics` table creation. It is unrelated to embedding. If the migration runs in an environment where `top_topics` already exists with data, the table and all its counters are dropped. If the schema needs changing, add a new migration instead of editing one that may already have run.

setnx followed by a separate expire can leave a throttle key with no TTL

`$redis.setnx` and `$redis.expire` are two separate commands. If the process dies or the connection drops between them, `retrieved:<url>` persists with no TTL. Non-staff users are then permanently throttled for that URL and it is never retried. Use one atomic command, `SET key 1 NX EX 60`.

Missing post for an existing embed causes NoMethodError on update

`post = embed.post` can be nil if the post was deleted. When the content hash differs, `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` raises NoMethodError on `@post.raw`. The stale embed row is never repaired, and in PollFeed this exception aborts the whole loop (poll_feed.rb:31), so every later item is skipped. Handle a missing post explicitly, for example by recreating the post or removing the stale embed.

Readability attribute whitelist does not restrict URL schemes

`attributes: %w[href src]` limits which attribute names survive, but it does not check URL schemes. A `<a href="javascript:...">` from the fetched page can survive into the body. That body is stored as raw_html (cook_method), so the link runs script on the forum when clicked. The source is the configured embeddable host, so exploiting this needs that site to be compromised or malicious, but the forum should not accept unsanitized HTML from it. Pass the output through the normal sanitizer with an allowed-scheme list.

embed_url is varchar(255) with no length check, so long URLs fail at insert

`t.string :embed_url` creates varchar(255) in PostgreSQL. The value comes from unauthenticated request params (embed_controller.rb:9) and from feed links, and nothing checks its length. A longer URL makes `TopicEmbed.create!` raise StatementInvalid after the page has been fetched and the post built. The transaction rolls back, and every retry fails the same way. Validate the length at the controller and model, or use a text column.

Adding a NOT NULL column with a default rewrites the entire posts table

On PostgreSQL releases before 11, `add_column` with a default and `null: false` rewrites the whole posts table while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. On a large forum, reads and writes to posts are blocked for the duration. Add the column nullable, backfill in batches, then add the default and NOT NULL constraint, or schedule the downtime explicitly.

The --category option is silently removed from the Disqus import CLI

Removing `method_option :category` means `thor disqus:import --category X` now fails with an unknown-option error, and imported topics no longer get a category. This is a breaking change to the command-line interface that the PR description does not mention. Restore the option or document the removal.

Disqus import now fetches every thread live with no error handling and duplicates comments on re-run

Replacing PostCreator with `TopicEmbed.import_remote` makes the import fetch each thread's live URL with `open(url).read`. There is no timeout, no rescue, and no per-thread handling, so one 404 or network error aborts the import midway. The `ensure` block restores settings, but earlier threads are already imported. Re-running the import also appends every comment again: `import` returns the existing post, and the loop keeps creating posts for it. Rescue per thread, and skip comment creation when the topic already existed.

New gems are added for both Rails modes, but only the Rails 4 lockfile is updated

`ruby-readability` and `simple-rss` are added unconditionally, and Rails 3 mode uses the same Gemfile with the default `Gemfile.lock`. Only `Gemfile_rails4.lock` is updated in this PR. In Rails 3 mode, `bundle install --deployment` or `--frozen` will fail because the lockfile is missing these gems. Update the Rails 3 lockfile too, or gate the gems by mode.

Test named 'is 404' asserts only failure, and no test renders the view

The example is titled 'is 404 without an embed_url' but only checks `should_not be_success`. It passes because the `ensure_embeddable` filter raises first when embeddable_host is unset, so `params.require` is never exercised. No spec renders the `best` or `loading` templates (no `render_views`), so a broken template like the one in best.html.erb:6 goes undetected. Add a request spec that checks the status code and renders the templates.

Every TopicRetriever example stubs the method under test, leaving the throttle and feed logic untested

Each example in the 'with a valid host' context stubs `retrieved_recently?` or `perform_retrieve`. The Redis throttle, the feed-first branch in `perform_retrieve` (topic_retriever.rb:40-43), the existing-embed early return, and `fetch_http` are never exercised. The most important behavior, that a second request within 60 seconds does not fetch again, has no coverage. Add examples that use a real or mock Redis and exercise `perform_retrieve` directly.

PollFeed import logic has no test coverage, only the gating conditions

The spec only checks when `poll_feed` is called and stubs `poll_feed` in the delegation example. The actual import path, including URL filtering, nil title or content handling, the `TopicEmbed.import` call per item, and the error behavior, is untested. That is the riskiest code in the feature (see the XSS and per-item abort findings above). Add examples that feed a sample RSS document through `poll_feed`.

String#scrub requires Ruby 2.1 or later

`String#scrub` was added in Ruby 2.1. If this application still targets Ruby 2.0 (as Discourse did in late 2013), every poll that reaches this line raises NoMethodError. Confirm the supported Ruby version, or use an encoding-safe alternative.

cook_method is accepted from any opts hash and can bypass sanitization

`setup_post` now copies `opts[:cook_method]` onto the post. Setting it to raw_html stores the body unsanitized, because `Post#cook` returns raw HTML directly. If any controller forwards request parameters into PostCreator, an API or web user could create raw_html posts. Check that user-facing controllers whitelist their params and never pass `cook_method`, or only honor it from trusted server-side callers.

Documented options list omits the new cook_method option

The header comment lists the accepted PostCreator options, but `cook_method`, which this PR adds and which changes how the body is rendered and sanitized, is not documented. Add it, with its accepted values and the fact that raw_html skips the sanitizer.

false_negatives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `downsize` definition silently replaces the (from, to, max_width, max_height) version

The PR adds `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` but leaves the existing `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 in place. Ruby does not overload by arity, so the later definition replaces the earlier one and the 4-argument form becomes dead. Any caller that passes width and height separately now fails: `downsize(src, dst, 500, 500, force_aspect_ratio: true)` raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments), and `downsize(src, dst, 500, 500)` passes 500 as `opts`, so `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` fails with a TypeError. Either remove the old method and migrate its callers, or keep a single definition that accepts both forms.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the duplicate downsize definitions and Ruby's lack of arity overloading: the later dimensions-string method replaces the max_width/max_height method, making the original unreachable and breaking callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size limit replaced with hardcoded 10 MB for images and attachments, ignoring site settings

The `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` lookup is replaced by a hardcoded 10 MB for every upload type. Consequences: images larger than max_image_size_kb now pass client validation up to 10 MB, and an admin who sets max_image_size_kb above 10 MB can never upload between 10 MB and that limit from the UI, so the setting above 10 MB has no effect. Attachments are now checked against 10 MB instead of max_attachment_size_kb, so attachments the admin has forbidden pass client validation. The 413 branch (line 246) also now always reports '10 MB' regardless of configuration. If the goal is to let large images through for server-side shrinking, only the image limit should change, and attachments should keep using their setting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: replacing the per-type Discourse.SiteSettings max size lookup with a hardcoded 10 MB client limit, causing divergence from server/admin settings and affecting the 413 error message.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores failures and never verifies the final size before uploading

The loop calls OptimizedImage.downsize at most five times and then continues to Upload.create_for with whatever is in tempfile. Two problems. First, nothing re-checks tempfile.size against max_image_size_kb after the loop, so an image that is still over the limit is stored. Each pass scales both dimensions by 0.8 (pixel count by 0.64), so five passes leave about 11% of the original pixels, which is not enough for a large original. Second, downsize returns false when convert exits non-zero (convert_with does not log that case), and the return value is discarded. A failing conversion is retried five times on an unchanged file and the failure is invisible. On this path nothing enforces max_image_size_kb for uploaded images any more.

Up to five ImageMagick and ImageOptim passes per oversized upload, run inline on the synchronous API path

Each loop iteration runs a full convert pass, and convert_with also runs ImageOptim.new.optimize_image! on the output, so an oversized upload can cost five decode/encode cycles plus five optimizer runs. On the synchronous API path (`synchronous` param) this runs inline in the request and blocks the web worker for the duration. This code does not bound the input size: the client-side check is browser-only, the URL path cap is 10 MB, and the multipart path has no size check in this diff. A very large image makes every pass expensive.

Downsizing writes in place to the uploaded file, so a failed pass can corrupt the only copy

OptimizedImage.downsize is called with the same path as input and output, so ImageMagick overwrites the uploaded file in place. If a pass fails partway (disk full, process killed, ImageMagick error during write), the file is left truncated or corrupt. Because the return value is ignored (see the loop above), the damaged file is then passed to Upload.create_for. Writing to a separate temp file and replacing the original only on success would avoid this.

Oversized animated GIFs are flattened to their first frame when allow_animated_thumbnails is off

The loop reuses the thumbnail setting `allow_animated_thumbnails` for the user's original upload. When that setting is off, OptimizedImage.optimize uses downsize_instructions, which reads `#{from}[0]`, so an oversized animated GIF is replaced by a static first frame. The animation is lost permanently in the stored upload, and the user is not told. This may be intended, but it is not documented or surfaced anywhere in the PR.

No specs for the changed downsize/optimize signatures or the new upload downsizing path

The PR changes the signatures of optimize, resize and downsize, removes the public OptimizedImage.dimensions helper, and adds a loop in UploadsController#create_upload. No spec changes accompany any of this. A single spec calling downsize with width and height would have caught the duplicate-definition bug, and nothing covers the '80%' percentage path, the loop's termination, or the behaviour when convert fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no topic_users row

Line 105 does `TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])`, which returns nil when the logged-in user has no row for this topic (they never visited or read it, or the link was opened while logged in as an account with no relation to the topic). Line 107 then calls `tu.notification_level` and raises NoMethodError, producing a 500. Use `TopicUser.change` (which creates the row when missing) or handle the nil case explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: TopicUser.find_by can return nil when no row exists, and the subsequent method call on tu crashes. The candidate's NoMethodError wording matches the golden's nil pointer concern.

false_positives.candidate:
tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change and can be silently undone by auto-tracking

The notification level is written with a direct `tu.save!` instead of `TopicUser.change(...)`. `change` sets `notifications_reason_id` (user_changed) and `notifications_changed_at`; this path sets neither and publishes no MessageBus `notification_level_change`. Consequence: when `notifications_reason_id` is NULL (common for rows created by reading, via the INSERT in `update_last_read`), `TopicUser.update_last_read` sets the level back to tracking once enough reading time accumulates, and `TopicUser.auto_track` does the same on new posts. The user's unsubscribe is silently reverted. Fix by calling `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic.id, notification_level: ...)`.

Unsubscribe leaves watching/tracking users at 'regular', which still sends reply and mention emails

The toggle sets watching/tracking topics to `regular` and only sets `muted` when the level is already `regular` or lower. `regular` still generates reply, quote and mention notifications and emails, so a user who clicks the one-click unsubscribe link on a watched or tracked topic keeps receiving email for that topic. The new page text (`topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`: 'You will stop receiving notifications for ...') is therefore false for those users, and they need a second click. The action should mute the topic from any level, or the copy must change.

State-changing action exposed over GET and authenticated only by session cookie `unsubscribe` changes the user's notification level on a GET request (routes.rb lines 440-441). Rails CSRF protection does not cover GET, so any cross-site GET to `/t/:id/unsubscribe` (for example an `` or link) performs the change for a logged-in visitor, and link prefetchers that carry the session do the same. Use a POST from a confirmation page, or a signed per-user token like the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` flow.

Email unsubscribe link carries no recipient identity; it acts on whichever session is logged in

The per-topic unsubscribe link in the email contains only the topic path, with no token identifying the recipient. The action uses `current_user` only. Consequences: (a) a recipient who is not logged in is redirected to login by `ensure_logged_in`, and the unsubscribe intent is lost, which is the common case for email clicks; (b) if the browser is logged in as a different account, that account's topic setting is changed while the actual recipient stays subscribed. The existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` route avoids this with a signed key; the topic link should do the same.

unsubscribe_link now requires :unsubscribe_url; other callers with add_unsubscribe_link will raise

`server.en.yml` now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}` in `unsubscribe_link`. This line (and the same key in `body`, line 90) passes `template_args`, which only contains `unsubscribe_url` if the caller supplied it. Any caller that passes `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without `unsubscribe_url` (only `send_notification_email` is updated in this PR; plugins or other mailers may call it too) will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` while building the email. Either default the value in `MessageBuilder` or guard the interpolation.

No specs for the new unsubscribe action, Topic#unsubscribe_url, or the topic link in emails

The new `unsubscribe` action has no controller spec. Untested paths include: the nil TopicUser case, the level transitions (regular to muted, tracking to regular), the login requirement, the slug-mismatch 301 redirect, and the rendered page. `Topic#unsubscribe_url` is untested. The only spec change adds an `unsubscribe_url:` argument to an existing test that checks only that the List-Unsubscribe header is present; no test checks that the email body contains the topic-specific link.

Unrelated route reordering and removed constraints bundled into the feature

The diff reorders the `moderator-liked` and `summary` routes and removes `post_number: /\d+/` from both `summary` routes. None of this is needed for the unsubscribe feature and the PR does not explain it. Dropping constraints from existing routes can change which requests match, so it should be split out or justified.

Top-level topicUnsubscribe route paired with a nested-style template path

The route is declared at top level as `topicUnsubscribe`, but its template is `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, the name a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route would use. Ember resolves a route's template from its route name, so this template may not be picked up and the page could render without its content. Worth verifying in the browser, or setting `templateName` explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only; on Linux the env update silently fails while the script still reports success

GNU sed interprets the empty string after -i as the script and then treats the substitution expression as a filename, so the substitution never happens. The script has no set -e or exit check, so it prints 'Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL' regardless. Use a portable approach (e.g. a temp file and mv) and check the result.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and fails on GNU/Linux sed, with the substitution not applied. It adds detail about silent success, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-denied case throws a plain Error, which tRPC reports as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR

A Response does not carry the token fields as enumerable properties, so the stored key either becomes an empty or garbage object (losing accessToken and refreshToken) or the update fails. The catch at lines 203-205 only logs, so nothing surfaces. The HubspotToken annotation on line 177 hides the mismatch from the type checker.

Zoom refresh sends appSlug 'zoomvideo' but the Zoom app slug is 'zoom'

Zoom credentials are created with appId 'zoom' (zoomvideo/api/callback.ts line 73), and the webhook resolves app slugs the same way. Here refreshOAuthTokens is called with 'zoomvideo', the directory name rather than the app slug. A self-hoster's sync endpoint keyed on appSlug will not recognize it or will look up the wrong app. Use 'zoom'.

Salesforce CalendarService uses prisma without importing it

The new refresh code calls prisma.credential.update (line 96), but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript compile error, and at runtime constructing the client throws a ReferenceError, so every Salesforce calendar operation (contact search, event creation, availability) fails for all users. Add the import.

Salesforce refreshes its token on every client construction, bypassing the sync endpoint

getClient now posts to login.salesforce.com and writes the credential row on every CalendarService construction, even when the stored access token is still valid. Each calendar operation therefore costs an extra network round trip and a DB write, and concurrent operations each refresh and overwrite the same row. The refresh also goes directly to Salesforce with the Cal.com consumer secret and does not use refreshOAuthTokens, so with CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set Salesforce still refreshes on its own, contrary to the sync design. Refresh only when the token is expired and route it through refreshOAuthTokens.

Webhook secret compared with !== instead of a constant-time comparison

The shared webhook secret is checked with plain string inequality, which short-circuits at the first differing byte and leaks timing information. For an authentication check on a network endpoint, compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers (for example, hash both values first).

Concurrent deliveries can create duplicate credentials for the same user and app

The handler does findFirst (line 62) then create (line 83) with no transaction or lock. Two deliveries for the same user and app can both see no row and both create one, unless the schema has a unique constraint on (userId, appId), which this PR does not add. Later lookups that take the first matching credential may then pick a row that is not the one just synced.

Sync update leaves a credential flagged invalid even after fresh tokens arrive

Refresh failure paths set invalid: true on the credential (for example googlecalendar CalendarService lines 112-118 on invalid_grant, and Webex/Zoom invalidateCredential). The update branch here only writes key (lines 73-80), so after the self-hoster pushes fresh tokens the credential stays flagged invalid and remains unusable in code paths that check the flag. Clear invalid on update.

Documented sync response contract is narrower than what the callers read

The comment says the endpoint should return only the access token and expiry date, but callers read more. Google reads expiry_date. Hubspot reads expiresIn. Zoom, Webex and Office365 video read expires_in, and Office365 video stores the whole response as the credential key. Lark parses a {code, data} envelope and needs refresh_token and refresh_expires_in. Following the comment gives NaN expiry, or in Office365 video expiry_date = now (line 84), which forces a sync call on every request, and loses refresh tokens. The actual contract (field names, units, envelope) should be documented, for example next to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT in .env.example (line 240, currently undocumented). The PR description also says docs are required, but none are included.

No tests for the webhook, the sync refresh path, or the schema helper

The PR adds a webhook that writes credentials, a refresh indirection touching about twelve integrations, and a new schema helper, and the PR description says no tests were added. Several defects above (wrapper stored as the key, stripped fields, placeholder refresh token, wrong userId, missing prisma import) would be caught by unit tests of parseRefreshTokenResponse and refreshOAuthTokens with sync on and off, and by webhook tests for auth, validation and create/update.

This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. The `cancelled: true` UPDATE that now decides whether the reminder is sent may not complete before the handler returns, and on a serverless runtime the process can be frozen after the response. Errors are swallowed inside the helper's try/catch, so a failed write leaves the booking cancelled with no record that its reminder must be stopped, and nothing retries it. The helper's result should be awaited and failures surfaced or retried.

The candidate focuses on deleteScheduledEmailReminder and serverless freeze/error swallowing, but it points to the same underlying reliability issue and locations.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Immediate cancel path reuses the call that hits SendGrid's 100-pending-cancellation cap

The `immediateDelete` branch sends `status: "cancel"` to SendGrid's `/v3/user/scheduled_sends`. The PR description identifies this exact mechanism as the root cause: each cancelled send stays pending until its scheduled date, and once 100 are pending new cancels fail while the emails are still sent. This branch is used for rescheduling (handleNewBooking.ts line 968), workflow deletion (workflows.tsx line 214) and step deletion (workflows.tsx line 521), which can cancel many reminders at once. When the cap is hit, the error is swallowed by the catch at the bottom of the function, so the reminders are silently still sent. The branch also returns without touching the DB row, so the reminder keeps `scheduled: true` and a `referenceId` pointing at a cancelled batch until its scheduled date passes. The name `immediateDelete` is also misleading because the row is not deleted. These paths should use the same deferred `cancelled` flag and cron-based cancellation as the rest of the PR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments target the immediateDelete path in deleteScheduledEmailReminder: it performs a SendGrid cancel but returns without updating/deleting the WorkflowReminder row, leaving an orphaned scheduled record. The candidate adds the pending-cancellation cap context, but the core bug is the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Paid-booking cancellation returns before workflow reminders are cancelled

For a paid booking the handler takes the `bookingToDelete.paid` branch (starts at line 363), refunds, sets status REJECTED, and returns at this line. The workflow reminder cancellation block (lines 484-493) and the zapier `cancelScheduledJobs` call come after this return, so they never run for paid bookings. The booking is cancelled, but its scheduled BEFORE_EVENT email and SMS reminders are still sent, which is the exact bug this PR is meant to fix. The same gap exists at line 437 (`return null` when the payment service is not implemented), and any throw between the status update at line 255 and line 484 leaves reminders uncancelled. Reminder cancellation should happen before the paid branch, or be duplicated into it.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation batch and skips all deletes

The loop awaits `client.request` for every cancelled reminder inside a single try block. If any call throws (for example SendGrid rejects a batch that was already sent or already cancelled), the catch at lines 75-77 runs and the loop is abandoned, so the remaining reminders in the window are never cancelled. Also, `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` returns a lazy PrismaPromise that only executes when awaited in `Promise.all` at line 74. Because that await is never reached after an error, the deletes for reminders already cancelled earlier in the loop never run either. Those rows keep `cancelled: true`, and the next cron run (about 15 minutes later) hits the same failing reminder first. A single bad batch therefore blocks cancellation of every other reminder in its one-hour window, and emails for cancelled bookings still go out. Each cancel should be isolated (try/catch per reminder), and the delete should be awaited right after its own successful cancel.

SMS reminder row is only deleted if the Twilio cancel succeeds

The Prisma `workflowReminder.delete` runs after `twilio.cancelSMS` in the same try block. If Twilio throws (for example because the message is already sent or no longer cancellable), the delete is skipped and the error is only logged. Before this change the callers deleted the row regardless of the Twilio result, so this is a regression: the row keeps `scheduled: true` and its `referenceId`. The row deletion should not depend on the external cancel succeeding.

If `CRON_API_KEY` is not configured and the request has neither an `authorization` header nor an `apiKey` query parameter, `apiKey` is `undefined` and the check `process.env.CRON_API_KEY !== apiKey` evaluates to `undefined !== undefined`, which is false, so the request proceeds. This is pre-existing, but the endpoint now also cancels SendGrid sends and deletes reminder rows, so an unauthenticated caller on a misconfigured deployment can trigger those side effects. The handler should reject when the key is missing.

The condition changes from `(isPhoneNumberNeeded || isSenderIdNeeded)` to `isPhoneNumberNeeded` and the phone block is unwrapped. This changes rendering for SMS_ATTENDEE steps, which no longer get an empty padded container. Nothing in the PR description or title mentions this UI change, and it is unrelated to cancelling reminders. It should be split into its own PR or described explicitly.
