The PR changes cancellation semantics across handleCancelBooking, bookings.tsx, handleNewBooking and workflows.tsx, adds a `cancelled` column with a migration, and adds a cron branch that calls SendGrid and deletes rows. None of this is covered by a test in the diff. The previous fix shipped broken with the failure silently swallowed. At minimum, tests should cover: a cancelled reminder inside the one-hour window being cancelled and deleted; a SendGrid failure for one reminder not blocking the others; and a paid booking's reminders being cancelled.

Guests array has no size limit; any attendee can mass-mail arbitrary addresses

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no max length and no per-user rate limit. Each new guest receives a calendar invite and an email containing booking details, and the handler also sends an email to every existing attendee. Any authenticated user who is merely an attendee (the handler allows `isAttendee`) can send a single request with thousands of addresses to third parties through the platform's mail infrastructure, with no cap.

The attendees are written to the DB at lines 92-106. `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` at line 165 is not wrapped in try/catch, unlike the email call. If the calendar update throws, the request fails after the guests were saved, and no invites are sent. Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

When a team admin or an attendee (not the organizer) adds guests, the calendar event belongs to the organizer's connected calendar, so `updateCalendarAttendees` runs against the wrong account's credentials and either fails or does not update the organizer's event. The catch block logs the constant string 'Error sending AddGuestsEmails' and discards `err`, so the failure cause is unrecoverable from logs. It should use the project logger and include the error. Swallowing the error is intentional, but the diagnostic detail should not be lost.

This change is unrelated to backup codes and is not mentioned in the PR description, but it applies to every PasswordField in the app. tabIndex={-1} removes the visibility toggle from the Tab order, so keyboard-only users can no longer reveal a password they typed. The button has only an sr-only label, so it is effectively unreachable without a pointer. This is an accessibility regression. PasswordField renders type={isPasswordVisible ? 'text' : 'password'} and then spreads {...props} afterward. The type='password' passed here wins, so the input never switches to text. Clicking the eye toggle changes the icon and label but the value stays hidden. This was previously a plain TextField; the swap introduces a dead control on the enable-2FA password step. req.body.backupCode is taken from a JSON body without type checking. Any truthy non-string value (number, object, array) makes .replaceAll throw, which escapes the handler as an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of a JSON error. Check typeof req.body.backupCode === 'string' before normalizing it.

missing_backup_codes tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such action exists

The message says 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' No UI in this PR generates codes outside the initial setup, and the setup endpoint refuses to run once 2FA is enabled. Users who enabled 2FA before this change (backupCodes null) are shown this message on login and sent to a screen where they cannot act. Their only path is disabling 2FA with a TOTP code and re-enabling it. Reword the message or add a regenerate action.

Enable test asserts on a switch behind the open backup-codes dialog, with a known-vacuous assertion left in place

The PR adds a FIXME stating that this assertion 'passes even when switch is not checked'. The enable test also never closes the backup-codes dialog that now sits on top of the page, so the switch is checked behind the modal. The assertion is therefore weak and knowingly so. Close the dialog and assert data-state='checked' as the disable test does, rather than shipping a check the author has already identified as not validating anything.

No test covers logging in with a backup code, the core new behavior

The TODO defers backup-code login testing, but this is the main user-facing addition of the PR (the 'Lost access' flow). Nothing exercises the authorize() backup-code branch, the consumption of a code, rejection of reuse, or the new error messages. The disable-endpoint backup path is also untested. At minimum, add an e2e test that logs in with a code, confirms it is accepted once, and confirms reuse is rejected.

navigator.clipboard.writeText returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast fires unconditionally. On insecure origins or when permission is denied, the write fails (or navigator.clipboard is undefined and throws), yet the user is told 'Backup codes copied!'. Backup codes are stored with symmetricEncrypt, so anyone holding CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, or a DB dump together with that key, can recover every unused code and log in as the user. These codes are bearer secrets. Because they are random and high-entropy, a one-way hash (for example SHA-256 with a comparison on the submitted code) would suffice and remove this exposure. Severity is low because the same key already protects TOTP secrets.

false_positives.candidate:
Video references are saved without credentialId

The `credentialId` mapping in `create()` was changed to `isCalendarType ? result.credentialId : undefined`. Previously non-calendar (video) results kept `result.credentialId`. Now every video reference is stored with a null credentialId. handleCancelBooking.ts only deletes the video meeting when `bookingVideoReference.credentialId` is set (around line 491), so cancelled bookings leave the Zoom/Daily/etc. meeting behind. The seated-cancellation video update path has the same dependency. Restore `result.credentialId` for the non-calendar branch.

Destinations without credentialId lose their externalId and can create duplicate events

For destinations without a credentialId, `createEvent(c, event)` is called without the destination's externalId. The result therefore has `externalId` undefined, and the booking reference is stored with a null externalCalendarId. Google picks its calendar only by credentialId, so the event goes to 'primary' and later update/delete cannot find the right calendar. The previous code stored `evt.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. In addition, this loop runs once per destination against the same list of credentials of that type, so N such destinations and K credentials produce N×K events.

Per-destination calendar is only honored by the Google service; other calendar apps still use the organizer's calendar

CalendarManager calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`. The destination externalId is only attached to the returned result, so the calendar implementation never sees which calendar this credential should write to. Only the Google service resolves its calendar by credentialId. Lark (googlecalendar-style `destinationCalendar[0]` at larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 129), Office365 (office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts line 75) and CalDAV (lib/CalendarService.ts line 161) always use the first destination, which for a collective event is usually the organizer's calendar. A team member's Lark or O365 credential therefore targets the organizer's calendar ID with the member's token, which fails. The collective-event fix works only for Google.

CalDAV reports success when no event was written for a team member

The filter keeps only calendars whose externalId equals the first destination's externalId. For a team member's CalDAV account that URL does not exist, so the filtered list is empty. `responses` is then empty, `responses.some((r) => !r.ok)` is false, and the function returns a uid as if the event was created. CalendarManager records success=true, the member never gets the event, and no error is logged.

deleteEvent fallback never finds the destination calendar and defaults to primary

Same dead predicate as in updateEvent: `find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` runs only when externalCalendarId is falsy, so it always returns undefined. `calendarId` then becomes 'primary' (line 322), so cancelling a booking whose reference has no externalCalendarId deletes from the user's primary calendar, not the calendar the event was created on, and the event remains on the destination calendar.

Hangout patch still uses selectedCalendar, which can now be undefined

The insert now falls back with `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `events.patch` (line 168) still passes the raw `selectedCalendar`. That value is undefined when no destination matches the credentialId, so the patch is sent without a calendarId. The patch is fire-and-forget with no callback or catch, so the failure is unhandled and the hangout link description is silently not updated. Use the same fallback in the patch.

Team members' calendars are dropped when the organizer and event type have no destination calendar

`destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer has one (around line 1067). `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is then a no-op, so every collective member's calendar is discarded. This is the scenario the PR is meant to fix. The array may also start with a team member's calendar, which the calendar services then treat as the organizer's main calendar.

Recurring cancellation deletes only the first calendar reference of each instance

The PR changed the top-level logic to iterate over all calendar references, but this recurring-cancel path still uses `updBooking.references.find(...)`, so only the first calendar reference per instance is considered. For a collective recurring booking with a second calendar reference (for example the team member's), that event is never deleted. The calls go to every calendar credential with the first reference's uid, which fails silently for the other accounts.

Recurring deletions are repeated once per calendar reference

This block sits inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. Each iteration re-runs the same deletion of every updated booking across all calendar credentials. With two calendar references and a recurring series, each instance's event is deleted twice (or more), producing duplicate API calls and duplicate entries in `apiDeletes`. The deletion should run once, outside the loop.

loadUsers error handling turns client errors into 500s and leaks Prisma messages

The new try/catch wraps the whole user-loading path. The `dynamicUserList` validation at line 728 throws a plain Error, which is not an HttpError, so it is rethrown as HttpError 500 'Unable to load users', losing the message and the 4xx status. Conversely, Prisma known-request errors are rethrown as HttpError 400 with the raw Prisma message, which exposes internal details. The old code let these errors propagate unchanged.

Webhook payload destinationCalendar changes from object to array without a breaking-change note

The event object is sent as-is in BOOKING_CREATED/REQUESTED webhook payloads (`...evt` in sendPayload). `destinationCalendar` changes from a DestinationCalendar object (or null) to an array (or null here, [] in other paths). Existing webhook consumers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` will break. The e2e test was edited to expect `[]` for BOOKING_REJECTED while still expecting `null` for BOOKING_CREATED, so the payload is now inconsistent across events and the contract change is undocumented.

Organization relation dropped from dynamic-group user query without explanation

The `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` selection was removed from the dynamic-user query. The PR does not explain why or add a replacement. If any downstream code in this handler reads `users[i].organization` for dynamic group bookings, it now receives undefined. The removal should be justified or reverted.

Error logging removed from updateAllCalendarEvents catch block

The `console.error(message)` call was removed. The catch now returns fallback results with success=false and emits no log, so calendar update failures disappear silently. The `message` string is still built but never output.

No tests cover the new multi-destination create/update/cancel logic

The PR states no tests were added. The new multi-destination logic in createAllCalendarEvents and updateAllCalendarEvents, and the Google calendar-id selection, are where most of the defects above sit (null-calendar regressions, dead predicates, lost credentialIds). A unit test per destination shape (with and without credentialId, empty and multiple destinations) would catch these.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Import failure in getVideoAdapters escapes the Cal Video fallback in createMeeting

getVideoAdapters now awaits a dynamic import from appStore. Line 52 calls it outside the try block that starts at line 70, and the catch at line 86 is where createMeeting falls back to Cal Video. If the dynamic import rejects (module evaluation error, missing dependency, or a chunk load failure), createMeeting rejects immediately instead of falling back, so the whole booking or reschedule that uses the video location fails. updateMeeting has the same shape at line 111, where the await is also outside its .catch. Before this change, appStore lookups were synchronous and could not reject. Move the adapter resolution inside the try, or catch the import failure and return the fallback.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the dynamic import await sits outside the existing try/catch, so an import rejection bypasses the Cal Video fallback. The candidate is more specific but points to the same fix of catching the import failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch dead and leaves calendar cancellations unawaited

The callback passed to bookingRefsFiltered.forEach is now async and awaits getCalendar(). forEach ignores the promises its callback returns, so the try/catch at lines 124-139 can no longer catch anything. Before this change, a synchronous throw from getCalendar (for example a CalendarService constructor error) was caught and logged. Now every throw becomes a rejected promise nobody handles, so it surfaces as an unhandledRejection and the logger.error branch never runs. The function also returns true at line 151 before the calendar and video cancellations have run. The identical change in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts line 125 has the same problem. Use a for...of loop with await inside the try so failures are caught and ordering is preserved.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify unawaited async forEach callbacks causing unhandled rejections and ineffective try/catch, and recommend awaiting via for...of.

false_positives.candidate:
requestReschedule fires async callbacks through forEach with no awaiting or error handling

The forEach callback is now async and awaits getCalendar() before calendar.deleteEvent(). forEach does not await these promises, so the mutation finishes and responds while calendar and video cancellations may still be in flight. Any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Before this change, a synchronous throw from getCalendar would propagate out of the mutation and fail it visibly; now that error is silently swallowed as an unhandled rejection. Use for...of with await, or Promise.allSettled with explicit logging, so the outcome of the cancellations is observed.

Recurring-cancel calendar deletions are no longer awaited before the response

The outer .forEach(async (credential) => {...}) pushes deletion results into apiDeletes from inside an async callback that nothing awaits. apiDeletes is snapshotted by prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes) in the later Promise.all, so these pushes arrive too late to be awaited, and their errors are unhandled. This PR adds another await before deleteEvent is called, so the calendar deletions are now issued a microtask later, after the handler has already moved on toward the response. The same PR converts the non-recurring 'old behaviour' branch just below to a for...of loop with await (lines 477-484), so the recurring branch is inconsistent with the intended pattern. On serverless runtimes, work still pending after the response can be frozen and never complete. Convert this to for...of with await and push into apiDeletes before the Promise.all.

Eagerly created import() promises can produce unhandled rejections

Each entry in the appStore object is an import() promise created at module evaluation. Only the keys that a caller actually awaits get a rejection handler. If any app module throws while evaluating, its promise rejects and nothing handles it, which Node reports as an unhandledRejection (process termination under default settings on modern Node). With the previous static imports, the same failure surfaced deterministically at startup. Consider storing factories (() => import(...)) and awaiting only the requested app, or attaching a handler to each promise.

import() in an object literal still loads every app eagerly

The object literal calls import() for all 28 apps as soon as the module is evaluated, so every app module still loads at startup, just asynchronously. The PR does not make app loading lazy, and the extra awaits at every call site add complexity without a corresponding saving. If the goal is lazy loading, the entries need to be functions such as () => import('./vital') that are invoked only when needed.

Default export values changed from modules to Promises; unconverted callers fail silently

appStore's values changed from module namespaces to Promise<module>. Any call site that still indexes appStore synchronously, including code outside the 12 changed files, now receives a Promise. The guard pattern used throughout, `if (!(app && 'lib' in app && 'CalendarService' in app.lib))`, evaluates `'lib' in promise` as false and takes the 'not implemented' branch, returning null with only a warning. Calendar events, video meetings, or payments would then be skipped silently rather than erroring. TypeScript does not flag this because `in` accepts any object type. Every consumer of the default export needs to be checked for a missing await.

Commented-out example import points at a path that does not exist

The old file used `// import * as example from "./_example";`. The new comment refers to `import("./example")`, which drops the leading underscore and so points to the wrong module if someone uncomments it.

getCalendarCredentials returns an unawaited Promise in the calendar field

getCalendarCredentials stays synchronous, but getCalendar is now async, so each returned entry's `calendar` field is a Promise<Calendar | null> that is never awaited here. The exported return shape changed silently. Callers that read `.calendar` as a Calendar would fail type-checking, and any rejection (for example an import failure) is unhandled if the entry is never consumed. Making this function async and awaiting each calendar, or documenting the Promise field, would make the contract explicit.
